lessons.title: 3.1 What Is the Chart of Accounts?
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 3: The Chart of Accounts

LESSON NOTE: WHAT IS THE CHART OF ACCOUNTS?

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingWhat Is the Chart of Accounts?Beginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Define the chart of accounts
  • Explain why it is the backbone of every report
  • Read an existing chart of accounts critically

1. Introduction

If QuickBooks is a filing cabinet, the chart of accounts is the set of labelled drawers. Every transaction must go into one, and every report is simply a summary of those drawers.

2. Meaning

Chart of accounts: The complete list of accounts an organisation uses to classify its transactions.

Nothing is recorded 'in general'. A fuel purchase is not just money out; it is money out into the Motor Vehicle Expenses drawer. Change which drawer and you change the reports.

3. The five account types

TypeMeaningAppears onExamples
AssetWhat you ownBalance SheetBank, Accounts Receivable, Equipment
LiabilityWhat you oweBalance SheetAccounts Payable, Loans, Tax payable
EquityThe owner's stakeBalance SheetOwner's Equity, Retained Earnings
IncomeWhat you earnProfit and LossSales, Grant income
ExpenseWhat you spendProfit and LossRent, Salaries, Fuel
Note: Assets, liabilities and equity form the Balance Sheet. Income and expenses form the Profit and Loss. Choosing the wrong type puts an item on the wrong statement entirely.

4. Judging a chart of accounts

A good chart is short enough to use and detailed enough to answer management's questions. Ask: can the manager see the numbers they actually make decisions on? If a shop owner keeps asking 'how much do we spend on transport?', transport deserves its own account.

Example: A 200-account chart where 180 accounts are never used is worse than a 30-account chart matched to real decisions.

Summary

  • The chart of accounts is the list of categories every transaction is filed into.
  • Five types: asset, liability, equity, income, expense.
  • Assets, liabilities and equity make the Balance Sheet; income and expense make the Profit and Loss.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
AccountA named category that transactions are recorded into.
Account typeThe classification that decides which financial statement an account appears on.
Balance SheetThe statement of assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What is the chart of accounts?

  1. The complete list of accounts used to classify transactions
  2. A list of customers
  3. The bank statement
  4. A tax return
Show answer

Answer: A. It is the organisation's full set of categories for recording transactions.

Which account types appear on the Profit and Loss?

  1. Income and expense
  2. Asset and liability
  3. Equity only
  4. Asset and equity
Show answer

Answer: A. Income and expenses determine profit; the rest belong to the Balance Sheet.

What happens if you give an account the wrong type?

  1. It appears on the wrong financial statement
  2. Nothing changes
  3. The transaction is deleted
  4. Tax is recalculated
Show answer

Answer: A. Type controls which statement the account reports on, so an error misplaces it entirely.

What makes a chart of accounts 'good'?

  1. It is detailed enough to answer the questions managers actually ask, without unused clutter
  2. It has as many accounts as possible
  3. It has exactly five accounts
  4. It copies another company exactly
Show answer

Answer: A. Usefulness for decisions, not size, is the test.

Short answer

Name the five account types and the statement each belongs to.

Model answer

Asset, liability and equity — Balance Sheet. Income and expense — Profit and Loss.

Why is a very large chart of accounts often a problem?

Model answer

Unused accounts create clutter and inconsistent coding, making reports harder to read without adding any decision value.

Class Activity

  1. List ten transactions from an organisation you know and name the account each belongs in.
  2. Review a sample chart of accounts and mark three accounts you would delete and one you would add.

Assignment

Design a chart of accounts of 25–35 accounts for a small organisation of your choice. Group by type and justify five of your choices in terms of the decisions they support.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 3.2 Account Types in QuickBooks
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 3: The Chart of Accounts

LESSON NOTE: ACCOUNT TYPES IN QUICKBOOKS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingAccount Types in QuickBooksBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Distinguish account type from detail type
  • Choose the correct type for a new account
  • Explain the consequence of choosing wrongly

1. Introduction

QuickBooks asks for two things when you create an account: an account type and a detail type. New users confuse them constantly, and the consequences differ enormously.

2. Type versus detail type

Account typeDetail type
What it decidesWhich financial statement the account appears onA finer label used for suggested reports and tax mapping
How many optionsFive broad groups plus bank/credit card variantsMany, within the chosen type
Cost of an errorSerious — the item lands on the wrong statementMinor — reports still work
Note: Get the account type right; treat the detail type as a helpful label rather than something to agonise over.

3. The types you will actually use

  • Bank — current, savings, mobile money
  • Accounts Receivable — what customers owe
  • Other Current Asset — inventory, prepayments
  • Fixed Asset — vehicles, equipment
  • Accounts Payable — what you owe suppliers
  • Credit Card — card balances
  • Other Current Liability — tax payable, payroll liabilities
  • Long Term Liability — loans over a year
  • Equity — owner's capital, drawings, retained earnings
  • Income / Other Income
  • Cost of Goods Sold — direct cost of what you sell
  • Expense / Other Expense

4. Cost of Goods Sold vs Expense

This is the classification learners get wrong most often. Cost of Goods Sold is the direct cost of the item you sold; Expense is the cost of running the business regardless of sales.

Example: A bakery: flour and sugar are Cost of Goods Sold. Shop rent and the accountant's fee are Expenses. Getting this wrong makes gross profit meaningless.

Summary

  • Account type sets the financial statement; detail type is a finer label.
  • Type errors are serious; detail type errors are cosmetic.
  • Cost of Goods Sold is the direct cost of goods sold; Expense is the cost of operating.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Detail typeA sub-classification within an account type used for suggested reporting.
Cost of Goods SoldThe direct cost of the goods or services sold.
Fixed assetAn item owned and used for more than a year.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does the account TYPE decide?

  1. Which financial statement the account appears on
  2. The colour of the report
  3. The user who can see it
  4. The tax rate
Show answer

Answer: A. Type determines placement on the Balance Sheet or Profit and Loss.

A bakery buys flour to bake bread for sale. Which type is correct?

  1. Cost of Goods Sold
  2. Expense
  3. Fixed Asset
  4. Equity
Show answer

Answer: A. Flour is a direct input to the goods sold, so it is Cost of Goods Sold.

Which error is more serious?

  1. Choosing the wrong account type
  2. Choosing the wrong detail type
  3. Misspelling the account name
  4. Using lower case
Show answer

Answer: A. The wrong type places the account on the wrong statement; detail type is only a label.

A delivery van bought for use over five years is which type?

  1. Fixed Asset
  2. Cost of Goods Sold
  3. Expense
  4. Other Current Asset
Show answer

Answer: A. An item owned and used beyond a year is a fixed asset.

Short answer

Explain the difference between account type and detail type.

Model answer

Type decides the financial statement the account reports on; detail type is a finer descriptive label that affects suggested reports and tax mapping only.

Give two examples each of Cost of Goods Sold and Expense for a restaurant.

Model answer

COGS: food ingredients, drinks bought for resale. Expense: shop rent, staff salaries not tied to production, electricity.

Class Activity

  1. Classify fifteen items from a business into account types.
  2. Find three accounts in a sample chart that you think have the wrong type and explain why.

Assignment

Take twenty transactions from a trading business and assign each an account type and detail type. Highlight every item you judged Cost of Goods Sold and defend the decision.

lessons.title: 3.3 Creating a New Account
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 3: The Chart of Accounts

LESSON NOTE: CREATING A NEW ACCOUNT

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCreating a New AccountBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create a new account correctly
  • Decide when a new account is actually needed
  • Name accounts so others can use them

1. Introduction

Creating an account is easy; deciding whether it should exist is the skill. Every new account is a permanent question your bookkeeper must answer for every future transaction.

2. The steps

  1. Gear → Chart of accounts → New.
  2. Choose the account type (the important choice).
  3. Choose a detail type.
  4. Give it a clear name.
  5. Optionally make it a sub-account of a parent.
  6. Enter an opening balance only if it genuinely had one on the start date.
Note: Do not enter an opening balance for an account whose balance will build up from transactions you are about to record — that would double-count.

3. When to create a new account

Create one only if you can answer yes to at least one of these:

  • Does a manager regularly ask about this figure separately?
  • Does a funder, tax rule or regulator require it to be reported separately?
  • Is it large enough that burying it in another account would mislead?
Example: A church asked repeatedly 'how much goes on the generator?' — fuel was buried inside General Expenses. Creating 'Generator Fuel' answered a real, recurring question, so it earned its place.

4. Naming accounts well

Names are read by people who did not create them. Use plain words, be consistent, and avoid abbreviations only you understand.

Poor nameBetter nameWhy
MiscSundry Office CostsSays what actually goes in it
Exp 2Staff TrainingMeaningful to any reader
JD acctLoan – J. DoeIdentifies the relationship

Summary

  • Type is the important choice when creating an account; the name is the second.
  • Only create an account if a manager, funder or materiality genuinely demands the split.
  • Never enter an opening balance for a balance that transactions will build up anyway.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Sub-accountAn account nested under a parent for grouping.
Opening balanceThe balance an account already held on the file's start date.
MaterialityWhether an amount is large enough to affect a reader's decision.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

When should you NOT enter an opening balance for a new account?

  1. When the balance will build up from transactions you are about to record
  2. When the account is an expense
  3. When the account has a parent
  4. Whenever the amount is large
Show answer

Answer: A. Entering both an opening balance and the transactions would double-count.

What is the strongest reason to create a new account?

  1. A manager or funder regularly needs that figure reported separately
  2. It makes the list longer
  3. Another company has one
  4. It looks more professional
Show answer

Answer: A. Accounts exist to answer real recurring questions.

Which is the best account name?

  1. Staff Training
  2. Exp 2
  3. Misc
  4. Acct 14
Show answer

Answer: A. A plain, descriptive name can be used correctly by anyone.

What is the most important choice when creating an account?

  1. The account type
  2. The colour
  3. The detail type
  4. The opening balance
Show answer

Answer: A. Type determines which financial statement the account appears on.

Short answer

Give the three tests for whether a new account is justified.

Model answer

A manager asks about it regularly; a funder or regulator requires it separately; or it is large enough that hiding it would mislead.

Why do account names matter to people other than the person who created them?

Model answer

Because bookkeepers, managers and auditors must code and read transactions consistently, and an unclear name causes inconsistent coding.

Class Activity

  1. Create five accounts in a sample company, one of each type, and note the detail type you chose.
  2. Rewrite five poorly named accounts into clear names.

Assignment

Propose five new accounts for an organisation you know. For each, state the type, the name, and which of the three justification tests it passes.

lessons.title: 3.4 Editing and Merging Accounts
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 3: The Chart of Accounts

LESSON NOTE: EDITING AND MERGING ACCOUNTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingEditing and Merging AccountsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Edit an account safely
  • Merge duplicate accounts
  • Know what can and cannot be undone

1. Introduction

Real charts of accounts get messy: the same cost ends up in 'Fuel', 'Petrol' and 'Motor Fuel'. Merging cleans this up — but it is permanent, so it deserves care.

2. Editing an account

Gear → Chart of accounts → find the account → Edit. You may safely change the name and detail type at any time. Changing the account type of an account that already has transactions moves all of that history to another statement, so treat it as a serious act, not a tidy-up.

Note: Renaming is cosmetic and safe. Retyping is structural and restates reports.

3. Merging duplicates

To merge, you rename one account to exactly match the other; QuickBooks then offers to merge them.

  1. Decide which name is the survivor.
  2. Edit the duplicate and give it the survivor's exact name (and same type and parent).
  3. Confirm the merge prompt.
RuleDetail
Same type requiredYou cannot merge an expense into an income account
Same parent levelBoth must be sub-accounts of the same parent, or both top level
PermanentMerging cannot be undone; history moves to the survivor
History movesAll past transactions re-point to the surviving account

4. Deciding what survives

Example: 'Fuel', 'Petrol' and 'Motor Fuel' all hold vehicle running costs. Choose 'Motor Fuel' as the survivor because it is unambiguous, then rename the other two to 'Motor Fuel' one at a time and confirm each merge. Reports for past periods will now show one combined figure.

5. What to do instead of deleting

QuickBooks does not truly delete an account that has history; it makes it inactive. Inactive accounts disappear from lists but their past transactions remain in reports, which is exactly what you want for audit purposes.

Summary

  • Renaming is safe; changing an account's type restates reports.
  • Merging is done by renaming one account to match another exactly, and it is permanent.
  • Accounts with history are made inactive rather than deleted, preserving the audit trail.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
MergeCombining two accounts so all history sits under one.
Inactive accountAn account hidden from lists but retained in historical reports.
Audit trailThe preserved record of what was entered and changed.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

How do you merge two accounts in QuickBooks?

  1. Rename one to exactly match the other and confirm the merge
  2. Click a Merge button in Reports
  3. Delete one of them
  4. Export and re-import
Show answer

Answer: A. Matching the name exactly triggers the merge prompt.

Which change restates past reports?

  1. Changing an account's type when it already has transactions
  2. Renaming an account
  3. Making an account inactive
  4. Adding a description
Show answer

Answer: A. Type controls which statement history appears on, so retyping moves that history.

What happens to an account with history when you 'delete' it?

  1. It becomes inactive and its past transactions remain in reports
  2. All its transactions are erased
  3. It is permanently removed
  4. It becomes an income account
Show answer

Answer: A. QuickBooks preserves history by making the account inactive.

Can an expense account be merged into an income account?

  1. No, merging requires the same account type
  2. Yes, always
  3. Only in the Advanced plan
  4. Only at year end
Show answer

Answer: A. Both accounts must share the same type and level to merge.

Short answer

State two rules that must be satisfied before two accounts can merge.

Model answer

They must be the same account type, and both must sit at the same level (both top level or both sub-accounts of the same parent).

Why is making an account inactive better than deleting it?

Model answer

Because past transactions stay in historical reports, preserving the audit trail while removing clutter from lists.

Class Activity

  1. Find three duplicate-looking accounts in a sample chart and write a merge plan naming the survivor.
  2. Explain in two sentences the risk of changing an account type after a year of transactions.

Assignment

Audit a chart of accounts of at least 25 accounts. Identify duplicates, propose merges with a named survivor for each, and list any accounts you would make inactive and why.

lessons.title: 3.5 Sub-Accounts and Organization
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 3: The Chart of Accounts

LESSON NOTE: SUB-ACCOUNTS AND ORGANIZATION

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSub-Accounts and OrganizationBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create sub-accounts under a parent
  • Use sub-accounts to group without clutter
  • Avoid nesting too deeply

1. Introduction

Sub-accounts let you keep detail for the bookkeeper while showing a manager a clean summary. They are the answer to 'I need the detail, but the report is unreadable'.

2. How they work

A parent account holds one or more sub-accounts. Transactions are posted to the sub-accounts, and reports can show either the detail or a collapsed total.

Example: Parent: Motor Vehicle Costs. Sub-accounts: Fuel, Repairs, Insurance, Licensing. The bookkeeper codes precisely; the board sees one Motor Vehicle Costs line when the report is collapsed.

3. Rules that keep them useful

RuleReason
Post to sub-accounts, not the parentMixing both makes the parent total confusing
Keep to one or two levelsDeep nesting is unreadable and hard to maintain
Sub-accounts share the parent's typeQuickBooks enforces this
Use them for grouping, not for customersCustomer detail belongs in customer records, not accounts
Note: A frequent mistake is creating a sub-account per customer or per project. Use customers, classes or projects for that — otherwise the chart of accounts grows without limit.

4. Collapsing reports

On most reports there is a Collapse control. Collapsed shows parent totals only; expanded shows every sub-account. This single feature is why sub-accounts are worth the effort — one chart serves both the bookkeeper and the board.

Summary

  • Sub-accounts group detail under a parent so reports can be collapsed or expanded.
  • Post to sub-accounts, never to the parent, and keep nesting shallow.
  • Never create a sub-account per customer or project; use customers, classes or projects instead.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Parent accountAn account that groups sub-accounts beneath it.
CollapseA report control that hides sub-account detail and shows parent totals.
NestingPlacing accounts within accounts.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why should you post transactions to sub-accounts rather than the parent?

  1. Mixing postings between parent and sub-accounts makes the totals confusing
  2. The parent cannot accept transactions
  3. Sub-accounts are cheaper
  4. Reports would not run
Show answer

Answer: A. Consistently posting to sub-accounts keeps the parent a clean total.

What is the benefit of collapsing a report?

  1. Managers see summary totals while the detail remains available
  2. It deletes sub-accounts
  3. It changes account types
  4. It hides income
Show answer

Answer: A. Collapse gives a readable summary without losing the underlying detail.

Why is a sub-account per customer a bad idea?

  1. The chart of accounts grows without limit; customer detail belongs in customer records
  2. Customers cannot be tracked at all
  3. QuickBooks forbids it
  4. It costs extra
Show answer

Answer: A. Customer, class and project features exist precisely for that kind of tracking.

How deep should sub-account nesting normally go?

  1. One or two levels
  2. At least five levels
  3. As deep as possible
  4. Nesting is not allowed
Show answer

Answer: A. Shallow nesting stays readable and maintainable.

Short answer

Give an example of a parent account with four sensible sub-accounts.

Model answer

Motor Vehicle Costs, with sub-accounts Fuel, Repairs, Insurance and Licensing.

How do sub-accounts serve both a bookkeeper and a board?

Model answer

The bookkeeper codes to detailed sub-accounts, while the board reads a collapsed report showing only parent totals.

Class Activity

  1. Design a parent account with sub-accounts for an area of spending you know well.
  2. Take a flat list of fifteen expense accounts and reorganise it into parents and sub-accounts.

Assignment

Restructure a flat chart of accounts into a grouped structure using parents and sub-accounts. Show the before and after, and explain how the collapsed report would read.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 3.6 Opening Balances
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 3: The Chart of Accounts

LESSON NOTE: OPENING BALANCES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingOpening BalancesBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Explain what an opening balance represents
  • Enter opening balances so the file balances
  • Diagnose an out-of-balance opening position

1. Introduction

An opening balance is the organisation's true financial position on the day the QuickBooks file starts. Get these wrong and every report afterwards is built on sand.

2. Meaning

Opening balance: The balance an account already held on the file's start date, carried over from the previous records.

If the business started trading long before QuickBooks did, it already owns things, owes things and has accumulated profit. Those balances must be carried in — they are not transactions you record again.

3. What needs an opening balance

AccountWhere the figure comes from
BankThe bank statement balance on the start date
Accounts ReceivableUnpaid customer invoices at the start date, entered individually
Accounts PayableUnpaid supplier bills at the start date, entered individually
InventoryValue of stock counted at the start date
Fixed assetsCost less accumulated depreciation
LoansAmount still owed
EquityThe balancing figure — Opening Balance Equity

4. Receivables and payables are special

Do not enter a single lump sum for Accounts Receivable. Enter each unpaid invoice as its own invoice dated before the start date. Otherwise you know the total owed but not who owes it, and you can never apply a customer's payment properly.

Note: Same rule for Accounts Payable: enter each unpaid bill individually.

5. Opening Balance Equity

QuickBooks posts the other side of opening balances to a holding account called Opening Balance Equity. When setup is complete this account should be cleared to Retained Earnings or Owner's Equity, so it ends at zero.

Example: Assets 500,000; liabilities 180,000. Opening Balance Equity holds 320,000, which is then reclassified to Owner's Equity. If Opening Balance Equity is still sitting there months later, setup was never finished.

Summary

  • Opening balances carry the true position into the file on the start date.
  • Receivables and payables must be entered invoice by invoice, not as a lump sum.
  • Opening Balance Equity is a temporary holding account that should end at zero.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Opening Balance EquityA temporary holding account for the other side of opening balances.
Accumulated depreciationTotal depreciation charged on an asset to date.
Balancing figureThe amount that makes total debits equal total credits.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why must unpaid customer invoices be entered individually?

  1. So you know who owes what and can apply their payments correctly
  2. Because QuickBooks forbids totals
  3. To increase sales income
  4. To calculate tax
Show answer

Answer: A. A lump sum tells you the total but leaves you unable to match customer payments.

What should the Opening Balance Equity account show once setup is complete?

  1. Zero, after being reclassified to equity
  2. The bank balance
  3. Total sales
  4. Total expenses
Show answer

Answer: A. It is a temporary holding account and should be cleared.

Where does the opening bank balance come from?

  1. The bank statement balance on the start date
  2. An estimate
  3. Last year's profit
  4. The customer list
Show answer

Answer: A. The statement balance on the start date is the verifiable figure.

An opening balance is best described as:

  1. The position carried in from previous records, not a new transaction
  2. A sale made on day one
  3. An expense
  4. A budget
Show answer

Answer: A. It represents history brought forward, not new activity.

Short answer

List four accounts that typically need an opening balance.

Model answer

Bank, Accounts Receivable, Accounts Payable, inventory, fixed assets and loans.

What does a non-zero Opening Balance Equity months after setup tell you?

Model answer

That the setup was never completed — the holding account has not been reclassified into proper equity.

Class Activity

  1. Given assets of 800,000 and liabilities of 250,000, calculate the opening equity figure.
  2. List the documents you would gather before entering opening balances for a real organisation.

Assignment

Prepare a full set of opening balances for a small organisation from a given trial balance. Show that total debits equal total credits and explain how you would clear Opening Balance Equity.

lessons.title: 3.7 Chart of Accounts Best Practices
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 3: The Chart of Accounts

LESSON NOTE: CHART OF ACCOUNTS BEST PRACTICES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingChart of Accounts Best PracticesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Apply professional conventions to a chart of accounts
  • Keep a chart stable over time
  • Review a chart annually

1. Introduction

A chart of accounts is a long-lived structure. Changing it constantly destroys comparability between years; never changing it leaves it useless. Good practice sits between the two.

2. The practices that matter

PracticeWhy
Keep it as small as it can usefully beFewer accounts means more consistent coding
Name in plain languageAnyone can code correctly without asking
Group with sub-accountsDetail for the bookkeeper, summary for the board
Never post to Accounts Receivable/Payable directlyQuickBooks maintains these through invoices and bills
Use one 'Ask My Accountant' accountA parking place for genuinely unclear items, reviewed monthly
Do not restructure mid-yearComparability between periods is destroyed
Review once a yearMerge dead accounts, add ones now needed

3. The comparability rule

If you split 'Travel' into 'Local Travel' and 'International Travel' in July, then a full-year report shows one combined figure for the first half and two split figures for the second. Make structural changes at the start of a financial year wherever possible.

Example: Plan structural changes in the last month of the year and switch them on from day one of the new year.

4. The annual review

  1. Run a Profit and Loss and Balance Sheet for the full year, expanded.
  2. Highlight every account with no activity — candidates to make inactive.
  3. Highlight every account with a very large 'General' or 'Miscellaneous' balance — that is a sign detail is missing.
  4. Ask management which figures they wanted last year and could not get — those become new accounts.
  5. Apply the changes from the first day of the new year.

Summary

  • Keep the chart small, plainly named and grouped, and review it once a year.
  • Never post directly to Accounts Receivable or Accounts Payable.
  • Make structural changes at a year boundary to protect comparability.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
ComparabilityThe ability to compare figures fairly across periods.
Ask My AccountantA holding account for unclear items pending review.
Annual reviewA yearly tidy-up of the chart of accounts.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why should structural changes be made at the start of a financial year?

  1. Splitting accounts mid-year destroys comparability within that year
  2. QuickBooks blocks changes mid-year
  3. It is cheaper
  4. Tax requires it
Show answer

Answer: A. A mid-year split makes the first and second halves of the year non-comparable.

Why should you never post directly to Accounts Receivable?

  1. QuickBooks maintains it automatically through invoices and payments
  2. It is an income account
  3. It cannot hold a balance
  4. It is inactive by default
Show answer

Answer: A. Direct postings break the link between the control account and customer records.

A large 'Miscellaneous' balance is a sign of what?

  1. Missing detail — real categories are being hidden
  2. Excellent bookkeeping
  3. Too many accounts
  4. A software fault
Show answer

Answer: A. A swollen catch-all account means useful detail is not being captured.

What is the purpose of an 'Ask My Accountant' account?

  1. A monitored parking place for genuinely unclear items
  2. To hide errors permanently
  3. To record all expenses
  4. To store customer balances
Show answer

Answer: A. It parks uncertain items visibly so they are resolved rather than mis-coded.

Short answer

Give three signs a chart of accounts needs review.

Model answer

Many accounts with no activity; a large miscellaneous balance; managers repeatedly asking for figures the chart cannot produce.

Why is a smaller chart often coded more consistently?

Model answer

Because there are fewer plausible places to put each transaction, so different people make the same choice.

Class Activity

  1. Run the five-step annual review against a sample chart and write your recommendations.
  2. List three accounts you would add for an organisation you know, based on questions its managers ask.

Assignment

Carry out a full annual review of a chart of accounts. Produce a written report listing accounts to merge, make inactive, rename or add, with the effective date you would apply the changes and why.

lessons.title: 4.1 Adding Customers
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 4: Customers, Sales and Invoicing

LESSON NOTE: ADDING CUSTOMERS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingAdding CustomersBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create a customer record with the fields that matter
  • Explain why customer records beat typing names
  • Set customer defaults that speed up invoicing

1. Introduction

A customer record is created once and reused forever. Typing a name freehand onto an invoice instead creates a stranger QuickBooks cannot track, report on, or chase.

2. The fields that matter

FieldWhy it matters
Display nameThe unique identifier; must be distinct
Company / individualControls how the name prints
EmailEnables sending invoices and reminders
Billing addressPrints on the invoice; may drive tax
Payment termsSets the due date automatically
Tax statusWhether this customer is charged sales tax
Opening balanceOnly if they owed you on the file start date

3. Why the record matters

With a real customer record QuickBooks can produce a statement, age the debt, apply a payment, and show lifetime sales. With a typed name it can do none of these.

Example: Invoice 'J. Doe' freehand three times and you have three unrelated invoices. Create the customer 'John Doe' once and you have one account with a running balance you can chase.

4. Naming consistently

Agree one convention and stick to it — usually the trading name for businesses and Surname, First name for individuals. Inconsistent naming creates duplicates, and duplicates split a customer's balance across two records.

Summary

  • Customer records enable statements, ageing, payment matching and sales history.
  • Display name must be unique; agree a naming convention to avoid duplicates.
  • Default terms and tax status on the record speed up and standardise invoicing.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Display nameThe unique name identifying a customer in QuickBooks.
Payment termsThe agreed number of days before an invoice is due.
AgeingGrouping unpaid invoices by how overdue they are.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why is typing a customer name freehand on an invoice a problem?

  1. QuickBooks cannot track a balance, age the debt or apply payments to them
  2. It looks unprofessional only
  3. It costs more
  4. Invoices cannot be printed
Show answer

Answer: A. Without a customer record there is no account to track, chase or report on.

What does setting payment terms on a customer record do?

  1. Sets the invoice due date automatically
  2. Changes the price
  3. Applies a discount
  4. Adds sales tax
Show answer

Answer: A. Terms drive the due date, which drives overdue reporting.

Why must the display name be unique?

  1. It is the identifier QuickBooks uses; duplicates split one customer's balance in two
  2. For legal reasons
  3. To calculate tax
  4. To allow printing
Show answer

Answer: A. Duplicate records fragment history and balances.

Which field decides whether sales tax is charged to a customer?

  1. Tax status
  2. Display name
  3. Billing address only
  4. Opening balance
Show answer

Answer: A. The customer's tax status controls taxability, alongside the item's own setting.

Short answer

Name four fields on a customer record and what each controls.

Model answer

Display name — unique identity; email — sending invoices; payment terms — due date; tax status — whether tax is charged.

How do duplicate customer records cause harm?

Model answer

A customer's invoices and payments split across two records, so neither shows the true balance and chasing becomes unreliable.

Class Activity

  1. Create five customer records in a sample company with full details.
  2. Write down the naming convention you would enforce and apply it to ten mixed business and individual names.

Assignment

Build a customer list of at least twelve records for an organisation, applying one naming convention, and state the default terms and tax status for each.

lessons.title: 4.2 Sub-Customers and Projects
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 4: Customers, Sales and Invoicing

LESSON NOTE: SUB-CUSTOMERS AND PROJECTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSub-Customers and ProjectsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Distinguish sub-customers from projects
  • Track income and cost for a job or funder
  • Choose the right tool for the reporting you need

1. Introduction

Sometimes one customer has several distinct jobs, or one funder finances several programmes. Sub-customers and Projects both solve this, in different ways.

2. The two tools compared

Sub-customerProject
What it isA customer nested under a parent customerA dedicated job record with its own profitability view
Best forBranches or departments of one clientA specific job with income and costs to compare
ReportingRolls up to the parent customerHas a built-in profitability report
AvailabilityAll plansPlus and above

3. Which to use

Ask what question you need answered. 'How much does this client owe us in total across their branches?' is a sub-customer question. 'Did we make money on this job?' is a Project question.

Example: A construction firm building three houses for one developer should use Projects: each house has its own income and costs, and the firm needs to know which was profitable.

4. Practical warning

Note: Do not use sub-customers as a substitute for classes when tracking funders across many customers. Sub-customers sit under one parent; classes cut across the whole file.

Summary

  • Sub-customers nest under a parent and roll up to their balance; Projects track profitability of a job.
  • Use sub-customers for branches, Projects for jobs with income and cost.
  • Projects require Plus or above.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Sub-customerA customer record nested beneath a parent customer.
ProjectA job record tracking income, cost and profitability.
Roll upTotalling child balances into the parent.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which tool answers 'did we make money on this job?'

  1. A Project
  2. A sub-customer
  3. A class only
  4. The dashboard
Show answer

Answer: A. Projects carry a built-in income-versus-cost profitability view.

Which tool suits tracking three branches of one client?

  1. Sub-customers
  2. Projects
  3. Products
  4. Bank rules
Show answer

Answer: A. Sub-customers nest under the parent and roll up into one balance.

Projects are available on which plans?

  1. Plus and above
  2. All plans
  3. Simple Start only
  4. Desktop only
Show answer

Answer: A. Project tracking is a Plus-tier feature.

Why are sub-customers a poor substitute for classes?

  1. Sub-customers sit under one parent, while classes cut across the whole file
  2. They cost more
  3. They cannot be reported on
  4. They delete history
Show answer

Answer: A. Cross-cutting reporting across many customers needs classes, not nesting.

Short answer

State one question best answered by a Project and one by a sub-customer.

Model answer

Project: was this job profitable? Sub-customer: what does this client owe across all its branches?

Why does a construction firm prefer Projects?

Model answer

Each build has its own income and costs, and the firm needs to compare them per job to see which was profitable.

Class Activity

  1. Set up one parent customer with two sub-customers in a sample file.
  2. Decide, for three scenarios you invent, whether a sub-customer or a Project is right.

Assignment

Design the customer structure for an organisation with at least two clients that have multiple jobs or branches. Justify each use of a sub-customer or a Project.

lessons.title: 4.3 Creating an Invoice
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 4: Customers, Sales and Invoicing

LESSON NOTE: CREATING AN INVOICE

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCreating an InvoiceBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create and send an invoice
  • Explain each field on the invoice form
  • State the accounting effect of an invoice

1. Introduction

The invoice is the single most important sales document. It tells the customer what they owe, and it tells QuickBooks to record income and a receivable.

2. The form field by field

FieldPurpose
CustomerWho owes the money
Invoice dateWhen the sale is recognised
Due dateDriven by terms; determines overdue status
Product/serviceWhat was sold; drives the income account used
Quantity and rateThe maths of the line
TaxApplied if both customer and item are taxable
MessageWhat the customer reads
AttachmentSupporting document such as a delivery note

3. The accounting effect

Saving an invoice posts: Debit Accounts Receivable, Credit Income (and Credit Sales Tax Payable if tax applies). No cash moves. The bank is untouched until the customer pays.

Example: Invoice for 3 chairs at $50 = $150. Debit Accounts Receivable $150, Credit Sales $150. The bank balance does not change.

4. Sending it

Save and send emails a PDF with a payment link if online payments are enabled. Save and close records it without sending — use this when the customer will collect a printed copy. Either way the accounting is identical.

Summary

  • An invoice debits Accounts Receivable and credits income; no cash moves until payment.
  • The product/service chosen decides which income account is credited.
  • Sending is a communication choice; the accounting effect is the same either way.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
InvoiceA request for payment that records income and a receivable.
Due dateThe date payment becomes overdue.
Product/service itemA saved item that determines the income account and default price.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does saving an invoice post?

  1. Debit Accounts Receivable, credit income
  2. Debit Bank, credit income
  3. Debit income, credit Bank
  4. Debit expenses, credit Bank
Show answer

Answer: A. An invoice creates a receivable and records the income; cash is untouched.

Which field determines the income account credited?

  1. The product/service item
  2. The invoice date
  3. The customer message
  4. The attachment
Show answer

Answer: A. Each item is mapped to an income account, which is what gets credited.

Does emailing rather than printing an invoice change the accounting?

  1. No, the accounting effect is identical
  2. Yes, emailing records cash
  3. Yes, printing doubles the income
  4. Only if tax applies
Show answer

Answer: A. Delivery method is communication; the posted entry is the same.

A $150 invoice is raised. What happens to the bank balance?

  1. Nothing until the customer pays
  2. It rises by $150
  3. It falls by $150
  4. It rises by the tax only
Show answer

Answer: A. Cash moves only when payment is received.

Short answer

Write the journal entry for a $400 invoice with no tax.

Model answer

Debit Accounts Receivable $400; Credit Sales income $400.

Why does the product/service item matter more than the description?

Model answer

Because the item is mapped to an income account, so it decides where the revenue is reported; the description is only text.

Class Activity

  1. Create three invoices in a sample company and view each Transaction journal.
  2. Explain to a shopkeeper why raising invoices has not increased their cash.

Assignment

Raise five invoices for a practice organisation with varied items, quantities and terms. For each, write the journal entry QuickBooks posted and the due date it calculated.

lessons.title: 4.4 Customizing Invoice Templates
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 4: Customers, Sales and Invoicing

LESSON NOTE: CUSTOMIZING INVOICE TEMPLATES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCustomizing Invoice TemplatesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Customise the layout and content of an invoice
  • Add a logo and payment instructions
  • Decide which optional fields to show

1. Introduction

Your invoice is often the only document a customer keeps. A clear invoice gets paid faster; a confusing one sits on a desk.

2. What can be changed

  • Logo, colours and font
  • Which columns appear (SKU, quantity, rate, tax)
  • Header and footer text, including bank details
  • Whether the due date and terms are displayed
  • Custom fields such as purchase-order number

3. What makes an invoice get paid

ElementWhy it speeds payment
Clear total, prominently placedThe reader finds the amount instantly
Explicit due date'Net 30' is vague; a date is not
Bank details or payment linkRemoves the excuse of not knowing how to pay
Your contact detailsQueries reach you instead of stalling
The customer's PO numberLets their finance team match and approve it
Note: Most late payments in small organisations are caused by unclear invoices, not unwilling customers.

4. How to customise

Gear → Custom form styles → Edit or New style. Work through Design (logo, colour, font), Content (fields and columns) and Emails (the covering message). Always use Preview before saving.

Summary

  • Customisation controls layout, visible fields and footer text such as bank details.
  • A prominent total, an explicit due date and payment instructions speed up payment.
  • Custom form styles are found under the Gear icon; always preview before saving.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Custom form styleA saved invoice design and content configuration.
Custom fieldAn extra field you define, such as a purchase-order number.
FooterThe bottom area of the invoice, often holding payment details.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What is the most common cause of late payment in small organisations?

  1. Unclear invoices rather than unwilling customers
  2. Bank failures
  3. Software errors
  4. High prices
Show answer

Answer: A. Ambiguous invoices stall in approval queues.

Why show an explicit due date rather than just 'Net 30'?

  1. A date is unambiguous, whereas terms must be interpreted
  2. It is legally required
  3. It reduces tax
  4. It shortens the invoice
Show answer

Answer: A. An actual date removes any calculation or doubt for the reader.

Where do you customise invoice layout?

  1. Gear → Custom form styles
  2. + New → Invoice
  3. Banking → Rules
  4. Reports
Show answer

Answer: A. Custom form styles under the Gear icon control design and content.

Why include the customer's purchase-order number?

  1. It lets their finance team match and approve the invoice
  2. It is required by QuickBooks
  3. It calculates tax
  4. It sets the due date
Show answer

Answer: A. Matching to a PO is often required before a customer will pay.

Short answer

List four things you would put on an invoice to get paid faster.

Model answer

A prominent total, an explicit due date, bank details or a payment link, and your contact details.

What is a custom field and give an example.

Model answer

An extra field you define yourself, such as the customer's purchase-order number or a job reference.

Class Activity

  1. Customise an invoice in a sample company: add a logo, bank details and a due date.
  2. Review a real invoice you have received and list three improvements.

Assignment

Design a complete invoice template for an organisation. Explain each element you included and how it helps the invoice get paid.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 4.5 Recurring Invoices
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 4: Customers, Sales and Invoicing

LESSON NOTE: RECURRING INVOICES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingRecurring InvoicesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Set up a recurring transaction
  • Choose between scheduled, reminder and unscheduled types
  • Identify which billing suits recurring invoices

1. Introduction

If you bill the same customer the same amount every month — rent, retainers, subscriptions, school fees — a recurring template removes the work and the risk of forgetting.

2. The three types

TypeBehaviourUse when
ScheduledCreated and optionally sent automaticallyThe amount and date never vary
ReminderQuickBooks prompts you to review, then you create itThe amount usually but not always the same
UnscheduledA saved template you create on demandA complex invoice you reuse occasionally

3. Setting one up

  1. Create the invoice as normal, or Gear → Recurring transactions → New.
  2. Choose Invoice and the type.
  3. Set the interval, start date and, if needed, an end date.
  4. Save the template.
Example: A landlord billing twelve tenants monthly sets twelve scheduled recurring invoices dated the 1st. On the 1st QuickBooks raises and emails all twelve automatically.

4. The risk to manage

Note: Scheduled invoices keep going after a customer leaves. Review the recurring list every quarter and end templates that should have stopped, or you will be billing — and reporting income from — customers who are gone.

Summary

  • Recurring transactions can be scheduled, reminder-based or unscheduled templates.
  • Scheduled suits fixed amounts and dates; reminder suits amounts that sometimes vary.
  • Review the recurring list regularly so templates stop when customers leave.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Recurring transactionA saved template that repeats on a defined schedule.
IntervalHow often the transaction repeats.
End dateThe date after which a recurring template stops.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which recurring type suits a fixed monthly rent invoice?

  1. Scheduled
  2. Reminder
  3. Unscheduled
  4. None
Show answer

Answer: A. Fixed amount and date is exactly the scheduled case.

Which type prompts you to review before creating?

  1. Reminder
  2. Scheduled
  3. Unscheduled
  4. Automatic
Show answer

Answer: A. Reminder templates prompt so you can adjust a varying amount.

What is the main risk of scheduled recurring invoices?

  1. They keep billing customers who have left, overstating income
  2. They cannot be edited
  3. They delete customers
  4. They double the tax
Show answer

Answer: A. Templates run until stopped, so a departed customer keeps being invoiced.

Where do you manage recurring templates?

  1. Gear → Recurring transactions
  2. Banking
  3. Reports
  4. + New only
Show answer

Answer: A. The recurring transactions list lives under the Gear icon.

Short answer

Name the three recurring types and one use for each.

Model answer

Scheduled — fixed monthly rent; Reminder — a retainer that sometimes varies; Unscheduled — a complex invoice reused occasionally.

Why review the recurring list every quarter?

Model answer

So templates for customers who have left are ended, preventing false invoices and overstated income.

Class Activity

  1. Create one scheduled and one reminder recurring invoice in a sample file.
  2. List the recurring billing an organisation you know could automate.

Assignment

Design the recurring invoice setup for an organisation with at least four repeating customers. State the type, interval and end date for each and the review routine you would run.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 4.6 Sales Receipts vs Invoices
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 4: Customers, Sales and Invoicing

LESSON NOTE: SALES RECEIPTS VS INVOICES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSales Receipts vs InvoicesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Distinguish a sales receipt from an invoice
  • Choose the right form for a transaction
  • State the different accounting effects

1. Introduction

Both record a sale. The difference is timing of payment, and choosing wrongly either invents a debt that does not exist or hides one that does.

2. The difference

InvoiceSales receipt
PaymentLater, on creditImmediately, at the time of sale
DebitAccounts ReceivableBank or Undeposited Funds
CreditIncomeIncome
Creates a debt?YesNo
Typical useB2B credit sale, monthly billingShop counter, market stall, instant payment

3. Choosing correctly

Ask one question: has the money already been received? If yes, sales receipt. If no, invoice.

Example: A shop selling a $20 item for cash uses a sales receipt — Debit Bank $20, Credit Sales $20. Using an invoice instead would create a $20 debt the customer does not actually owe, which then sits on the ageing report forever.

4. The common error

Note: Raising an invoice and a sales receipt for the same sale records the income twice and leaves a phantom receivable. If a customer pays immediately against an invoice, receive the payment against that invoice — do not add a sales receipt as well.

Summary

  • An invoice is for payment later and creates a receivable; a sales receipt is for payment now and hits the bank directly.
  • The test is simply whether the money has already been received.
  • Never record both an invoice and a sales receipt for the same sale.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Sales receiptA form recording a sale paid for at the time of sale.
Phantom receivableA debt shown in the records that the customer does not actually owe.
Undeposited FundsA holding account for payments received but not yet banked.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

A customer pays cash at the counter. Which form?

  1. Sales receipt
  2. Invoice
  3. Estimate
  4. Credit memo
Show answer

Answer: A. Payment received at the time of sale is a sales receipt.

What does an invoice create that a sales receipt does not?

  1. A receivable — a debt owed by the customer
  2. Income
  3. A tax entry
  4. A bank record
Show answer

Answer: A. Both record income, but only the invoice creates a debt.

What is the result of recording both an invoice and a sales receipt for one sale?

  1. Income is doubled and a phantom receivable remains
  2. Nothing, they cancel out
  3. The sale is deleted
  4. Tax is halved
Show answer

Answer: A. Two documents post two lots of income and leave an uncollectable balance.

What single question decides which form to use?

  1. Has the money already been received?
  2. Is the customer local?
  3. Is the amount large?
  4. Is tax charged?
Show answer

Answer: A. Timing of payment is the whole distinction.

Short answer

Give the journal entries for a $20 cash sale and a $20 credit sale.

Model answer

Cash sale: Debit Bank $20, Credit Sales $20. Credit sale: Debit Accounts Receivable $20, Credit Sales $20.

How would you spot phantom receivables caused by this error?

Model answer

They appear on the Accounts Receivable ageing as old unpaid invoices for customers who in fact paid at the time.

Class Activity

  1. Classify ten sales as invoice or sales receipt and justify each.
  2. Find an aged receivable in a sample file and decide whether it might be a phantom.

Assignment

Take fifteen sales from a business, decide the correct form for each, and write the journal entry. Then explain how you would find and correct any sale recorded on the wrong form.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 4.7 Estimates and Quotes
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 4: Customers, Sales and Invoicing

LESSON NOTE: ESTIMATES AND QUOTES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingEstimates and QuotesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create an estimate and convert it to an invoice
  • Explain why an estimate has no accounting effect
  • Track estimate status

1. Introduction

An estimate is a proposal: 'this is what the job would cost'. It is a sales tool, not an accounting record, and understanding that distinction prevents a common reporting error.

2. No accounting effect

Saving an estimate posts nothing. No income, no receivable, no tax. It appears in sales reports as a pipeline figure only. Income arises only when the estimate becomes an invoice.

Note: If your Profit and Loss looks too low, do not go hunting for missing estimates. Estimates are meant to be invisible to it.

3. Statuses

StatusMeaning
PendingSent, awaiting the customer's answer
AcceptedCustomer agreed; ready to invoice
ClosedConverted to an invoice or otherwise finished
RejectedCustomer declined

4. Converting to an invoice

  1. Open the accepted estimate.
  2. Choose Create invoice.
  3. Invoice the whole estimate, a percentage, or selected lines — useful for staged work.
  4. Save; the estimate is marked closed and linked to the invoice.
Example: A builder quotes $9,000. On acceptance he invoices 40% ($3,600) to start, then the remaining 60% on completion. Both invoices link back to one estimate.

Summary

  • An estimate posts no accounting entries; it is a proposal only.
  • Statuses track pending, accepted, closed and rejected.
  • An estimate can be converted wholly, partly or in stages into invoices.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
EstimateA quotation of expected price, with no accounting effect.
Progress invoicingInvoicing an estimate in stages.
PipelineExpected future sales not yet earned.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does saving an estimate post to the accounts?

  1. Nothing
  2. Income and a receivable
  3. A bank entry
  4. An expense
Show answer

Answer: A. An estimate is a proposal and has no accounting effect until invoiced.

When does income from a quoted job get recorded?

  1. When the estimate is converted into an invoice
  2. When the estimate is created
  3. When the estimate is sent
  4. When it is accepted verbally
Show answer

Answer: A. Income arises on the invoice, not the estimate.

What is progress invoicing?

  1. Invoicing an estimate in stages rather than all at once
  2. Invoicing twice by mistake
  3. Cancelling an estimate
  4. Adding tax later
Show answer

Answer: A. Staged invoicing bills a percentage or selected lines of an estimate.

An estimate the customer declined should be marked:

  1. Rejected
  2. Accepted
  3. Closed as invoiced
  4. Pending forever
Show answer

Answer: A. Marking it rejected keeps the pipeline figure honest.

Short answer

Why does an estimate not affect the Profit and Loss?

Model answer

Because no sale has occurred yet — it is only a proposal, so no income or receivable exists.

Describe how a builder might use progress invoicing on a $9,000 quote.

Model answer

Invoice 40% on acceptance to fund materials, then the remaining 60% on completion, with both invoices linked to the one estimate.

Class Activity

  1. Create an estimate in a sample file and convert 50% of it to an invoice.
  2. List three situations where progress invoicing would help cash flow.

Assignment

Prepare an estimate for a realistic job, then show the staged invoices you would raise. Explain at each stage what is posted to the accounts and what is not.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 4.8 Credit Memos and Refunds
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 4: Customers, Sales and Invoicing

LESSON NOTE: CREDIT MEMOS AND REFUNDS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCredit Memos and RefundsBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create a credit memo and apply it
  • Distinguish a credit memo from a refund receipt
  • Reverse a sale correctly

1. Introduction

Sometimes a sale must be reduced: goods returned, an overcharge, a service not delivered. Doing this by deleting the original invoice destroys the audit trail; a credit memo does it properly.

2. Credit memo vs refund receipt

Credit memoRefund receipt
What it doesReduces what the customer owesGives money back
Cash moves?NoYes
Use whenThe customer has an unpaid balance or will buy againThe customer already paid and wants cash back
PostsDebit Sales/Returns, Credit Accounts ReceivableDebit Sales/Returns, Credit Bank

3. Applying a credit memo

A credit memo sits as an unapplied credit until you attach it to an invoice. Apply it via Receive payment, ticking both the invoice and the credit.

Example: A customer owes $500 and returns $120 of goods. Raise a credit memo for $120, apply it, and the balance becomes $380. Sales for the period fall by $120.

4. Never delete the invoice

Note: Deleting the original invoice hides that a sale ever happened, breaks the numbering sequence and removes the evidence of the return. Auditors and tax authorities treat missing invoice numbers as a red flag. Always reverse with a credit memo.

Summary

  • A credit memo reduces what a customer owes; a refund receipt returns cash.
  • A credit memo must be applied to an invoice to reduce the balance.
  • Never delete an invoice to reverse a sale — use a credit memo to preserve the audit trail.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Credit memoA document reducing the amount a customer owes.
Refund receiptA document recording money paid back to a customer.
Unapplied creditA credit not yet attached to an invoice.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

A customer who has already paid wants money back. Which document?

  1. Refund receipt
  2. Credit memo
  3. Invoice
  4. Estimate
Show answer

Answer: A. Cash going back to the customer is a refund receipt.

What happens if a credit memo is never applied to an invoice?

  1. It sits as an unapplied credit and the invoice still shows as owing
  2. It is deleted automatically
  3. It doubles the sale
  4. Tax is refunded
Show answer

Answer: A. An unapplied credit does not reduce any specific invoice balance.

Why should you never delete an invoice to reverse a sale?

  1. It destroys the audit trail and breaks the invoice number sequence
  2. It is impossible in QuickBooks
  3. It increases tax
  4. It creates a refund
Show answer

Answer: A. Missing invoice numbers are a red flag to auditors and tax authorities.

A customer owing $500 returns $120 of goods. What is the new balance after a credit memo is applied?

  1. $380
  2. $620
  3. $500
  4. $120
Show answer

Answer: A. The credit reduces the receivable from $500 to $380.

Short answer

State the accounting difference between a credit memo and a refund receipt.

Model answer

A credit memo debits sales/returns and credits Accounts Receivable, moving no cash. A refund receipt debits sales/returns and credits Bank, moving cash out.

Why is preserving the invoice number sequence important?

Model answer

Gaps suggest deleted or hidden sales, which auditors and tax authorities treat as a sign of possible concealment.

Class Activity

  1. Create a credit memo in a sample file and apply it to an open invoice.
  2. Decide, for five return scenarios, whether a credit memo or refund receipt is correct.

Assignment

Handle three return scenarios end to end: state the document used, the journal entry posted, and the effect on the customer balance and on reported sales.

lessons.title: 5.1 Receiving Customer Payments
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 5: Receiving Payments and Deposits

LESSON NOTE: RECEIVING CUSTOMER PAYMENTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingReceiving Customer PaymentsBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Record a payment against the correct invoice
  • Explain why payments must be matched, not just banked
  • Handle a payment covering several invoices

1. Introduction

Receiving a payment is not simply money arriving. It is the settlement of a specific debt, and QuickBooks needs to know which one.

2. The correct process

  1. + New → Receive payment.
  2. Choose the customer; QuickBooks lists their open invoices.
  3. Enter the date, amount and method.
  4. Tick the invoice or invoices being paid.
  5. Choose where the money goes — the bank account or Undeposited Funds.

3. Why matching matters

If you match the paymentIf you just record a deposit
The invoice is marked paidThe invoice stays open forever
Ageing reports are accurateThe customer looks like a debtor when they are not
Income is recorded onceIncome is recorded twice — once by the invoice, once by the deposit
Note: Recording a bank deposit instead of receiving a payment is the single most common error in QuickBooks. It doubles income and leaves phantom debts.

4. One payment, several invoices

Example: A customer owes $200, $150 and $90 and pays $350. Receive payment for $350 and tick the $200 and $150 invoices. The $90 stays open. If they pay $360, the extra $10 sits as a credit on their account for next time.

Summary

  • Payments must be applied to specific invoices, not merely banked.
  • Recording a deposit instead of a payment doubles income and leaves the invoice open.
  • One payment can settle several invoices; an overpayment becomes a customer credit.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Receive paymentThe form that applies money received against open invoices.
Open invoiceAn invoice not yet fully paid.
Customer creditAn overpayment held against future invoices.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What is the most common QuickBooks error described in this lesson?

  1. Recording a bank deposit instead of receiving a payment against the invoice
  2. Sending an invoice twice
  3. Using the wrong font
  4. Creating too many customers
Show answer

Answer: A. It doubles income and leaves the original invoice permanently open.

A customer pays $350 against invoices of $200, $150 and $90. What happens?

  1. The $200 and $150 are settled and the $90 stays open
  2. All three are marked paid
  3. Nothing is settled
  4. The $90 is deleted
Show answer

Answer: A. You tick the invoices the payment covers; the rest remains outstanding.

A customer overpays by $10. What happens to the $10?

  1. It sits as a credit on their account for future invoices
  2. It is recorded as income
  3. It is refunded automatically
  4. It is deleted
Show answer

Answer: A. Overpayments become customer credits available against later invoices.

Why does matching keep ageing reports accurate?

  1. Settled invoices drop off, so only genuine debts remain listed
  2. Because ageing ignores payments
  3. Because it deletes old invoices
  4. It does not affect ageing
Show answer

Answer: A. Only correctly applied payments clear invoices from the ageing report.

Short answer

Explain in one sentence why recording a deposit instead of a payment doubles income.

Model answer

The invoice already recorded the income, so recording a separate deposit to an income account records the same sale a second time.

What happens to an invoice if a payment is never applied to it?

Model answer

It remains open on the ageing report, making the customer appear to owe money they have already paid.

Class Activity

  1. Receive three payments in a sample file, one covering two invoices.
  2. Find an open invoice in a sample file and decide whether it is genuine or a matching error.

Assignment

Process six customer payments including one part-payment, one covering two invoices, and one overpayment. Show the effect of each on the customer balance and explain the treatment of the overpayment.

lessons.title: 5.2 Undeposited Funds Explained
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 5: Receiving Payments and Deposits

LESSON NOTE: UNDEPOSITED FUNDS EXPLAINED

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingUndeposited Funds ExplainedBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Explain what Undeposited Funds is for
  • Decide when to use it
  • Clear a stuck Undeposited Funds balance

1. Introduction

Undeposited Funds confuses more new users than any other account, yet its purpose is simple: it mirrors the physical reality of holding cheques and cash in a drawer before you walk to the bank.

2. Meaning

Undeposited Funds: A temporary holding account for money received but not yet deposited at the bank.

The bank statement will show one lump deposit of $1,000, not five separate customer payments. If each payment went straight to the bank account in QuickBooks, you would have five entries facing one statement line and reconciliation would fail.

3. The workflow

  1. Receive each customer payment into Undeposited Funds.
  2. When you physically bank them, use + New → Bank deposit.
  3. Tick the payments included in that trip to the bank.
  4. QuickBooks creates one deposit matching the one statement line.
Example: Five payments of $200 each go into Undeposited Funds. One bank deposit of $1,000 is recorded. The bank feed shows $1,000 and matches perfectly.

4. When NOT to use it

Note: If money arrives directly in the bank — a transfer, a card settlement, mobile money — send it straight to the bank account. Routing it through Undeposited Funds then creates an extra step for nothing.

5. Clearing a stuck balance

A growing Undeposited Funds balance means payments were received but never included in a bank deposit. Run the Undeposited Funds account register, find the old items, and either include them in a deposit or, if they were separately recorded as deposits, delete the duplicate.

Summary

  • Undeposited Funds holds received money until it is banked as one deposit.
  • It exists so several payments can match one bank statement line.
  • Money arriving directly in the bank should bypass it; a growing balance means deposits were never completed.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Undeposited FundsA holding account for received but unbanked money.
Bank depositThe form that groups held payments into one banked amount.
RegisterThe transaction list for a single account.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why does Undeposited Funds exist?

  1. So several payments can be grouped into one deposit that matches one bank statement line
  2. To hide income
  3. To calculate tax
  4. To store customer details
Show answer

Answer: A. It mirrors physically holding payments before banking them together.

Money is transferred directly into your bank by a customer. What should you do?

  1. Receive it straight to the bank account, bypassing Undeposited Funds
  2. Always route it through Undeposited Funds
  3. Record it as an expense
  4. Ignore it
Show answer

Answer: A. Direct arrivals need no holding step.

A growing Undeposited Funds balance usually means:

  1. Payments were received but never included in a bank deposit
  2. The bank is holding money
  3. Income is overstated
  4. Tax is unpaid
Show answer

Answer: A. The holding account only clears when a bank deposit is recorded.

Five $200 payments are banked together. What should QuickBooks show?

  1. One bank deposit of $1,000 matching one statement line
  2. Five separate bank entries
  3. One expense of $1,000
  4. Nothing until month end
Show answer

Answer: A. Grouping them produces a single deposit matching the statement.

Short answer

Explain Undeposited Funds using the drawer analogy.

Model answer

It represents cash and cheques held in a drawer after being received but before being physically taken to the bank.

How would you clear an old Undeposited Funds balance?

Model answer

Open the account register, identify the unbanked payments, and either include them in a bank deposit or remove duplicates if a separate deposit was already recorded.

Class Activity

  1. Receive three payments into Undeposited Funds and combine them into one deposit.
  2. Check a sample company's Undeposited Funds balance and explain what it represents.

Assignment

Process a week of takings: receive at least six payments, group them into two bank deposits, and show how each deposit matches a single bank statement line.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 5.3 Making Bank Deposits
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 5: Receiving Payments and Deposits

LESSON NOTE: MAKING BANK DEPOSITS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingMaking Bank DepositsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Record a bank deposit
  • Include several payments in one deposit
  • Record non-sales money received

1. Introduction

The bank deposit form is where held payments become a single banked amount, and it is also how you record money that is not a customer sale.

2. Depositing held payments

  1. + New → Bank deposit.
  2. Choose the bank account and the deposit date.
  3. Tick the payments from Undeposited Funds included in this deposit.
  4. Check the total matches the physical deposit slip.
  5. Save.

3. Adding other money

Below the payments list is an 'Add funds to this deposit' section for money that is not a customer payment:

Money receivedAccount to use
Owner putting money inOwner's Equity
A loan receivedLoan liability
Interest paid by the bankInterest Income
Refund from a supplierThe original expense account
A grant or donationGrant/Donation income
Note: Never post these to Sales. A loan is not revenue, and an owner's contribution is not profit. Misposting them inflates income and distorts tax.

4. Handling bank charges on a deposit

Example: You bank $1,000 and the bank deducts a $5 handling fee, crediting $995. Record the deposit as $1,000 of payments plus a negative $5 line coded to Bank Charges. The deposit then nets to $995 and matches the statement exactly.

Summary

  • Bank deposits group held payments into one banked amount.
  • The 'Add funds' section records non-sales money such as loans, owner contributions and interest.
  • Never code loans or owner contributions to sales income.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Bank depositThe form recording money banked into an account.
Add fundsThe part of the deposit form for money that is not a customer payment.
Bank chargeA fee the bank deducts.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Where do you record a loan received?

  1. On the deposit, coded to a loan liability account
  2. As sales income
  3. As an expense
  4. As a customer payment
Show answer

Answer: A. A loan is money owed, not revenue.

How do you handle a $5 bank fee deducted from a $1,000 deposit?

  1. Add a negative $5 line coded to Bank Charges so the deposit nets to $995
  2. Ignore it
  3. Reduce sales by $5
  4. Record a separate invoice
Show answer

Answer: A. Netting the fee inside the deposit makes it match the statement exactly.

Why must an owner's contribution not be coded to Sales?

  1. It is not revenue; it inflates income and distorts tax
  2. Sales accounts are locked
  3. It would reduce equity
  4. It has no effect
Show answer

Answer: A. Owner contributions are equity, not earnings.

What should the deposit total match?

  1. The physical deposit slip and the bank statement line
  2. The invoice total
  3. The month's sales
  4. The customer balance
Show answer

Answer: A. The deposit is a banking event and must agree to the bank.

Short answer

List three kinds of money recorded through 'Add funds to this deposit'.

Model answer

Owner contributions, loans received, bank interest, supplier refunds and grants or donations.

Why net a bank charge inside the deposit rather than recording it separately?

Model answer

So the deposit total equals the amount the bank actually credited, allowing a clean match during reconciliation.

Class Activity

  1. Record a deposit combining four payments plus $50 of bank interest.
  2. List five kinds of non-sales money an organisation you know receives and the account for each.

Assignment

Record a week of deposits for an organisation, including at least one loan or owner contribution and one deposit with a bank charge deducted. Show that each matches its statement line.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 5.4 Partial Payments and Overpayments
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 5: Receiving Payments and Deposits

LESSON NOTE: PARTIAL PAYMENTS AND OVERPAYMENTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingPartial Payments and OverpaymentsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Record a part-payment against an invoice
  • Handle an overpayment
  • Explain the effect on the ageing report

1. Introduction

Customers rarely pay exactly. They pay part now, or round up, or pay two invoices with one transfer. QuickBooks handles all of this, provided you record it deliberately.

2. Part-payments

Enter the amount actually received and apply it to the invoice. QuickBooks reduces the balance and leaves the invoice open for the remainder.

Example: A $500 invoice, $200 received. The invoice shows $300 outstanding and remains on the ageing report at its original date — which is correct, because the debt is that old.

3. Overpayments

SituationTreatment
Customer pays more than owedThe excess becomes an unapplied credit on their account
They will buy againLeave the credit to offset the next invoice
They want it backIssue a refund receipt for the excess
It is a small rounding amountWrite it off to a Sundry Income account

4. The ageing consequence

Note: A part-paid invoice keeps its original date for ageing. Do not edit the invoice date to make it look current — the age of a debt is a management warning, and resetting it hides a collection problem.

Summary

  • A part-payment reduces the balance and leaves the invoice open at its original date.
  • Overpayments become customer credits, which can offset future invoices or be refunded.
  • Never change an invoice date to make an old debt look current.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Part-paymentA payment settling only some of an invoice.
Unapplied creditMoney held on a customer account not yet offset against an invoice.
AgeingHow long a debt has been outstanding.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

A $500 invoice receives a $200 payment. What is shown?

  1. The invoice remains open with $300 outstanding at its original date
  2. The invoice is closed
  3. A new $300 invoice is created
  4. The payment is rejected
Show answer

Answer: A. Part-payment reduces the balance without closing the invoice.

Why should an old part-paid invoice keep its original date?

  1. The age of a debt is a management warning that should not be hidden
  2. QuickBooks forbids editing
  3. To calculate tax
  4. To please the customer
Show answer

Answer: A. Re-dating conceals a genuine collection problem.

A customer overpays and will buy again soon. Best treatment?

  1. Leave the credit on their account to offset the next invoice
  2. Refund immediately
  3. Record it as sales
  4. Delete the payment
Show answer

Answer: A. An unapplied credit naturally offsets the next invoice.

A customer overpays by $2 in rounding and will not return. Reasonable treatment?

  1. Write it off to a sundry income account
  2. Keep it forever as a credit
  3. Refund $2 by bank transfer
  4. Record it as a loan
Show answer

Answer: A. Trivial amounts are cleared to sundry income rather than kept indefinitely.

Short answer

Describe two ways to deal with an overpayment.

Model answer

Leave it as a credit against future invoices, or issue a refund receipt returning the money.

What does the ageing of a part-paid invoice tell a manager?

Model answer

How long the remaining debt has actually been outstanding, which signals whether collection is failing.

Class Activity

  1. Record a part-payment and an overpayment in a sample company and view the ageing report.
  2. Decide the treatment for four overpayment scenarios you invent.

Assignment

Handle five awkward payment situations, including at least one part-payment and one overpayment. For each, state what you recorded and how the ageing report was affected.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.
