lessons.title: 5.5 Accounts Receivable Ageing
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 5: Receiving Payments and Deposits

LESSON NOTE: ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE AGEING

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingAccounts Receivable AgeingBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Run and read an ageing report
  • Explain the ageing bands
  • Use ageing to drive collection

1. Introduction

The ageing report answers the question every organisation needs answered weekly: who owes us money, how much, and for how long?

2. Reading the report

BandMeaningAction
CurrentNot yet dueNo action
1–30 daysRecently overduePolite reminder
31–60 daysA problem is developingPhone the customer
61–90 daysSeriousEscalate; stop further credit
90+ daysLikely uncollectableDecide: pursue or write off

3. Summary vs detail

The Ageing Summary gives one row per customer with columns per band — the management view. The Ageing Detail lists every unpaid invoice — the collections working list. Use summary to see the shape of the problem, detail to act on it.

4. Using it properly

  1. Run it weekly, not monthly — a debt found at 45 days is far more collectable than at 90.
  2. Sort by the oldest band, not the largest amount; old debt hardens.
  3. Check for phantom debts caused by unmatched payments before chasing anyone.
  4. Record every chase, so escalation is evidenced.
Example: An ageing summary shows one customer with $4,000 in the 90+ band. That single line is worth more management attention than twenty small current balances.

5. The credibility check

Note: Before sending reminders, confirm the debts are real. Chasing a customer who paid last month, because the payment was recorded as a deposit rather than matched, damages the relationship and your credibility.

Summary

  • Ageing groups unpaid invoices into bands by how overdue they are.
  • Summary is the management view; detail is the collections working list.
  • Run it weekly and verify debts are genuine before chasing.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Ageing reportA report grouping unpaid invoices by how long they are overdue.
Ageing bandA range of days used to group overdue debts.
Write offRecognising a debt as uncollectable.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does the 90+ band usually indicate?

  1. A debt that is likely uncollectable and needs a decision
  2. A recent sale
  3. A prepayment
  4. A supplier balance
Show answer

Answer: A. The older a debt, the less likely it is ever recovered.

Which report is the collections working list?

  1. Ageing Detail
  2. Ageing Summary
  3. Profit and Loss
  4. Balance Sheet
Show answer

Answer: A. Detail lists every unpaid invoice so each can be actioned.

What should you check before sending reminders?

  1. That the debts are genuine and not caused by unmatched payments
  2. The weather
  3. The customer's address only
  4. The invoice font
Show answer

Answer: A. Chasing paid invoices damages credibility and the relationship.

Why run ageing weekly rather than monthly?

  1. A debt found at 45 days is far more collectable than at 90
  2. Reports expire
  3. Monthly reports cost more
  4. QuickBooks requires it
Show answer

Answer: A. Early action materially improves recovery.

Short answer

List the ageing bands and one action for each.

Model answer

Current — none; 1–30 — reminder; 31–60 — phone; 61–90 — escalate and stop credit; 90+ — pursue or write off.

What is the difference between the summary and detail ageing reports?

Model answer

Summary shows one row per customer across bands for management; detail lists every unpaid invoice for action.

Class Activity

  1. Run both ageing reports in a sample file and write three actions you would take.
  2. Explain how you would verify a debt is genuine before chasing it.

Assignment

Produce an ageing analysis for an organisation, identify the three most serious balances, and write the collection action and escalation step for each.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 5.6 Sending Statements and Reminders
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 5: Receiving Payments and Deposits

LESSON NOTE: SENDING STATEMENTS AND REMINDERS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSending Statements and RemindersBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Send a customer statement
  • Choose the right statement type
  • Automate payment reminders

1. Introduction

An invoice asks for one payment. A statement shows the whole relationship — everything invoiced, everything paid, and what remains. For customers with many transactions it is far more effective.

2. The three statement types

TypeShowsBest for
Balance ForwardOpening balance, activity in the period, closing balanceRegular customers with ongoing accounts
Open ItemEvery unpaid invoice individuallyChasing specific overdue invoices
Transaction StatementAll transactions in a date rangeCustomers who query their account

3. Sending them

  1. Sales → Customers → select customers.
  2. Batch actions → Create statements.
  3. Choose the type and date range.
  4. Preview, then print or email.

Statements can be sent to many customers at once, which makes a monthly statement run realistic even for a small team.

4. Automated reminders

QuickBooks can email reminders automatically at chosen intervals — for example three days before due, on the due date, and seven days after. Set these once and routine chasing happens without anyone remembering.

Note: Keep reminder wording courteous. Automated reminders reach good customers who are simply slow, and an aggressive tone costs more in goodwill than the delay costs in cash.

Summary

  • Statements show the whole account relationship, not just one invoice.
  • Balance Forward suits ongoing accounts; Open Item suits chasing specific invoices.
  • Automated reminders handle routine chasing; keep the wording courteous.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
StatementA summary of a customer's account over a period.
Open Item statementA statement listing each unpaid invoice.
Automated reminderA scheduled email prompting payment.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which statement type lists every unpaid invoice individually?

  1. Open Item
  2. Balance Forward
  3. Transaction Statement
  4. Ageing Summary
Show answer

Answer: A. Open Item is designed for chasing specific overdue invoices.

What is the advantage of a statement over an invoice?

  1. It shows the whole account: invoiced, paid and outstanding
  2. It is legally stronger
  3. It charges interest
  4. It replaces the invoice
Show answer

Answer: A. Statements give the customer the full picture of the relationship.

Why keep automated reminder wording courteous?

  1. They reach good customers who are merely slow, and goodwill is worth more than the delay
  2. It is legally required
  3. Rude emails are blocked
  4. It reduces tax
Show answer

Answer: A. Automation is indiscriminate, so the tone must suit your best customers.

How can a small team make monthly statements realistic?

  1. Send them as a batch to many customers at once
  2. Write each by hand
  3. Only send one per year
  4. Use invoices instead
Show answer

Answer: A. Batch statement runs make the task practical.

Short answer

Name the three statement types and one use for each.

Model answer

Balance Forward for ongoing accounts; Open Item for chasing overdue invoices; Transaction Statement for customers querying their account.

Describe a sensible automated reminder schedule.

Model answer

A courteous note three days before the due date, one on the due date, and a firmer one about a week after.

Class Activity

  1. Generate statements for three customers in a sample file, using two different types.
  2. Draft the wording for a before-due and an after-due reminder email.

Assignment

Design a complete customer communication routine: which statement type, how often, and the reminder schedule and wording at each stage.

lessons.title: 5.7 Writing Off Bad Debts
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 5: Receiving Payments and Deposits

LESSON NOTE: WRITING OFF BAD DEBTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingWriting Off Bad DebtsBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Decide when a debt should be written off
  • Write off a bad debt correctly
  • Explain the effect on profit and tax

1. Introduction

Some debts will never be paid. Leaving them on the books overstates your assets and flatters your profit. Writing them off is honesty, not defeat.

2. When to write off

  • The customer has ceased trading or cannot be traced
  • Reasonable collection efforts have failed over a long period
  • The cost of pursuing exceeds the amount owed
  • A settlement has been agreed for less than the full amount
Note: Write off only after genuine effort, and keep evidence of that effort. Tax authorities usually allow a deduction for a bad debt only where recovery was genuinely attempted.

3. How to write it off

  1. Create an expense account called Bad Debt Expense if one does not exist.
  2. Create a product/service item called 'Bad debt' pointing to that account.
  3. Raise a credit memo to the customer using that item for the unpaid amount.
  4. Apply the credit memo to the unpaid invoice.

This clears the receivable, records the loss as an expense, and leaves the original invoice intact for the audit trail.

4. The accounting effect

AccountMovement
Accounts ReceivableDecreases — the debt is removed
Bad Debt ExpenseIncreases — the loss is recognised
ProfitDecreases by the amount written off
SalesUnchanged — the original sale stays recorded
Example: A $600 debt written off: Debit Bad Debt Expense $600, Credit Accounts Receivable $600. Sales still show the original $600; the loss appears separately as an expense, which is exactly what a reader needs to see.

Summary

  • Write off only after genuine collection effort, and keep the evidence.
  • Use a credit memo with a Bad Debt item, then apply it to the unpaid invoice.
  • The receivable falls and an expense is recognised; original sales remain intact.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Bad debtA receivable judged uncollectable.
Bad Debt ExpenseThe expense account recording uncollectable amounts.
Write offRemoving an uncollectable debt from receivables.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What is the journal effect of writing off a $600 bad debt?

  1. Debit Bad Debt Expense $600, credit Accounts Receivable $600
  2. Debit Sales $600, credit Bank $600
  3. Debit Bank $600, credit Sales $600
  4. No entry is needed
Show answer

Answer: A. The loss is expensed and the receivable removed.

Why not simply delete the original invoice?

  1. It would erase the sale and the audit trail; the loss should be shown separately
  2. Deleting is impossible
  3. It would increase tax
  4. It refunds the customer
Show answer

Answer: A. The sale genuinely happened; the loss is a separate, visible event.

Why do tax authorities usually require evidence of collection effort?

  1. A deduction is generally allowed only where recovery was genuinely attempted
  2. To delay the refund
  3. To increase the tax owed
  4. They do not require it
Show answer

Answer: A. Evidence prevents write-offs being used to reduce tax artificially.

What happens to reported Sales when a bad debt is written off?

  1. Sales are unchanged; the loss appears as an expense
  2. Sales fall by the same amount
  3. Sales double
  4. Sales are deleted
Show answer

Answer: A. Keeping sales intact and showing the loss separately is more informative.

Short answer

List three circumstances justifying a write-off.

Model answer

The customer has ceased trading; collection has failed over a long period; the cost of pursuing exceeds the debt.

Why does leaving bad debts on the books flatter the accounts?

Model answer

Receivables are overstated as assets and past profit is overstated, because income was recorded for money that will never arrive.

Class Activity

  1. Write off a bad debt in a sample company and check the Profit and Loss before and after.
  2. List the evidence you would keep to justify a write-off to a tax inspector.

Assignment

Review an ageing report, identify debts you would write off, justify each with reference to the criteria, and show the journal entry and profit effect for each.

lessons.title: 6.1 Adding Vendors
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 6: Vendors, Bills and Expenses

LESSON NOTE: ADDING VENDORS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingAdding VendorsBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create a vendor record with the right fields
  • Explain why vendor records matter for reporting
  • Set default terms and expense accounts

1. Introduction

A vendor (supplier) record is the mirror image of a customer record. Created once, it lets QuickBooks track what you owe, when, and what you have spent with each supplier over time.

2. Key fields

FieldWhy it matters
Display nameUnique identifier for the supplier
EmailSending purchase orders and remittances
TermsSets when their bill becomes due
Default expense accountSpeeds coding of repeat purchases
Tax IDNeeded for contractor reporting in some countries
Opening balanceOnly if you owed them on the start date

3. Why it matters

Without vendor records you can still record spending, but you cannot answer 'how much did we spend with this supplier this year?', you cannot age what you owe, and you cannot produce a remittance advice.

Example: Setting a default expense account of 'Fuel' on the fuel station vendor means every future bill from them is coded correctly by default, cutting errors and keystrokes.

Summary

  • Vendor records enable payables ageing, spend analysis and remittances.
  • Default terms drive the bill due date; a default account speeds coding.
  • Enter an opening balance only for amounts owed on the file's start date.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
VendorA supplier the organisation buys from.
Remittance adviceA note telling a supplier which invoices a payment covers.
Default expense accountThe account automatically suggested for that vendor's bills.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does setting a vendor's terms control?

  1. When their bill becomes due
  2. The price charged
  3. The tax rate
  4. The payment method
Show answer

Answer: A. Terms drive the due date and therefore payables ageing.

Why set a default expense account on a vendor?

  1. Repeat purchases are coded correctly and faster
  2. It reduces the price
  3. It is legally required
  4. It changes the currency
Show answer

Answer: A. Defaults reduce both keystrokes and coding errors.

Without a vendor record, which question cannot be answered?

  1. How much have we spent with this supplier this year?
  2. What is our bank balance?
  3. What did we sell today?
  4. What is our profit?
Show answer

Answer: A. Spend by supplier requires the supplier to exist as a record.

When should a vendor opening balance be entered?

  1. Only if you owed them money on the file's start date
  2. For every vendor
  3. Never
  4. Only at year end
Show answer

Answer: A. Opening balances represent debts existing at the start date.

Short answer

Name four useful fields on a vendor record.

Model answer

Display name, email, payment terms, default expense account and tax ID.

How does a vendor record improve control over spending?

Model answer

It allows spend per supplier to be reported and what you owe to be aged, so nothing is paid twice or forgotten.

Class Activity

  1. Create five vendor records with terms and default accounts in a sample file.
  2. List your organisation's ten most frequent suppliers and the account each should default to.

Assignment

Build a vendor list of at least ten suppliers with terms and default expense accounts, and explain how the defaults you chose reduce coding errors.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 6.2 Entering Bills
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 6: Vendors, Bills and Expenses

LESSON NOTE: ENTERING BILLS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingEntering BillsBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Enter a supplier bill
  • Explain the difference between a bill and an expense
  • State the accounting effect of a bill

1. Introduction

A bill records something you owe but have not yet paid. It is the purchases mirror of a customer invoice, and it is what makes accrual accounting work.

2. Bill vs expense

BillExpense
When to useYou will pay laterYou have already paid
DebitExpense accountExpense account
CreditAccounts PayableBank / card
Creates a debt?YesNo
Needs a later payment step?Yes — Pay BillsNo
Note: Entering a bill and then also recording an expense for the same purchase double-counts the cost and leaves a payable that never clears.

3. The accounting effect

Example: A $300 bill for stationery: Debit Office Supplies $300, Credit Accounts Payable $300. The bank is untouched. When paid: Debit Accounts Payable $300, Credit Bank $300.

4. Why bother with bills

If you only record spending when money leaves, your reports never show what you owe. A supplier owed $8,000 is invisible until payday, so profit looks healthy and cash planning fails. Bills make obligations visible before they bite.

Summary

  • A bill records a purchase to be paid later; an expense records one already paid.
  • A bill debits the expense and credits Accounts Payable; payment clears the payable.
  • Bills make obligations visible before payment, which is essential for cash planning.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
BillA record of an amount owed to a supplier.
Accounts PayableTotal owed to suppliers.
AccrualRecognising a cost when incurred rather than when paid.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

You buy goods and will pay in 30 days. Which form?

  1. Bill
  2. Expense
  3. Sales receipt
  4. Estimate
Show answer

Answer: A. Paying later means a bill, which creates a payable.

What does entering a bill credit?

  1. Accounts Payable
  2. Bank
  3. Sales
  4. Equity
Show answer

Answer: A. The obligation is recorded as a payable until paid.

What happens if you record both a bill and an expense for one purchase?

  1. The cost is double-counted and a payable never clears
  2. Nothing
  3. The bill is deleted
  4. Tax is halved
Show answer

Answer: A. Two records post the cost twice and leave a permanent payable.

Why do bills matter for cash planning?

  1. They make future obligations visible before payment falls due
  2. They increase the bank balance
  3. They reduce expenses
  4. They replace budgets
Show answer

Answer: A. Knowing what is owed and when is the basis of cash planning.

Short answer

Give the two journal entries for a $300 bill later paid in full.

Model answer

Bill: Debit Office Supplies $300, Credit Accounts Payable $300. Payment: Debit Accounts Payable $300, Credit Bank $300.

Why does recording only paid expenses distort the accounts?

Model answer

Amounts already owed are invisible, so profit looks better than it is and cash requirements are underestimated.

Class Activity

  1. Enter four bills in a sample company and view the Accounts Payable balance.
  2. Classify ten purchases as bill or expense.

Assignment

Enter a week of purchases for an organisation, choosing correctly between bills and expenses, and produce the resulting Accounts Payable balance with an explanation.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 6.3 Paying Bills
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 6: Vendors, Bills and Expenses

LESSON NOTE: PAYING BILLS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingPaying BillsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Pay a bill correctly
  • Pay several bills at once
  • Explain why Pay Bills is not the same as writing a cheque

1. Introduction

Once a bill exists, it must be settled through Pay Bills. Paying by any other route leaves the payable open and records the cost twice.

2. The process

  1. + New → Pay bills.
  2. Choose the bank or card account paying.
  3. Set the payment date.
  4. Tick the bills to pay; adjust the amount for a part-payment.
  5. Save.

3. The critical rule

CorrectWrong
Enter bill, then Pay BillsEnter bill, then write a separate cheque or expense
Payable clears to zeroPayable stays open forever
Cost recorded onceCost recorded twice
Note: If your Accounts Payable keeps growing even though suppliers are paid, this is almost always the cause.

4. Part-payments and batches

Example: Three bills of $200, $350 and $150 are due. You pay $400 to the first two suppliers: tick both, pay $200 in full and $200 of the $350, leaving $150 open on that bill. QuickBooks records one bank payment per supplier.

Summary

  • Bills must be settled through Pay Bills so the payable clears.
  • Paying a bill with a separate cheque or expense double-counts the cost.
  • Several bills can be paid at once, and part-payments leave the remainder open.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Pay BillsThe form that settles recorded bills.
Part-paymentPaying less than the full bill amount.
Payable ageingHow long amounts owed to suppliers have been outstanding.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why must you use Pay Bills rather than writing a separate cheque?

  1. Otherwise the payable stays open and the cost is recorded twice
  2. Cheques are not allowed
  3. It is faster only
  4. Tax requires it
Show answer

Answer: A. Only Pay Bills links the payment to the bill and clears the payable.

Accounts Payable keeps growing although suppliers are paid. Likely cause?

  1. Bills are being paid outside Pay Bills
  2. The bank is wrong
  3. Too many vendors
  4. Sales are too low
Show answer

Answer: A. Unlinked payments leave the original bills permanently open.

Can one Pay Bills transaction settle several bills?

  1. Yes, tick each bill to include
  2. No, one at a time only
  3. Only at month end
  4. Only for one vendor per year
Show answer

Answer: A. Batch payment is a normal and efficient use of the form.

A $350 bill is paid $200. What remains?

  1. $150 stays open on that bill
  2. The bill closes
  3. A new bill is created
  4. Nothing
Show answer

Answer: A. Part-payment reduces the balance and leaves the remainder outstanding.

Short answer

What are the two symptoms of paying bills the wrong way?

Model answer

Accounts Payable grows despite payments being made, and expenses are overstated because the cost was recorded twice.

Describe how to part-pay a bill.

Model answer

In Pay Bills, tick the bill and change the payment amount to the sum actually paid; the balance remains open on that bill.

Class Activity

  1. Pay three bills in one transaction in a sample company.
  2. Check a sample file's Accounts Payable for bills that look wrongly settled.

Assignment

Settle a set of at least six bills including one part-payment, then produce the Accounts Payable ageing and explain every remaining balance.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 6.4 Recording Expenses
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 6: Vendors, Bills and Expenses

LESSON NOTE: RECORDING EXPENSES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingRecording ExpensesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Record an expense paid immediately
  • Choose the right account and payment method
  • Split one payment across several accounts

1. Introduction

An expense records money already gone: cash, card or instant transfer. It is the fastest form in QuickBooks and the one most often coded carelessly.

2. The form

  1. + New → Expense.
  2. Choose the payee and the account the money came from.
  3. Enter the date and reference.
  4. Code the category — the expense account.
  5. Split across several lines if the payment covers different things.
  6. Attach the receipt.

3. Splitting a payment

Example: A $250 payment at a supermarket covers $180 of stock for resale and $70 of cleaning materials. Enter two lines: Cost of Goods Sold $180 and Cleaning $70. Coding all $250 to one account would distort gross profit.

4. Attaching receipts

Note: Attach a photo of the receipt to the expense. It costs seconds, satisfies auditors and tax inspectors, and means the paper copy fading in a drawer no longer matters. This single habit separates records that survive an audit from records that do not.

Summary

  • An expense records money already paid and credits the bank or card directly.
  • Split a payment across accounts when it covers different kinds of cost.
  • Attaching the receipt to the transaction is the habit that makes records audit-proof.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
ExpenseA record of money already spent.
SplitCoding one payment across several accounts.
AttachmentA document stored against a transaction.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

A $250 payment covers stock and cleaning materials. What should you do?

  1. Split it across two accounts on separate lines
  2. Code it all to one account
  3. Record two separate payments
  4. Ignore the smaller part
Show answer

Answer: A. Splitting keeps gross profit and expense reporting accurate.

What does an expense credit?

  1. The bank or card account the money left
  2. Accounts Payable
  3. Sales
  4. Equity
Show answer

Answer: A. Money has already gone, so the funding account is credited directly.

Why attach receipts to expenses?

  1. It satisfies auditors and tax inspectors and survives lost paper
  2. It reduces the amount
  3. It changes the account
  4. It is required to save the form
Show answer

Answer: A. A stored image is durable evidence tied to the transaction.

When is an expense the wrong form to use?

  1. When the purchase will be paid later — that needs a bill
  2. When paying by card
  3. When paying cash
  4. When the amount is small
Show answer

Answer: A. Deferred payment requires a bill so the payable is recorded.

Short answer

When would you split an expense across accounts?

Model answer

When a single payment covers genuinely different kinds of cost, such as stock for resale and cleaning materials.

Why is attaching receipts described as the habit that separates audit-proof records?

Model answer

Because the evidence is stored with the transaction permanently, rather than depending on paper that fades or is lost.

Class Activity

  1. Record four expenses in a sample file, one of them split across three accounts.
  2. Photograph three real receipts and describe how you would code each.

Assignment

Record fifteen expenses for an organisation, including at least two splits, attach a document to each, and list the accounts used with a justification for the splits.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 6.5 Writing Checks
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 6: Vendors, Bills and Expenses

LESSON NOTE: WRITING CHECKS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingWriting ChecksBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Write and record a cheque
  • Distinguish a cheque from a bill payment
  • Handle unpresented cheques

1. Introduction

Cheques remain common in West Africa and in NGO and church finance, where dual signatures are a control. QuickBooks records them like any payment, with one important timing difference.

2. Writing a cheque

  1. + New → Cheque.
  2. Choose the payee and the bank account.
  3. Enter the cheque number — this is what you will match at reconciliation.
  4. Code the category or, if it settles a bill, use Pay Bills instead.
  5. Print or handwrite, then save.
Note: If the payment settles a bill you already entered, use Pay Bills and choose Cheque as the method. Writing a separate cheque leaves the bill open.

3. Unpresented cheques

Unpresented cheque: A cheque you have written and recorded that the recipient has not yet cashed.

The money has left your records but not your bank. This is the normal and correct reason your QuickBooks balance is lower than the bank's.

Example: Bank statement $10,000; QuickBooks $9,400. Two cheques totalling $600 are uncashed. Nothing is wrong — reconciliation will show them as outstanding.

4. Control over cheques

Record cheques in strict number order and account for spoiled ones. A missing cheque number in the records is a serious control gap; mark voided cheques as void rather than deleting them.

Summary

  • Record cheques with their number, which is the key to reconciliation.
  • If a cheque settles an existing bill, pay it through Pay Bills.
  • Unpresented cheques legitimately explain a lower QuickBooks balance than the bank's.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Cheque numberThe sequential number identifying a cheque.
Unpresented chequeA written cheque not yet cashed by the recipient.
VoidMarking a cheque cancelled while keeping its number in the records.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

A cheque settles a bill already entered. What should you use?

  1. Pay Bills with Cheque as the payment method
  2. A separate cheque form
  3. An expense
  4. A deposit
Show answer

Answer: A. Otherwise the bill remains open and the cost is doubled.

What is an unpresented cheque?

  1. One written and recorded but not yet cashed by the recipient
  2. One never written
  3. A cancelled cheque
  4. A cheque received from a customer
Show answer

Answer: A. It has left your records but not the bank.

Why should a spoiled cheque be voided rather than deleted?

  1. The number stays accounted for, closing a control gap
  2. Deleting is impossible
  3. It refunds the money
  4. It changes the bank balance
Show answer

Answer: A. A missing number in a sequence looks like a concealed payment.

Bank shows $10,000 and QuickBooks shows $9,400 with $600 of uncashed cheques. What is wrong?

  1. Nothing; this is the expected effect of unpresented cheques
  2. The bank has stolen money
  3. A cheque was recorded twice
  4. Sales are missing
Show answer

Answer: A. Timing differences of this kind are exactly what reconciliation resolves.

Short answer

Why is the cheque number important?

Model answer

It is the reference used to match the payment to the bank statement during reconciliation, and it evidences an unbroken sequence.

Explain why unpresented cheques make the QuickBooks balance lower than the bank's.

Model answer

The payment is recorded when written, but the bank only reduces the balance when the recipient presents the cheque.

Class Activity

  1. Write three cheques in a sample company with sequential numbers.
  2. Explain how you would account for a spoiled cheque.

Assignment

Record a month of cheque payments in sequence, including one void, then reconcile and list which cheques remain unpresented and why.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 6.6 Purchase Orders
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 6: Vendors, Bills and Expenses

LESSON NOTE: PURCHASE ORDERS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingPurchase OrdersBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Raise a purchase order
  • Convert a purchase order into a bill
  • Explain why purchase orders are a control

1. Introduction

A purchase order (PO) is a formal instruction to a supplier: send these goods at this price. Like an estimate, it has no accounting effect until it becomes a bill.

2. No accounting effect

Raising a PO posts nothing. It creates a commitment record you can report on, but no expense and no payable exist until the goods arrive and a bill is entered.

3. Why POs are a control

ControlHow the PO delivers it
AuthorisationSpending is approved before it is committed, not after
Price agreementThe agreed price is documented before delivery
Three-way matchPO, delivery note and bill are compared before payment
Budget disciplineCommitments are visible before the money is spent
Note: Three-way matching — PO against goods received against supplier bill — is the standard defence against being overcharged or billed for goods never delivered.

4. Converting to a bill

  1. Turn POs on in Account and settings → Expenses.
  2. + New → Purchase order; send it to the supplier.
  3. When goods arrive, open the PO and choose Copy to bill.
  4. Adjust quantities if the delivery was partial; the PO stays partly open.
Example: A PO for 100 bags at $12 arrives as 80 bags. Copy to bill for 80 at $12 ($960). The PO remains open for the outstanding 20.

Summary

  • A purchase order commits to a purchase but posts no accounting entries.
  • POs deliver authorisation, agreed pricing, three-way matching and budget visibility.
  • Converting a PO to a bill is where the expense and payable are finally recorded.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Purchase orderA formal order to a supplier, with no accounting effect until billed.
Three-way matchComparing purchase order, goods received and supplier bill before paying.
Open POA purchase order not yet fully received and billed.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does raising a purchase order post to the accounts?

  1. Nothing until it is converted to a bill
  2. An expense
  3. A payable
  4. A bank payment
Show answer

Answer: A. A PO is a commitment record, not an accounting entry.

What is three-way matching?

  1. Comparing the purchase order, the goods received and the supplier bill before paying
  2. Paying three suppliers at once
  3. Matching three bank accounts
  4. Splitting a bill three ways
Show answer

Answer: A. It is the standard control against overcharging and phantom deliveries.

A PO for 100 units is delivered as 80. What happens?

  1. Bill the 80 received; the PO stays open for 20
  2. Bill all 100
  3. Cancel the PO
  4. Delete the PO
Show answer

Answer: A. Partial receipt bills what arrived and leaves the balance open.

Why is authorisation before commitment better than approval after?

  1. It prevents unapproved spending rather than merely detecting it
  2. It is faster
  3. It reduces the price
  4. It avoids tax
Show answer

Answer: A. Prevention is the point of the control.

Short answer

Name three controls a purchase order provides.

Model answer

Authorisation before commitment, documented agreed pricing, and three-way matching before payment.

Why does a PO have no accounting effect?

Model answer

Because nothing has yet been received or owed — it is only an instruction to supply.

Class Activity

  1. Raise a PO in a sample file and convert part of it to a bill.
  2. Describe how three-way matching would catch a supplier overcharge.

Assignment

Design a purchase-order procedure for an organisation: who raises, who approves, how goods received are checked, and how the three-way match is evidenced before payment.

lessons.title: 6.7 Vendor Credits
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 6: Vendors, Bills and Expenses

LESSON NOTE: VENDOR CREDITS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingVendor CreditsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Record a vendor credit
  • Apply a credit to a bill or payment
  • Distinguish a credit from a refund received

1. Introduction

When you return goods to a supplier or are overcharged, they owe you. A vendor credit records that, and it is the purchases mirror of a customer credit memo.

2. Credit vs refund received

Vendor creditRefund received
What happensReduces what you owe the supplierSupplier sends money back
Cash moves?NoYes
Use whenYou still owe them, or will buy againYou have already paid and they repay you
PostsDebit Accounts Payable, Credit the expenseDebit Bank, Credit the expense

3. Applying a credit

  1. + New → Vendor credit.
  2. Choose the vendor and enter the returned items or the overcharge.
  3. Code to the same expense account as the original bill.
  4. Save, then apply it in Pay Bills by ticking both the bill and the credit.
Example: You owe a supplier $900 and return $150 of damaged goods. Record a $150 vendor credit and apply it; the next payment is $750. The original bill and the return both remain visible.

4. Coding it correctly

Note: Always code the credit to the same account as the original purchase. Coding it to a generic income account overstates both expenses and income and misstates gross profit.

Summary

  • A vendor credit reduces what you owe; a refund received brings money back.
  • Credits must be applied against bills in Pay Bills to take effect.
  • Code the credit to the same account as the original purchase.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Vendor creditA reduction in what you owe a supplier.
Refund receivedMoney returned to you by a supplier.
Applying a creditOffsetting a credit against an outstanding bill.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

You return goods but have not yet paid the supplier. Which record?

  1. Vendor credit
  2. Refund received
  3. Expense
  4. Purchase order
Show answer

Answer: A. Nothing has been paid, so the credit reduces what you owe.

Where should a vendor credit be coded?

  1. To the same expense account as the original purchase
  2. To sales income
  3. To equity
  4. To Accounts Receivable
Show answer

Answer: A. Matching the original account keeps expense reporting correct.

What happens if a vendor credit is never applied?

  1. You keep owing the full bill amount despite the credit
  2. It is refunded automatically
  3. The bill is deleted
  4. Tax is reduced
Show answer

Answer: A. An unapplied credit does not reduce any particular bill.

You owe $900 and record a $150 credit. What should the next payment be?

  1. $750
  2. $900
  3. $1,050
  4. $150
Show answer

Answer: A. Applying the credit reduces the amount payable to $750.

Short answer

State the accounting difference between a vendor credit and a refund received.

Model answer

A vendor credit debits Accounts Payable and credits the expense with no cash movement; a refund received debits Bank and credits the expense.

Why does coding a credit to income distort the accounts?

Model answer

It leaves expenses overstated and invents income that never existed, so gross profit and margins are both wrong.

Class Activity

  1. Record and apply a vendor credit in a sample file.
  2. Decide the correct record for four supplier-return scenarios.

Assignment

Handle three supplier return or overcharge situations end to end, showing the record used, the account coded, the journal entry, and the effect on the amount payable.

lessons.title: 6.8 Accounts Payable Ageing
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 6: Vendors, Bills and Expenses

LESSON NOTE: ACCOUNTS PAYABLE AGEING

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingAccounts Payable AgeingBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Run and read the payables ageing report
  • Use it to plan payments
  • Protect supplier relationships and cash at once

1. Introduction

Payables ageing is receivables ageing in reverse: it shows who you owe, how much, and how late you are. It is the foundation of paying suppliers deliberately rather than reactively.

2. Reading it

BandMeaningTypical action
CurrentNot yet dueSchedule for its due date
1–30Slightly latePay promptly; a relationship risk is starting
31–60LateContact the supplier before they contact you
61–90Seriously lateSupply may be stopped; negotiate a plan
90+CriticalExpect legal or credit consequences

3. Using it to plan

  1. Run payables ageing alongside the bank balance and expected receipts.
  2. Pay anything where a discount for early settlement exceeds the cost of paying early.
  3. Pay critical suppliers — those who could stop supply — before non-critical ones.
  4. Where cash is short, contact the supplier before the due date, not after.
Example: Cash available $5,000; payables due $8,000. Pay the two suppliers who could halt operations, then call the third to agree a two-week extension. Silence turns a cash-flow problem into a relationship problem.

4. The honesty check

Note: A payables report is only true if every bill has been entered. An organisation that enters bills only when paying them will always see an empty payables report and believe it owes nothing.

Summary

  • Payables ageing shows who you owe, how much and how late.
  • Use it with the bank balance to plan which suppliers to pay first.
  • The report is only meaningful if every bill has actually been entered.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Payables ageingA report grouping amounts owed to suppliers by how overdue they are.
Critical supplierOne whose withdrawal would halt operations.
Early settlement discountA reduction for paying before the due date.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

An empty payables ageing report in a busy organisation most likely means:

  1. Bills are not being entered until they are paid
  2. No money is owed
  3. The report is broken
  4. Suppliers are generous
Show answer

Answer: A. If bills are only entered at payment, obligations never appear.

Which supplier should be paid first when cash is short?

  1. One who could stop supply and halt operations
  2. The one owed least
  3. The newest supplier
  4. The one who complains least
Show answer

Answer: A. Protecting operations comes first when funds are limited.

What should you do if you cannot pay a supplier on time?

  1. Contact them before the due date to agree a plan
  2. Say nothing and hope
  3. Delete the bill
  4. Pay a different supplier twice
Show answer

Answer: A. Early communication preserves the relationship and credit terms.

What makes an early settlement discount worth taking?

  1. When the discount exceeds the cost of paying early
  2. Always
  3. Never
  4. Only at year end
Show answer

Answer: A. It is a straightforward comparison of discount against the value of holding cash.

Short answer

List the payables ageing bands and one action for each.

Model answer

Current — schedule; 1–30 — pay promptly; 31–60 — contact the supplier; 61–90 — negotiate a plan; 90+ — expect legal or credit consequences.

Why is communicating before the due date better than after?

Model answer

It preserves trust and credit terms, and turns a payment delay into an agreed arrangement rather than a default.

Class Activity

  1. Run a payables ageing report in a sample file and draft a payment plan for the next two weeks.
  2. Rank five suppliers by how critical they are to operations.

Assignment

Produce a payment plan from a payables ageing report and a limited bank balance. Justify the order of payment and draft the message you would send to any supplier you cannot pay in full.

lessons.title: 7.1 The Banking Centre
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 7: Banking and Reconciliation

LESSON NOTE: THE BANKING CENTRE

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingThe Banking CentreBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Navigate the banking screen
  • Explain the review queue
  • Distinguish the three tabs

1. Introduction

The Banking centre is where downloaded transactions arrive and wait for you to say what they are. Most day-to-day bookkeeping in a connected file happens on this one screen.

2. The three tabs

TabContainsYour job
For reviewNewly downloaded transactionsCategorise, match or exclude each one
CategorisedItems you have acceptedSpot-check for coding errors
ExcludedItems you told QuickBooks to ignoreReview occasionally; excluded items never reach the accounts

3. What the review queue is not

Note: Items sitting in For review are not yet in your accounts. A file with 400 unreviewed transactions has reports that are simply wrong, however healthy the dashboard looks.

4. A good routine

  1. Open Banking two or three times a week, not once a month.
  2. Work oldest first so nothing ages.
  3. Deal with every item: categorise, match, or exclude with a reason.
  4. Aim to end each session with For review empty.
Example: Ten minutes twice a week keeps a small organisation's file continuously accurate. One four-hour session a month produces the same total work but a month of unreliable reports.

Summary

  • Banking has three tabs: For review, Categorised and Excluded.
  • Transactions in For review are not yet in the accounts.
  • Frequent short sessions keep reports reliable; monthly batches do not.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
For reviewThe queue of downloaded transactions awaiting a decision.
ExcludedTransactions deliberately kept out of the accounts.
CategorisedTransactions already accepted into the accounts.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Are transactions in the For review tab already in your accounts?

  1. No, they have no effect until accepted
  2. Yes, immediately on download
  3. Only if over a set amount
  4. Only at month end
Show answer

Answer: A. They are proposals until you categorise or match them.

What does a file with 400 unreviewed transactions imply?

  1. Its reports are currently unreliable
  2. It is well maintained
  3. Its bank balance is wrong at the bank
  4. Nothing
Show answer

Answer: A. Unreviewed activity is missing from the accounts, so reports understate reality.

Why review the Excluded tab occasionally?

  1. Excluded items never reach the accounts, so a wrongly excluded item is silently lost
  2. It deletes them
  3. It increases income
  4. Exclusion is temporary
Show answer

Answer: A. An accidental exclusion permanently hides a real transaction.

What is the recommended banking routine?

  1. Short sessions two or three times a week, oldest first
  2. One long session per year
  3. Only at year end
  4. Only when the bank calls
Show answer

Answer: A. Frequent short reviews keep the file continuously accurate.

Short answer

Name the three banking tabs and what each holds.

Model answer

For review — new downloads awaiting a decision; Categorised — accepted items; Excluded — items deliberately kept out of the accounts.

Why is a monthly batch review worse than twice-weekly reviews for the same total effort?

Model answer

The work is identical, but reports are unreliable for most of the month, so decisions are made on wrong numbers.

Class Activity

  1. Open Banking in a sample file and count the items in each tab.
  2. Write the weekly banking routine you would give a junior bookkeeper.

Assignment

Clear a review queue in a sample company, recording how many items you categorised, matched and excluded, and justify each exclusion.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 7.2 Bank Feeds and Downloaded Transactions
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 7: Banking and Reconciliation

LESSON NOTE: BANK FEEDS AND DOWNLOADED TRANSACTIONS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingBank Feeds and Downloaded TransactionsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Explain how a bank feed works
  • Refresh and troubleshoot a feed
  • Handle duplicate downloads

1. Introduction

A bank feed is a one-way, read-only stream of transactions from the bank into QuickBooks. Understanding what it can and cannot do prevents most banking confusion.

2. What the feed carries

The feed sendsThe feed does not send
Date, description, amountWhich account the item belongs to
Whether money went in or outThe invoice or bill it relates to
A running bank balanceAny supporting document

The feed provides facts. Every piece of meaning — the category, the match, the purpose — is added by you.

3. Refreshing and troubleshooting

  1. Use Update to pull the latest transactions manually.
  2. If a feed stops, the usual cause is a changed online-banking password or an expired consent — reconnect the account.
  3. If transactions are missing, check the date range and whether they were excluded.
  4. If the feed is unavailable, upload a CSV; the workflow is identical from then on.

4. Duplicates

Note: Duplicates usually arise from uploading a CSV that overlaps a live feed, or reconnecting an account and pulling history again. Always check the date of the last transaction you have before uploading anything, and exclude rather than delete when unsure.

Summary

  • The feed supplies date, description and amount; you supply category and meaning.
  • Feeds break most often because of changed banking credentials or expired consent.
  • Duplicates come from overlapping CSV uploads or re-pulled history.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Bank feedA read-only download of transactions from the bank.
ConsentPermission given to the bank to share data, which expires periodically.
DuplicateThe same bank transaction recorded twice.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does a bank feed NOT provide?

  1. The account a transaction should be categorised to
  2. The date
  3. The amount
  4. The description
Show answer

Answer: A. Categorisation is the user's judgement, not data the bank supplies.

A feed suddenly stops updating. Most likely cause?

  1. A changed online banking password or expired consent
  2. The bank closed
  3. QuickBooks deleted the account
  4. Too many transactions
Show answer

Answer: A. Feeds rely on credentials and consent that periodically expire.

What most commonly creates duplicate transactions?

  1. Uploading a CSV that overlaps the live feed
  2. Categorising twice
  3. Running reports
  4. Adding a vendor
Show answer

Answer: A. Overlapping date ranges import the same items again.

Why is the feed described as read-only?

  1. It can download data but cannot move money
  2. It can only be read once
  3. It cannot be refreshed
  4. It shows only balances
Show answer

Answer: A. The connection has no payment authority.

Short answer

What three pieces of information does a bank feed provide?

Model answer

The date, the description and the amount, plus the direction of the money and a running balance.

How would you avoid creating duplicates when uploading a statement?

Model answer

Check the date of the most recent transaction already in QuickBooks and upload only the period after it.

Class Activity

  1. Refresh a bank feed in a sample company and note how many new items arrive.
  2. Write a short troubleshooting checklist for a feed that has stopped.

Assignment

Document the bank feed for an organisation: how often it is refreshed, who checks it, what to do if it breaks, and how duplicates are prevented and detected.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 7.3 Categorizing Bank Transactions
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 7: Banking and Reconciliation

LESSON NOTE: CATEGORIZING BANK TRANSACTIONS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCategorizing Bank TransactionsBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Categorise a downloaded transaction
  • Split a transaction across accounts
  • Handle transactions you do not recognise

1. Introduction

Categorising is the core daily skill. Each downloaded line must be told what it is, and that single decision determines every report the organisation will read.

2. The decision for each line

SituationAction
It matches an invoice or bill already recordedMatch — never categorise, or you double-count
It is a new cost or income not yet recordedCategorise to the correct account
It is a transfer between your own accountsRecord as Transfer, not income or expense
It is personal or already recorded elsewhereExclude
Note: Match before you categorise. Categorising a customer payment that already has an invoice records the income twice and leaves the invoice open.

3. Splitting

Example: A $400 card payment covers $250 of stock and $150 of fuel. Use Split, enter both lines, and the single bank line is coded to two accounts.

4. Unknown transactions

Never guess. Guessing puts a wrong number into a report that someone will rely on. Instead:

  1. Check the reference against receipts and invoices.
  2. Ask whoever made the payment.
  3. If still unknown, code to 'Ask My Accountant' and review it within the month.

5. Transfers

Moving money from current to savings is not income or expense — nothing has been earned or spent. Coding transfers as income is a common error that inflates revenue, sometimes dramatically for organisations that move money often.

Summary

  • Match first, categorise second, to avoid double-counting.
  • Transfers between your own accounts are never income or expense.
  • Never guess an unknown item; park it in Ask My Accountant and resolve it.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
MatchLinking a downloaded item to a transaction already recorded.
SplitCoding one bank line to several accounts.
TransferMoving money between accounts you own.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

A downloaded receipt matches an invoice you already raised. What should you do?

  1. Match it, not categorise it
  2. Categorise it to sales
  3. Exclude it
  4. Delete the invoice
Show answer

Answer: A. Categorising would record the income a second time.

How should a transfer from current to savings be recorded?

  1. As a Transfer
  2. As income
  3. As an expense
  4. As a customer payment
Show answer

Answer: A. No income or expense arises from moving your own money.

You cannot identify a transaction. What is the correct action?

  1. Code it to Ask My Accountant and resolve it within the month
  2. Guess the most likely account
  3. Delete it
  4. Exclude it permanently
Show answer

Answer: A. Guessing puts a wrong figure into reports people rely on.

A $400 payment covers stock and fuel. What feature do you use?

  1. Split
  2. Exclude
  3. Transfer
  4. Match
Show answer

Answer: A. Split codes one bank line across several accounts.

Short answer

State the four possible actions for a downloaded transaction.

Model answer

Match it to an existing record, categorise it as new activity, record it as a transfer, or exclude it.

Why does coding transfers as income distort reports?

Model answer

It invents revenue that was never earned, inflating income every time money is moved between your own accounts.

Class Activity

  1. Categorise fifteen transactions in a sample file, including one split and one transfer.
  2. List five transaction descriptions you would find ambiguous and say how you would resolve each.

Assignment

Clear a bank review queue of at least twenty items. Record how many you matched, categorised, transferred and excluded, and explain your treatment of any you could not identify immediately.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 7.4 Bank Rules for Automation
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 7: Banking and Reconciliation

LESSON NOTE: BANK RULES FOR AUTOMATION

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingBank Rules for AutomationBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create a bank rule
  • Decide which transactions deserve a rule
  • Avoid rules that hide errors

1. Introduction

A bank rule tells QuickBooks: whenever a transaction looks like this, code it like that. Rules turn repetitive categorising into a glance.

2. Building a rule

  1. Banking → Rules → New rule.
  2. Name it clearly, e.g. 'Fuel – Total station'.
  3. Set conditions: description contains, amount, or bank account.
  4. Set the action: payee, category, and optionally a class.
  5. Choose whether to auto-add or leave for review.

3. Auto-add or review

SettingBehaviourUse for
Leave for reviewPre-fills the coding; you still confirmMost rules, especially early on
Auto-addPosts straight into the accounts unseenOnly fixed, certain, repeating items
Note: Auto-add is where rules become dangerous. An auto-add rule that is slightly wrong will silently mis-code every future transaction, and nobody looks because nobody sees it.

4. Good rule design

  • Make conditions specific — a rule matching 'PAY' will match far too much.
  • One rule per real pattern; resist a single rule with many conditions.
  • Review rules quarterly, because supplier names and bank descriptions change.
  • Never write a rule for something you do not fully understand.
Example: Rule: description contains 'TOTAL FILLING' AND account is the business card → payee Total, category Motor Fuel, leave for review. Specific, safe and saves a decision every week.

Summary

  • Rules pre-code recurring transactions based on conditions you define.
  • Prefer 'leave for review' over 'auto-add' unless the pattern is completely certain.
  • Keep conditions specific and review rules quarterly.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Bank ruleAn automation that codes transactions matching set conditions.
Auto-addA rule setting that posts matching transactions without review.
ConditionThe test a transaction must meet for a rule to apply.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why is auto-add risky?

  1. A slightly wrong rule silently mis-codes every future matching transaction
  2. It slows the software
  3. It deletes transactions
  4. It cannot be undone
Show answer

Answer: A. Nobody reviews what they never see, so the error persists invisibly.

What makes a good rule condition?

  1. Specific text that only the intended transactions contain
  2. A single common word
  3. No conditions at all
  4. The amount only
Show answer

Answer: A. Broad conditions capture unintended transactions.

How often should rules be reviewed?

  1. Quarterly, because bank descriptions and suppliers change
  2. Never
  3. Every ten years
  4. Only when the bank changes
Show answer

Answer: A. Descriptions drift, so rules silently stop matching or start over-matching.

What is the safest default for a new rule?

  1. Leave for review so you confirm the coding
  2. Auto-add immediately
  3. Delete after one use
  4. Apply to all past transactions
Show answer

Answer: A. Reviewing lets you verify the rule behaves as intended.

Short answer

Give an example of a well-designed bank rule.

Model answer

Description contains 'TOTAL FILLING' and the account is the business card, coding to payee Total and category Motor Fuel, left for review.

Why should you never write a rule for a transaction you do not understand?

Model answer

The rule will repeat your misunderstanding automatically on every future occurrence, multiplying a single error indefinitely.

Class Activity

  1. Create two bank rules in a sample file, one auto-add and one review.
  2. Identify five recurring transactions in an organisation that deserve rules.

Assignment

Design a set of at least six bank rules for an organisation. For each state the conditions, the action, whether it auto-adds, and why that choice is safe.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 7.5 Matching Transactions
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 7: Banking and Reconciliation

LESSON NOTE: MATCHING TRANSACTIONS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingMatching TransactionsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Match a downloaded transaction to an existing record
  • Resolve a match QuickBooks suggests wrongly
  • Match one deposit to several payments

1. Introduction

Matching links a bank line to something you already recorded. It is the step that keeps the bank feed and your records as one set of books rather than two.

2. When to match

If a downloaded item corresponds to an invoice payment, a bill payment, a recorded expense or a deposit already in QuickBooks, it must be matched, never categorised.

3. Multi-item matches

Example: The bank shows one deposit of $1,000. QuickBooks holds five $200 customer payments in Undeposited Funds. Choose Find match, tick all five, and the totals agree — one bank line, five payments, correctly linked.

4. When the suggestion is wrong

SymptomCauseFix
Suggested match is a different invoice of the same amountTwo invoices share an amountOpen Find match and pick the right one
No match offeredThe transaction was never recordedCategorise it, or record the missing invoice first
Amount differs slightlyA bank fee was deductedMatch and add a fee line for the difference
Note: Never accept a suggested match without reading it. QuickBooks matches on amount and date, so two invoices for the same value are easily confused, and the wrong customer's invoice gets closed.

5. Fees inside a match

Where the bank credited $995 against a $1,000 payment, use Resolve difference and code the $5 to Bank Charges. The match then balances without editing the customer's payment.

Summary

  • Match anything already recorded; categorise only genuinely new activity.
  • One bank line can match several payments, as with a grouped deposit.
  • Always read a suggested match — equal amounts are easily confused.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
MatchLinking a bank line to an existing QuickBooks transaction.
Find matchThe tool for choosing which records a bank line corresponds to.
Resolve differenceAdding a line, such as a fee, so a match balances.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

A downloaded item corresponds to a bill payment you already recorded. What do you do?

  1. Match it
  2. Categorise it as an expense
  3. Exclude it
  4. Delete the bill
Show answer

Answer: A. Categorising would record the cost a second time.

The bank shows $1,000 but you hold five $200 payments. How do you handle it?

  1. Use Find match and tick all five payments
  2. Categorise it as sales
  3. Record a new deposit
  4. Exclude it
Show answer

Answer: A. One bank line can match several underlying payments.

Why must a suggested match be read before accepting?

  1. Equal amounts on different invoices are easily confused, closing the wrong one
  2. Suggestions are always wrong
  3. It is legally required
  4. It speeds up the software
Show answer

Answer: A. QuickBooks matches on amount and date, which is not unique.

The bank credited $995 against a $1,000 payment. Best action?

  1. Match and code the $5 difference to bank charges
  2. Edit the customer payment to $995
  3. Exclude the item
  4. Record a $5 sale
Show answer

Answer: A. Resolving the difference keeps the customer's payment intact and explains the shortfall.

Short answer

What is the difference between matching and categorising?

Model answer

Matching links a bank line to a transaction already recorded; categorising creates a new accounting entry for activity not yet recorded.

How do you handle a bank fee deducted from a customer payment?

Model answer

Match the payment and use Resolve difference to add the fee as a bank-charges line so the match balances.

Class Activity

  1. Match five transactions in a sample file, including one grouped deposit.
  2. Find a wrongly suggested match and explain how you would identify it.

Assignment

Work through a bank feed of at least fifteen items, matching everything that should be matched. Report any suggested matches you rejected and why.

lessons.title: 7.6 Bank Reconciliation Step by Step
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 7: Banking and Reconciliation

LESSON NOTE: BANK RECONCILIATION STEP BY STEP

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingBank Reconciliation Step by StepBeginner to Advanced45 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Reconcile a bank account
  • Explain what reconciliation proves
  • Complete a reconciliation that balances

1. Introduction

Reconciliation compares your records against the bank's and proves they agree. Until an account is reconciled, its balance is a claim; afterwards it is verified.

2. What it proves

A completed reconciliation says three things: every transaction the bank processed is in your books, everything in your books that should have reached the bank has, and any difference is explained by timing.

3. The steps

  1. Banking → Reconcile; choose the account.
  2. Enter the statement's ending balance and ending date exactly as printed.
  3. Tick every transaction that appears on the statement.
  4. Watch the Difference figure; it must reach zero.
  5. Finish now, and save the reconciliation report.

4. Reading the difference

DifferenceLikely cause
Equals one transaction's valueThat transaction is missing or ticked in error
Twice a transaction's valueSomething is recorded twice, or a sign is reversed
Small and oddA fee, interest or a typing error in an amount
Matches an old uncleared itemA stale cheque or deposit never cleared
Example: Difference of $45.00 exactly equals a bank charge on the statement that was never recorded. Add it as an expense and the difference goes to zero.

5. Discipline

Note: Never force a reconciliation to balance with an unexplained adjustment. That converts a findable error into a permanent one and destroys the value of every future reconciliation of the account.

Summary

  • Reconciliation proves your records and the bank agree, with differences explained by timing.
  • Enter the statement ending balance and date exactly, then tick until the difference is zero.
  • Never force a balance with an unexplained adjustment.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
ReconciliationComparing recorded transactions against a bank statement.
Ending balanceThe closing balance printed on the statement.
DifferenceThe unexplained gap between records and statement.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What must the Difference figure be before finishing?

  1. Zero
  2. Any small number
  3. Under $10
  4. Equal to the bank charges
Show answer

Answer: A. A zero difference is what proves the account agrees.

The difference exactly equals one transaction's amount. Likely cause?

  1. That transaction is missing from your records or was ticked in error
  2. The bank is wrong
  3. Reconciliation is impossible
  4. Too many transactions
Show answer

Answer: A. A difference equal to a single item points straight at that item.

Why is forcing a balance with an unexplained adjustment harmful?

  1. It converts a findable error into a permanent one and devalues future reconciliations
  2. It is slower
  3. It deletes transactions
  4. It has no effect
Show answer

Answer: A. The error is buried rather than fixed, and the account can never be trusted again.

What does a completed reconciliation prove?

  1. Records and bank agree, with any gap explained by timing
  2. That profit is correct
  3. That tax is paid
  4. That customers have paid
Show answer

Answer: A. It verifies completeness and accuracy of the bank account only.

Short answer

List the five steps of a reconciliation.

Model answer

Choose the account; enter the statement ending balance and date; tick items on the statement; drive the difference to zero; finish and save the report.

What does a difference of exactly twice a transaction's value suggest?

Model answer

That the transaction has been recorded twice, or that its sign or direction has been reversed.

Class Activity

  1. Reconcile one month in a sample company and save the report.
  2. Given a difference equal to a known bank charge, describe the fix.

Assignment

Reconcile a full month for an organisation from a supplied statement. Submit the reconciliation report and a note listing every difference you investigated and how you resolved it.

lessons.title: 7.7 Fixing Reconciliation Discrepancies
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 7: Banking and Reconciliation

LESSON NOTE: FIXING RECONCILIATION DISCREPANCIES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingFixing Reconciliation DiscrepanciesBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Diagnose why a reconciliation will not balance
  • Use the discrepancy report
  • Correct errors without breaking past reconciliations

1. Introduction

Sooner or later a reconciliation refuses to balance, or a previously reconciled month changes. Both have systematic causes and systematic fixes.

2. Why a previously reconciled month changes

Someone edited, deleted or re-dated a transaction that had already been reconciled. QuickBooks allows this unless a closing date prevents it, and the beginning balance of the next reconciliation then no longer matches.

Note: This is why a closing date matters. Lock each month once it is reconciled and this class of problem disappears.

3. The tools

ToolWhat it shows
Reconciliation Discrepancy reportTransactions changed since they were reconciled
Previous reconciliation reportWhat the account looked like when it last balanced
Audit logWho changed what, and when

4. A systematic approach

  1. Check the beginning balance. If it is wrong, the problem is in a past period, not this one.
  2. Run the Reconciliation Discrepancy report and reverse any unauthorised change.
  3. Compare the count of transactions on the statement with the number ticked.
  4. Look for a difference equal to one item, twice an item, or a transposition (a difference divisible by 9).
  5. Only when the cause is found, correct it — then set a closing date.
Example: A difference of $270 is divisible by 9, suggesting a transposition: $1,530 was entered as $1,260. Finding the item confirms it.

Summary

  • A changed beginning balance means someone altered a previously reconciled transaction.
  • The Reconciliation Discrepancy report and audit log identify what changed and who changed it.
  • A difference divisible by 9 suggests transposed digits.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Discrepancy reportA report listing transactions altered after reconciliation.
Beginning balanceThe opening figure carried from the last reconciliation.
TranspositionDigits entered in the wrong order, such as 1,530 as 1,260.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

The beginning balance is wrong. Where is the problem?

  1. In a previously reconciled period, not the current one
  2. In the current month only
  3. At the bank
  4. In the customer list
Show answer

Answer: A. A wrong opening figure means past reconciled data has changed.

A difference is divisible by 9. What does this suggest?

  1. Transposed digits in an amount
  2. A missing bank charge
  3. A duplicate deposit
  4. Nothing
Show answer

Answer: A. Differences from transposition are always divisible by nine.

Which tool shows who changed a transaction and when?

  1. The audit log
  2. The Profit and Loss
  3. The customer list
  4. The dashboard
Show answer

Answer: A. The audit log records user actions with timestamps.

What prevents previously reconciled months from changing?

  1. Setting a closing date
  2. Deleting old transactions
  3. Turning off the bank feed
  4. Running more reports
Show answer

Answer: A. A closing date locks the period against edits.

Short answer

Give three systematic checks when a reconciliation will not balance.

Model answer

Verify the beginning balance; run the discrepancy report; test whether the difference equals one item, twice an item, or is divisible by 9.

Why does a closing date reduce reconciliation problems?

Model answer

It stops anyone editing transactions in periods already reconciled, so the beginning balance stays fixed.

Class Activity

  1. Given a difference of $180 (divisible by 9), describe how you would search for the error.
  2. Run an audit log in a sample company and identify one edited transaction.

Assignment

Investigate an unbalanced reconciliation. Document each check you performed, the cause you found, the correction you made, and the control you would put in place to stop it recurring.

lessons.title: 7.8 Handling Bank Errors and Adjustments
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 7: Banking and Reconciliation

LESSON NOTE: HANDLING BANK ERRORS AND ADJUSTMENTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingHandling Bank Errors and AdjustmentsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Deal with a genuine bank error
  • Undo a reconciliation when necessary
  • Use adjustments responsibly

1. Introduction

Banks do make mistakes: a duplicated debit, a charge that should not apply, a payment credited to the wrong account. These need recording honestly and chasing separately.

2. Recording a bank error

The bank statement is the record of what the bank did, even when the bank is wrong. So record what actually happened, then record the correction when it arrives.

Example: The bank debits a $200 charge twice. Record both debits — they truly happened — and code the erroneous one to a receivable from the bank or to Bank Charges. When the bank refunds it, record the credit against the same account. Both events are then visible and the account reconciles at each stage.

3. Undoing a reconciliation

Sometimes a month must be reopened, for example when a whole batch was reconciled against the wrong statement. In QuickBooks Online an accountant user can undo a reconciliation; otherwise transactions can be un-ticked individually.

Note: Undoing is a last resort. Reconciling again is real work, and a reopened month can cascade into every later month. Exhaust the discrepancy report first.

4. Adjustments

AcceptableNot acceptable
Recording a real bank charge you had missedPlugging an unexplained gap
Recording interest the bank creditedForcing a balance to finish quickly
Correcting a known typing errorAdjusting because the cause was not found

An adjustment must always name a real event. If you cannot name it, you have not finished investigating.

Summary

  • Record what the bank actually did, then record the correction separately when it arrives.
  • Undoing a reconciliation is a last resort and can cascade into later months.
  • Every adjustment must name a real event; unexplained plugs are never acceptable.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Bank errorA mistake made by the bank on the account.
Undo reconciliationReopening a previously reconciled period.
AdjustmentAn entry made to correct a known, identified difference.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

The bank debits a charge twice in error. What should you record?

  1. Both debits, because both really happened, then the refund when it arrives
  2. Only one debit
  3. Nothing until it is refunded
  4. A sale
Show answer

Answer: A. The statement records reality; the correction is a separate later event.

When is an adjustment acceptable?

  1. When it records a real, identified event such as a missed bank charge
  2. Whenever the difference is small
  3. Whenever you are short of time
  4. Whenever the cause is unknown
Show answer

Answer: A. An adjustment must name the event it represents.

Why is undoing a reconciliation a last resort?

  1. It can cascade into every later month and means redoing real work
  2. It deletes the account
  3. It is impossible
  4. It changes the bank balance
Show answer

Answer: A. Reopening a period disturbs everything reconciled after it.

What should you do before making any adjustment?

  1. Investigate until the cause is identified
  2. Make it immediately
  3. Ask the bank to change the statement
  4. Delete the month
Show answer

Answer: A. An unexplained adjustment hides an error permanently.

Short answer

Explain why you record a bank error rather than ignoring it.

Model answer

Because the statement reflects what the bank actually did; recording it keeps the account reconcilable, and the correction is recorded separately when it arrives.

What distinguishes a legitimate adjustment from a plug?

Model answer

A legitimate adjustment names a real, identified event; a plug simply forces the numbers to agree without explanation.

Class Activity

  1. Describe how you would record and then clear a duplicated bank charge.
  2. List three situations that would justify undoing a reconciliation.

Assignment

Handle three banking problems: a duplicated charge, a payment credited to the wrong account, and an unexplained small difference. For each, state exactly what you would record and what you would refuse to record.
