lessons.title: 8.1 Setting Up Products and Services
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 8: Products, Services and Inventory

LESSON NOTE: SETTING UP PRODUCTS AND SERVICES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSetting Up Products and ServicesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create product and service items
  • Explain how items drive the accounts used
  • Choose between the four item types

1. Introduction

Items are what you put on an invoice. Each one carries the account it posts to, so items are how non-accountants code transactions correctly without thinking about accounts at all.

2. The four item types

TypeUse forTracks quantity?
ServiceLabour, consulting, rentNo
Non-inventoryGoods bought and sold without counting stockNo
InventoryGoods you count and valueYes
BundleA group of items sold togetherFollows components

3. Why items matter

An item links a name a salesperson understands to an account an accountant needs. 'Consulting – half day' means nothing to the ledger, but the item behind it posts to Consulting Income every time.

Example: Create 'Bag of cement' as an inventory item with income account Sales – Materials and expense account Cost of Goods Sold. Every future sale codes itself.

4. Setup fields

  • Name and SKU
  • Category, for grouping in reports
  • Sales price and description
  • Income account
  • Cost and expense/COGS account
  • Taxable or not
  • For inventory: quantity on hand, as-of date and reorder point

Summary

  • Items link everyday names to the correct accounts, so coding happens automatically.
  • Four types: service, non-inventory, inventory and bundle.
  • Only inventory items track quantity and value.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
ItemA product or service that can be placed on a sales form.
SKUA stock-keeping code identifying an item.
BundleA group of items sold as one line.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which item type tracks quantity on hand?

  1. Inventory
  2. Service
  3. Non-inventory
  4. Bundle
Show answer

Answer: A. Only inventory items maintain a counted quantity and value.

Why do items reduce coding errors?

  1. Each item carries the account it posts to, so users pick a familiar name rather than an account
  2. They are cheaper
  3. They calculate tax
  4. They speed up printing
Show answer

Answer: A. The accounting decision is made once, at item setup.

Which type suits consulting labour?

  1. Service
  2. Inventory
  3. Bundle
  4. Non-inventory
Show answer

Answer: A. Labour has no quantity of stock to track.

What does an inventory item need that a service does not?

  1. Quantity on hand, an as-of date and a cost account
  2. A name
  3. A sales price
  4. A description
Show answer

Answer: A. Stock tracking requires an opening quantity, date and cost.

Short answer

Name the four item types with one example each.

Model answer

Service — consulting; Non-inventory — a one-off part; Inventory — bags of cement; Bundle — a starter kit of several items.

Explain how items help a salesperson code correctly.

Model answer

They choose a familiar product name, and the item silently posts to the correct income and cost accounts.

Class Activity

  1. Create six items in a sample file, at least one of each type.
  2. List ten things an organisation you know sells and assign an item type to each.

Assignment

Build a product and service list of at least twelve items for an organisation, stating the type, income account and cost account for each.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 8.2 Inventory vs Non-Inventory Items
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 8: Products, Services and Inventory

LESSON NOTE: INVENTORY VS NON-INVENTORY ITEMS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingInventory vs Non-Inventory ItemsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Decide whether an item should be tracked as inventory
  • Explain the accounting difference
  • Avoid unnecessary inventory tracking

1. Introduction

Turning on inventory tracking for everything you sell is a common and expensive mistake. Inventory items demand counting, adjusting and valuing; non-inventory items do not.

2. The accounting difference

Inventory itemNon-inventory item
On purchaseDebit Inventory AssetDebit expense/COGS immediately
On saleDebit COGS, credit Inventory AssetNo further entry
Balance sheetShows a stock valueShows nothing
Requires stock countsYesNo

Inventory accounting delays the cost until the item is sold, which is more accurate. Non-inventory expenses it on purchase, which is simpler.

3. When to use inventory

  • You hold significant stock at period end
  • You need to know what stock is worth
  • You need reorder alerts
  • Stock loss or theft is a real risk
Note: If you buy goods that are sold within days and hold nothing at month end, non-inventory is usually the right answer. Tracking inventory you do not hold creates work with no reporting benefit.

4. Worked comparison

Example: A bakery buying flour used within the week: non-inventory, expensed on purchase. A hardware shop holding 400 bags of cement at month end: inventory, because that stock is a real asset that must appear on the balance sheet.

Summary

  • Inventory items capitalise cost until sale; non-inventory items expense it on purchase.
  • Use inventory when you hold meaningful stock at period end or need its value.
  • Tracking inventory you do not really hold creates work without benefit.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Inventory assetThe balance sheet value of stock held.
COGSCost of goods sold, the cost of items actually sold.
Reorder pointA stock level triggering a reminder to buy more.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

When is an item's cost recognised for an inventory item?

  1. When it is sold
  2. When it is bought
  3. At year end
  4. When it is counted
Show answer

Answer: A. Inventory capitalises the cost until the sale occurs.

A bakery buys flour used within days and holds none at month end. Best treatment?

  1. Non-inventory, expensed on purchase
  2. Inventory with monthly counts
  3. Bundle
  4. Service
Show answer

Answer: A. With no stock held at period end, inventory tracking adds work but no information.

What appears on the balance sheet for inventory items?

  1. The value of stock held
  2. Nothing
  3. The sales price
  4. The reorder point
Show answer

Answer: A. Unsold stock is an asset until it is sold.

What is the main cost of tracking inventory unnecessarily?

  1. Ongoing counting, adjusting and valuing work with no reporting benefit
  2. Higher tax
  3. Loss of customers
  4. Slower invoices
Show answer

Answer: A. Inventory tracking imposes a real administrative burden.

Short answer

State the accounting difference between inventory and non-inventory purchases.

Model answer

Inventory debits an asset until sale, then moves to COGS. Non-inventory debits the expense immediately on purchase.

Give two questions that decide whether to track something as inventory.

Model answer

Do we hold meaningful stock at period end, and do we need to know what that stock is worth?

Class Activity

  1. Classify twelve products as inventory or non-inventory with a reason for each.
  2. Explain the balance sheet effect of holding 400 bags of cement at month end.

Assignment

Review the product list of a trading organisation and decide, item by item, which should be inventory-tracked. Justify each decision and estimate the counting workload you have created.

lessons.title: 8.3 Tracking Inventory Quantities
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 8: Products, Services and Inventory

LESSON NOTE: TRACKING INVENTORY QUANTITIES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingTracking Inventory QuantitiesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Turn on inventory tracking
  • Record purchases and sales that move stock
  • Read quantity on hand and reorder points

1. Introduction

Once inventory tracking is on, QuickBooks maintains a running quantity for every inventory item, updated by every purchase and sale.

2. Turning it on

  1. Gear → Account and settings → Sales → Products and services.
  2. Switch on 'Track quantity and price/rate' and 'Track inventory quantity on hand'.
  3. Set opening quantity and as-of date on each inventory item.
Note: Inventory tracking requires the Plus plan or above, and once quantities exist the as-of date should not be changed casually.

3. What moves stock

TransactionEffect on quantity
Bill or expense for an inventory itemIncreases
Invoice or sales receiptDecreases
Vendor credit for returned goodsDecreases
Credit memo for customer returnIncreases
Inventory adjustmentIncreases or decreases to a counted figure

4. Reorder points

Set a reorder point on each item and QuickBooks flags it as low when quantity falls below. This turns stock management from memory into a report.

Example: Cement reorder point 50 bags. When stock falls to 48, the item is flagged low so it is reordered before it runs out and sales are lost.

Summary

  • Inventory tracking is switched on in Sales settings and needs the Plus plan.
  • Purchases increase quantity, sales decrease it, and adjustments correct it to a count.
  • Reorder points turn stock management into a report rather than a memory task.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Quantity on handThe number of units QuickBooks believes you hold.
Reorder pointThe level at which an item is flagged for reordering.
As-of dateThe date an opening inventory quantity applies from.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which transaction increases inventory quantity?

  1. A bill for inventory items purchased
  2. An invoice
  3. A sales receipt
  4. A customer payment
Show answer

Answer: A. Buying stock increases quantity on hand.

What does a reorder point do?

  1. Flags an item as low when quantity falls below it
  2. Orders stock automatically
  3. Sets the price
  4. Blocks sales
Show answer

Answer: A. It converts reordering from memory into a visible flag.

Which plan is needed for inventory quantity tracking?

  1. Plus or above
  2. Simple Start
  3. Essentials
  4. Any plan
Show answer

Answer: A. Inventory tracking is a Plus-tier feature.

A customer returns goods on a credit memo. What happens to quantity?

  1. It increases, because the goods came back
  2. It decreases
  3. Nothing
  4. It resets to zero
Show answer

Answer: A. Returned goods re-enter stock.

Short answer

List three transactions that decrease inventory quantity.

Model answer

An invoice, a sales receipt, and a vendor credit for goods returned to the supplier.

Why is a reorder point better than relying on memory?

Model answer

Because it produces a visible flag before stock runs out, preventing lost sales when nobody happens to notice.

Class Activity

  1. Turn on inventory tracking in a sample file and set reorder points for three items.
  2. Record a purchase and a sale and observe the quantity change.

Assignment

Set up inventory tracking for at least eight items with opening quantities and reorder points, then record a week of purchases and sales and produce the resulting stock position.

lessons.title: 8.4 Adjusting Inventory
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 8: Products, Services and Inventory

LESSON NOTE: ADJUSTING INVENTORY

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingAdjusting InventoryBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Perform an inventory adjustment
  • Explain why book and physical stock differ
  • Account for shrinkage honestly

1. Introduction

QuickBooks tells you what stock you should have. A physical count tells you what you do have. When they differ, the count wins and an adjustment records the truth.

2. Why differences arise

  • Theft or pilferage
  • Breakage and spoilage
  • Goods issued without being recorded
  • Receiving errors — short deliveries accepted as full
  • Data entry mistakes

3. Making the adjustment

  1. Count the stock physically and record it on a count sheet.
  2. + New → Inventory qty adjustment.
  3. Enter the counted quantity for each item that differs.
  4. Choose an adjustment account — normally Inventory Shrinkage or Cost of Goods Sold.
  5. Add a note explaining the reason and save the count sheet.
Example: Books show 120 bags; the count finds 114. Adjust to 114. Six bags at $8 cost = $48 charged to Inventory Shrinkage. Stock value falls by $48 and profit falls by $48.

4. Treating shrinkage honestly

Note: Do not bury shrinkage inside Cost of Goods Sold where nobody sees it. A separate Inventory Shrinkage account makes losses visible, and visible losses get investigated. Persistent shrinkage in one item or one location is a control finding, not an accounting one.

Summary

  • A physical count overrides the book quantity; the adjustment records the difference.
  • Differences arise from theft, breakage, unrecorded issues and receiving errors.
  • Post shrinkage to its own account so losses stay visible and get investigated.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
ShrinkageStock lost through theft, damage or error.
Inventory adjustmentAn entry aligning book quantity to a physical count.
Count sheetThe written record of a physical stock count.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Books show 120 units but a count finds 114. What should you do?

  1. Adjust the book quantity to 114 and record the loss
  2. Change the count to 120
  3. Ignore the difference
  4. Delete the item
Show answer

Answer: A. The physical count is the fact; the records must follow it.

Why post shrinkage to its own account?

  1. Losses stay visible and get investigated instead of hiding inside COGS
  2. It reduces tax
  3. It increases stock value
  4. It is required by the software
Show answer

Answer: A. Visibility is what turns a number into an action.

Which of these is NOT a normal cause of shrinkage?

  1. The bank charging a fee
  2. Theft
  3. Breakage
  4. Unrecorded issues
Show answer

Answer: A. Bank fees have nothing to do with stock quantities.

Six bags at $8 cost are lost. What is the profit effect?

  1. Profit falls by $48
  2. Profit rises by $48
  3. No effect
  4. Profit falls by $8
Show answer

Answer: A. The lost cost is charged to expense, reducing profit by $48.

Short answer

Why does the physical count override the book quantity?

Model answer

Because the count is direct evidence of what actually exists, while the book figure is only what the records predict.

What does persistent shrinkage in one item or location indicate?

Model answer

A control weakness such as theft or poor receiving discipline, which is a management issue rather than an accounting one.

Class Activity

  1. Perform an inventory adjustment in a sample file and check the profit effect.
  2. Design a simple stock count sheet for a shop.

Assignment

Carry out a full stock count for at least ten items, record the adjustments, calculate the total shrinkage value, and write a short note on the likely causes and the controls you would recommend.

lessons.title: 8.5 Inventory Valuation in QuickBooks
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 8: Products, Services and Inventory

LESSON NOTE: INVENTORY VALUATION IN QUICKBOOKS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingInventory Valuation in QuickBooksBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Explain how QuickBooks values inventory
  • Describe FIFO and its effect
  • Read the inventory valuation report

1. Introduction

Two organisations holding identical stock can report different inventory values, because valuation depends on which costs are assumed to have been sold. QuickBooks Online resolves this by using FIFO.

2. FIFO

FIFO (First In, First Out): The assumption that the oldest stock purchased is the first to be sold.

QuickBooks Online uses FIFO automatically; there is no setting to change it. So the cost charged when you sell is the cost of your oldest remaining units, and the stock left on the balance sheet is valued at the most recent prices.

3. Worked example

Example: Buy 10 bags at $8 = $80, then 10 bags at $10 = $100. Sell 12 bags. FIFO charges 10 at $8 plus 2 at $10 = $100 to COGS. The 8 bags remaining are valued at $10 each = $80.

4. Why it matters in a rising market

Prices risingEffect under FIFO
Cost charged to COGSLower, because older cheaper units are used first
Reported gross profitHigher
Closing stock valueHigher, valued at recent prices
TaxPotentially higher, because profit is higher
Note: This matters in Liberia and anywhere with significant inflation: FIFO can flatter reported profit, because you are matching today's selling prices against older, cheaper costs.

5. The valuation report

Reports → Inventory Valuation Summary shows, per item, the quantity on hand, the asset value and the average cost. Reconcile the total to the Inventory Asset account on the balance sheet — they should agree exactly.

Summary

  • QuickBooks Online values inventory using FIFO, with no option to change it.
  • FIFO charges the oldest costs to COGS and values remaining stock at recent prices.
  • In a rising market FIFO raises reported gross profit; the valuation report should agree with the Inventory Asset account.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
FIFOFirst in, first out — oldest costs are charged to sales first.
Inventory Valuation SummaryA report showing quantity and value per item.
Inventory AssetThe balance sheet account holding stock value.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which valuation method does QuickBooks Online use?

  1. FIFO
  2. LIFO
  3. Weighted average only
  4. Whatever you choose
Show answer

Answer: A. QuickBooks Online applies FIFO automatically.

Buy 10 at $8 then 10 at $10, and sell 12. What is charged to COGS under FIFO?

  1. $100
  2. $120
  3. $96
  4. $80
Show answer

Answer: A. Ten units at $8 ($80) plus two at $10 ($20) equals $100.

In a period of rising prices, FIFO tends to:

  1. Increase reported gross profit
  2. Decrease reported gross profit
  3. Have no effect
  4. Eliminate tax
Show answer

Answer: A. Older cheaper costs are matched against current selling prices.

What should the Inventory Valuation Summary total agree with?

  1. The Inventory Asset account on the balance sheet
  2. Total sales
  3. The bank balance
  4. Accounts payable
Show answer

Answer: A. Both represent the value of stock held and must reconcile.

Short answer

Explain FIFO in one sentence with an example.

Model answer

FIFO assumes the oldest stock is sold first, so selling 12 units after buying 10 at $8 and 10 at $10 charges $80 plus $20 to cost of sales.

Why does FIFO matter in an inflationary economy?

Model answer

It matches current selling prices against older cheaper costs, which flatters reported profit and can increase the tax charge.

Class Activity

  1. Work through a FIFO calculation for three purchases and two sales.
  2. Run an inventory valuation report and reconcile it to the balance sheet.

Assignment

Given a series of purchases at different prices and several sales, calculate cost of goods sold and closing stock value under FIFO, and explain how the result would differ if prices had been falling.

lessons.title: 8.6 Buying and Selling Inventory Items
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 8: Products, Services and Inventory

LESSON NOTE: BUYING AND SELLING INVENTORY ITEMS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingBuying and Selling Inventory ItemsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Record a purchase of inventory
  • Record a sale of inventory
  • Trace the full cycle through the accounts

1. Introduction

The inventory cycle is buy, hold, sell. Each stage posts a different entry, and following one item through all three is the clearest way to understand inventory accounting.

2. The full cycle

StageEntryEffect
Buy 10 bags at $8Debit Inventory Asset $80, Credit Accounts Payable $80Stock and payables rise; no expense yet
HoldNo entry$80 sits on the balance sheet
Sell 4 bags at $15Debit Accounts Receivable $60, Credit Sales $60Revenue recorded
Same sale, cost sideDebit COGS $32, Credit Inventory Asset $32Cost of the 4 bags sold is recognised

Notice the sale posts two entries: one for revenue and one for cost. QuickBooks does this automatically for inventory items, which is precisely why the item type matters.

3. Gross profit falls out automatically

Example: Sales $60 less COGS $32 gives gross profit $28. Six bags remain on the balance sheet at $48. Nothing had to be calculated by hand.

4. Common errors

  • Coding an inventory purchase directly to COGS, which expenses it before it is sold and destroys the stock figure.
  • Selling using a non-inventory item, so no cost is recorded and gross profit is overstated.
  • Recording the purchase as an expense and the sale as an inventory item, leaving negative stock.

Summary

  • Buying inventory debits an asset; selling posts both revenue and cost entries.
  • QuickBooks calculates cost of goods sold automatically for inventory items.
  • Coding an inventory purchase straight to COGS destroys the stock figure and misstates profit.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Inventory cycleThe sequence of buying, holding and selling stock.
Gross profitSales less cost of goods sold.
Negative stockA quantity below zero, caused by inconsistent recording.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

How many entries does selling an inventory item post?

  1. Two: one for revenue and one for cost
  2. One
  3. Three
  4. None
Show answer

Answer: A. Revenue and the matching cost of goods sold are recorded together.

What is wrong with coding an inventory purchase to COGS?

  1. The cost is expensed before the sale and stock value disappears
  2. Nothing
  3. Tax is higher
  4. The supplier is not paid
Show answer

Answer: A. It breaks the matching of cost to sale and removes the asset.

Sell 4 bags costing $8 for $15 each. What is gross profit?

  1. $28
  2. $60
  3. $32
  4. $88
Show answer

Answer: A. Sales $60 minus cost $32 gives $28.

Selling with a non-inventory item instead of an inventory item causes:

  1. No cost to be recorded, so gross profit is overstated
  2. No sale to be recorded
  3. Double tax
  4. Negative sales
Show answer

Answer: A. Only inventory items post the cost side of a sale.

Short answer

Write the four entries for buying 10 bags at $8 and selling 4 at $15.

Model answer

Purchase: Debit Inventory $80, Credit Payables $80. Sale: Debit Receivables $60, Credit Sales $60; and Debit COGS $32, Credit Inventory $32.

Why is gross profit automatic for inventory items?

Model answer

Because QuickBooks posts the cost of goods sold at the moment of sale, so sales less cost is calculated without manual work.

Class Activity

  1. Record a full buy-hold-sell cycle in a sample file and check gross profit.
  2. Explain how negative stock could arise and how to prevent it.

Assignment

Trace three inventory items through a complete purchase and sale cycle. Show every journal entry, the closing stock value, and the gross profit earned on each item.

lessons.title: 8.7 Inventory Reports
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 8: Products, Services and Inventory

LESSON NOTE: INVENTORY REPORTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingInventory ReportsBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Run the main inventory reports
  • Interpret each report
  • Use inventory reports to make buying decisions

1. Introduction

Inventory data is only worth collecting if it is read. Four reports answer nearly every stock question a small organisation has.

2. The four reports

ReportAnswers
Inventory Valuation SummaryWhat is our stock worth right now?
Physical Inventory WorksheetWhat should we count, and what do the books say?
Sales by Product/Service SummaryWhat sells, and what earns the most?
Inventory Stock StatusWhat is low and needs reordering?

3. Using them for decisions

  1. Print the Physical Inventory Worksheet before every count; it deliberately hides book quantities on some layouts so counters are not influenced.
  2. Use Sales by Product to identify slow movers — stock that is quietly consuming cash.
  3. Compare valuation to total sales; stock worth more than a month's sales usually signals over-buying.
  4. Act on the stock status list weekly, not when a customer is turned away.
Example: Sales by Product shows one line of goods worth $3,000 in stock that has sold twice in six months. That is $3,000 of cash sitting on a shelf and a candidate for discounting.

4. Reconciling

Note: The Inventory Valuation Summary total must equal the Inventory Asset balance on the balance sheet. If it does not, something was posted directly to the Inventory Asset account instead of through an item — find it and correct it.

Summary

  • Four core reports cover value, counting, sales performance and reorder status.
  • Slow-moving stock is cash sitting on a shelf; the sales report exposes it.
  • Valuation must reconcile to the Inventory Asset account on the balance sheet.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Physical Inventory WorksheetA count sheet listing items to be counted.
Slow moverStock that sells rarely and ties up cash.
Stock statusA report of items at or below reorder point.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which report tells you what stock is worth today?

  1. Inventory Valuation Summary
  2. Sales by Product
  3. Physical Inventory Worksheet
  4. Profit and Loss
Show answer

Answer: A. It gives quantity and value per item.

Why might a count sheet hide book quantities?

  1. So counters record what they see rather than confirming what is expected
  2. To save paper
  3. To speed up counting
  4. It never does
Show answer

Answer: A. Showing the expected figure biases the count.

Stock worth more than a month's sales usually indicates:

  1. Over-buying and cash tied up
  2. Excellent management
  3. A pricing error
  4. A tax problem
Show answer

Answer: A. Excess stock consumes cash without generating return.

The valuation total does not match the Inventory Asset account. Likely cause?

  1. Something was posted directly to the Inventory Asset account instead of through an item
  2. The bank is wrong
  3. Sales are missing
  4. Nothing, this is normal
Show answer

Answer: A. Direct postings bypass item tracking and break the link.

Short answer

Name the four inventory reports and the question each answers.

Model answer

Valuation Summary — what is stock worth; Physical Inventory Worksheet — what to count; Sales by Product — what sells; Stock Status — what to reorder.

How would you identify slow-moving stock and what would you do?

Model answer

Compare stock value against units sold over several months; discount, bundle or stop reordering lines that barely move.

Class Activity

  1. Run all four inventory reports in a sample file and note one decision from each.
  2. Identify the slowest-moving item in a sample company and propose an action.

Assignment

Produce an inventory report pack for an organisation, identify the three slowest-moving lines and the three most profitable, and recommend buying decisions with reasons.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 9.1 Payroll Overview and Setup
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 9: Payroll in QuickBooks

LESSON NOTE: PAYROLL OVERVIEW AND SETUP

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingPayroll Overview and SetupBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Explain what payroll in QuickBooks does
  • Complete the payroll setup steps
  • Identify what must be right before the first pay run

1. Introduction

Payroll is the highest-risk area in bookkeeping: people notice immediately when it is wrong, and tax authorities impose penalties when it is late. Setup discipline matters more here than anywhere else.

2. What payroll must produce

  • The correct net pay for each employee
  • Correct deductions withheld and recorded as liabilities
  • Payment of those liabilities to the authorities on time
  • Payslips for employees and records for auditors

3. Setup steps

  1. Confirm the business details and tax registration numbers.
  2. Set the pay schedule — weekly, fortnightly or monthly.
  3. Add each employee with their pay rate and start date.
  4. Enter deductions and benefits that apply.
  5. Enter year-to-date figures if you are switching mid-year.
  6. Run a test pay run and check every figure before finalising.

4. The mid-year switch

Note: If you move to QuickBooks payroll part-way through a tax year, year-to-date figures must be entered for every employee. Skipping this makes annual totals and tax certificates wrong for the entire year, and the error is usually discovered only at year end when it is expensive to fix.

5. Availability

QuickBooks Payroll is a paid add-on and is not offered in every country. Where it is unavailable, payroll is calculated outside QuickBooks and entered as a journal entry — the accounting in the next lessons still applies exactly.

Summary

  • Payroll must produce correct net pay, recorded liabilities, timely payments and proper records.
  • Setup covers business details, pay schedule, employees, deductions and year-to-date figures.
  • A mid-year switch requires year-to-date figures or annual totals will be wrong.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Net payWhat the employee actually receives after deductions.
Statutory deductionAn amount the law requires to be withheld.
Year-to-dateTotals accumulated since the start of the tax year.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What must be entered when switching to QuickBooks payroll mid-year?

  1. Year-to-date figures for every employee
  2. Nothing extra
  3. Only new employees
  4. Last year's accounts
Show answer

Answer: A. Without them, annual totals and tax certificates are wrong for the whole year.

Why is payroll described as the highest-risk area?

  1. Errors are noticed immediately by staff and penalised by tax authorities
  2. It involves the largest numbers
  3. It is the hardest to learn
  4. It cannot be corrected
Show answer

Answer: A. Both people and regulators react quickly to payroll errors.

QuickBooks Payroll is unavailable in your country. What can you do?

  1. Calculate payroll outside QuickBooks and record it as a journal entry
  2. Skip payroll entirely
  3. Use invoices instead
  4. Stop paying staff
Show answer

Answer: A. The accounting treatment is the same however the figures are calculated.

What should you do before finalising the first pay run?

  1. Run a test pay run and check every figure
  2. Pay immediately
  3. Skip checking
  4. Only check the total
Show answer

Answer: A. A test run catches setup errors before money moves.

Short answer

List four things payroll must produce.

Model answer

Correct net pay, correctly recorded deductions as liabilities, timely payment of those liabilities, and payslips and records.

Why does skipping year-to-date figures cause problems only at year end?

Model answer

Because monthly pay looks correct, but the annual totals used for tax certificates are understated, and this only surfaces when the annual return is prepared.

Class Activity

  1. List the setup steps you would follow for an organisation with five employees.
  2. Explain the risk of a mid-year switch in your own words.

Assignment

Produce a payroll setup plan for an organisation of at least five staff, covering pay schedule, deductions, year-to-date treatment and the checks you would run before the first live pay run.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 9.2 Adding Employees
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 9: Payroll in QuickBooks

LESSON NOTE: ADDING EMPLOYEES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingAdding EmployeesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Add an employee record
  • Identify the information legally required
  • Keep employee data secure

1. Introduction

An employee record drives every future pay run, every deduction and every tax certificate. Errors here repeat every single month until someone notices.

2. Information needed

CategoryDetails
IdentityFull legal name, date of birth, address
TaxTax identification number, tax status
EmploymentStart date, job title, employment type
PayRate, frequency, salary or hourly
PaymentBank account or mobile money details
DeductionsPension, union dues, loan repayments
LeaveEntitlement and balance

3. Accuracy that matters most

  • Legal name must match tax records, or certificates will be rejected.
  • Start date drives leave accrual and year-to-date totals.
  • Pay rate is the figure repeated every period; a small error compounds.
  • Bank details — a wrong digit sends money to a stranger and is rarely recoverable.

4. Confidentiality

Note: Payroll data is among the most sensitive information an organisation holds. Restrict payroll access to the minimum number of users, never share payslips by group email, and never leave payroll reports on a shared printer. A breach here damages trust permanently.

5. Leavers

Mark leavers as terminated with the correct date rather than deleting them. Their history must remain for tax certificates, and deletion breaks the year's totals.

Summary

  • Employee records drive every future pay run, so errors repeat monthly.
  • Legal name, start date, pay rate and bank details are the highest-risk fields.
  • Restrict payroll access tightly and terminate leavers rather than deleting them.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Employment typeWhether a worker is permanent, temporary or a contractor.
Termination dateThe date employment ended, used for final pay and certificates.
ConfidentialityThe duty to keep personal and pay data private.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why should a leaver be marked terminated rather than deleted?

  1. Their history is needed for tax certificates and year totals
  2. Deletion is impossible
  3. It saves money
  4. It keeps them on payroll
Show answer

Answer: A. Deleting destroys the records the year-end filing depends on.

Which error is hardest to recover from?

  1. Wrong bank account details
  2. A misspelled job title
  3. An incorrect address
  4. A missing phone number
Show answer

Answer: A. Money sent to the wrong account is rarely recovered.

Why must the legal name match tax records?

  1. Otherwise tax certificates are rejected
  2. It looks neater
  3. It affects the pay rate
  4. It is not important
Show answer

Answer: A. Authorities match filings on the registered legal name.

How should payslips be distributed?

  1. Individually and confidentially
  2. By group email
  3. On a shared printer
  4. Posted on a noticeboard
Show answer

Answer: A. Pay data is sensitive and must reach only the individual.

Short answer

Name four categories of information needed for an employee record.

Model answer

Identity details, tax information, employment terms, pay details, payment method, deductions and leave.

Why is confidentiality a control issue and not just courtesy?

Model answer

Because a pay-data breach permanently damages trust between staff and the organisation and can create legal liability.

Class Activity

  1. Create three employee records in a sample file with full details.
  2. List the documents you would collect from a new employee before their first pay run.

Assignment

Design an employee onboarding checklist for payroll purposes, covering every field required, the documents collected, who may access the data, and how a leaver is processed.

lessons.title: 9.3 Setting Up Pay Schedules
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 9: Payroll in QuickBooks

LESSON NOTE: SETTING UP PAY SCHEDULES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSetting Up Pay SchedulesBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create a pay schedule
  • Choose a frequency that suits the organisation
  • Explain the cash-flow effect of pay frequency

1. Introduction

A pay schedule tells QuickBooks how often staff are paid and on which dates. It drives the pay run, the liability due dates and a large part of your cash planning.

2. Frequencies compared

FrequencyPay runs a yearSuitsCash-flow effect
Weekly52Casual and daily-rated labourFrequent small outflows
Fortnightly26Mixed workforcesModerate
Semi-monthly24Salaried staffPredictable, twice monthly
Monthly12Most salaried organisationsOne large outflow

3. Setting one up

  1. Payroll → Employees → Pay schedules.
  2. Choose the frequency and the first pay date.
  3. Set the pay period end date — the last day worked that this run covers.
  4. Assign each employee to a schedule.
Note: Distinguish the pay period (the days worked) from the pay date (the day money moves). Deductions are usually due based on the pay date, not the period.

4. Cash-flow planning

Example: A monthly payroll of $12,000 is one large outflow on the 28th. The same wage bill paid weekly is roughly $2,770 every Friday. The annual cost is identical, but the second pattern is far easier to fund from weekly takings.

Summary

  • A pay schedule sets frequency, pay dates and the period each run covers.
  • Weekly suits casual labour; monthly suits salaried staff.
  • Pay frequency does not change the annual cost but changes how easily it can be funded.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Pay periodThe range of days worked that a pay run covers.
Pay dateThe date employees actually receive money.
Pay frequencyHow often payroll is run.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What is the difference between the pay period and the pay date?

  1. The pay period is the days worked; the pay date is when money moves
  2. They are the same
  3. The pay date is always earlier
  4. The pay period is always a month
Show answer

Answer: A. Deductions are generally due based on the pay date, not the period worked.

Which frequency usually suits daily-rated casual labour?

  1. Weekly
  2. Monthly
  3. Annually
  4. Semi-monthly
Show answer

Answer: A. Casual workers typically need frequent payment.

Does paying weekly rather than monthly change the annual wage cost?

  1. No, but it changes how easily it can be funded
  2. Yes, it is cheaper
  3. Yes, it is more expensive
  4. It removes deductions
Show answer

Answer: A. The total is the same; only the timing of outflows differs.

How many pay runs a year does a semi-monthly schedule have?

  1. 24
  2. 12
  3. 26
  4. 52
Show answer

Answer: A. Twice a month for twelve months gives 24 runs.

Short answer

Name four pay frequencies and one organisation type suited to each.

Model answer

Weekly — casual labour; fortnightly — mixed workforce; semi-monthly — salaried staff; monthly — most salaried organisations.

Why does pay frequency matter to cash planning?

Model answer

It determines whether the wage bill leaves as one large monthly outflow or as smaller, more frequent amounts that are easier to fund from ongoing income.

Class Activity

  1. Set up two pay schedules in a sample file and assign employees.
  2. Calculate the weekly equivalent of a $12,000 monthly payroll and comment on funding.

Assignment

Recommend a pay schedule for an organisation with both salaried and casual staff. Justify the frequencies chosen and show the cash-flow pattern each creates over a month.

lessons.title: 9.4 Running Payroll
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 9: Payroll in QuickBooks

LESSON NOTE: RUNNING PAYROLL

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingRunning PayrollBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Run a payroll cycle end to end
  • Check a pay run before finalising
  • Correct a mistake found after submission

1. Introduction

Running payroll is a routine, but it is a routine that must never be rushed. Once payments leave the bank, corrections are awkward and public.

2. The steps

  1. Payroll → Run payroll and choose the schedule.
  2. Confirm the pay period and pay date.
  3. Enter hours for hourly staff and any overtime, bonuses or unpaid leave.
  4. Review each employee's gross pay, deductions and net pay.
  5. Check the total cost against last period and investigate any large change.
  6. Submit, then distribute payslips.

3. The pre-submission check

CheckWhy
Compare total net pay to last periodA large change signals an error unless you know the cause
Confirm the employee countA leaver still being paid, or a starter missing
Scan for zero or unusually high net payUsually a data-entry error in hours or rate
Confirm the pay dateA wrong date misstates the period and deduction due dates
Note: Two minutes on these four checks catches most payroll errors before they become payments.

4. Fixing mistakes

If the run has not been submitted, edit and re-review. If it has been submitted but not paid, most versions allow the run to be deleted or voided and re-run. If money has already reached the employee, correct it in the next period and tell the employee immediately — never quietly adjust someone's pay without explaining it.

Summary

  • Run payroll by confirming the period, entering variable inputs, reviewing every employee and submitting.
  • Four checks before submission catch most errors: totals, headcount, outliers and pay date.
  • If money has already been paid, correct openly in the next period and inform the employee.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Gross payPay before any deductions.
Net payWhat the employee receives after deductions.
Pay runOne complete payroll cycle for a schedule.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What is the fastest check that a pay run is wrong?

  1. Comparing total net pay with the previous period
  2. Reading every payslip line by line
  3. Checking the office address
  4. Running a balance sheet
Show answer

Answer: A. An unexplained change in the total is the quickest signal of error.

An error is found after employees have been paid. What is the correct response?

  1. Correct it in the next period and tell the employee immediately
  2. Adjust their pay quietly
  3. Ignore it
  4. Delete the employee
Show answer

Answer: A. Transparency is essential; silent adjustments destroy trust.

Why check the employee count before submitting?

  1. A leaver may still be included or a new starter omitted
  2. It affects tax rates
  3. It is legally required
  4. It speeds up processing
Show answer

Answer: A. Headcount errors are common and immediately visible to staff.

Why does the pay date matter beyond the payment itself?

  1. Deduction due dates are usually based on it
  2. It sets the employee's start date
  3. It changes gross pay
  4. It has no other effect
Show answer

Answer: A. Statutory liabilities are generally due by reference to the pay date.

Short answer

List the four pre-submission checks.

Model answer

Compare total net pay to last period; confirm the employee count; scan for zero or unusually high net pay; confirm the pay date.

Why must a payroll error affecting an employee be disclosed rather than quietly corrected?

Model answer

Because staff notice changes to their pay, and an unexplained adjustment looks like concealment and destroys trust in the whole payroll process.

Class Activity

  1. Run a payroll in a sample file and apply all four pre-submission checks.
  2. Describe how you would handle an overpayment discovered a week after payday.

Assignment

Process a complete pay run for at least four employees including overtime and one unpaid absence. Document each pre-submission check and its result, then explain how you would correct an error found after payment.

lessons.title: 9.5 Payroll Taxes and Deductions
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 9: Payroll in QuickBooks

LESSON NOTE: PAYROLL TAXES AND DEDUCTIONS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingPayroll Taxes and DeductionsBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Distinguish employee deductions from employer costs
  • Explain how deductions become liabilities
  • Identify common statutory deductions

1. Introduction

The gap between what an employee costs and what they receive is made up of deductions and employer contributions. Confusing the two is the most common payroll misunderstanding.

2. Two different things

Employee deductionEmployer contribution
Whose moneyThe employee'sThe organisation's
Effect on net payReduces itNo effect
Effect on employer costNoneIncreases it
ExamplesIncome tax withheld, pension employee shareEmployer pension share, payroll levies
Example: Gross pay $500; income tax withheld $60; employee pension $25 → net pay $415. Employer pension $25 is an extra cost, so the true cost to the organisation is $525, not $500.

3. Deductions are liabilities, not expenses

Payroll liability: Money withheld from employees or owed by the employer that must be paid to a third party.

Tax withheld from an employee is not the organisation's money and is never income. It sits as a liability until it is paid to the authority.

Note: Spending withheld tax on operating costs is one of the most serious errors a small organisation can make. The money is held on behalf of the authority and remains payable in full, whatever the cash position.

4. Common deductions

  • Income tax withheld at source
  • Social security or national pension contributions
  • Health insurance
  • Union dues
  • Salary advances and staff loan repayments
  • Court-ordered deductions

Summary

  • Employee deductions reduce net pay; employer contributions increase employer cost.
  • Withheld amounts are liabilities held on behalf of third parties, never income.
  • True employment cost is gross pay plus employer contributions.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
WithholdingDeducting tax from pay and remitting it to the authority.
Employer contributionAn amount the employer pays on top of gross pay.
Payroll liabilityAmounts owed to authorities or third parties from payroll.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Gross pay is $500, deductions $85, employer pension $25. What is the true cost to the organisation?

  1. $525
  2. $500
  3. $415
  4. $585
Show answer

Answer: A. Employer cost is gross pay plus employer contributions: $500 + $25.

Tax withheld from an employee should be recorded as:

  1. A liability until paid to the authority
  2. Income
  3. An expense of the employer
  4. Equity
Show answer

Answer: A. It is the employee's money held on behalf of the authority.

Which of these does NOT reduce an employee's net pay?

  1. Employer pension contribution
  2. Income tax withheld
  3. Union dues
  4. Employee pension share
Show answer

Answer: A. Employer contributions are an additional employer cost, not a deduction.

Why is spending withheld tax on operating costs so serious?

  1. The money belongs to the authority and remains payable in full regardless
  2. It reduces profit
  3. It is merely untidy
  4. It has no consequence
Show answer

Answer: A. The liability does not disappear, and penalties usually follow.

Short answer

Explain the difference between a deduction and an employer contribution.

Model answer

A deduction is taken out of the employee's gross pay and reduces what they receive; an employer contribution is paid by the organisation on top of gross pay and increases its cost.

Why is withheld tax not income?

Model answer

It was never the organisation's money — it belongs to the employee and is owed to the tax authority, so it is recorded as a liability.

Class Activity

  1. Calculate net pay and total employer cost for three employees with given deductions.
  2. List the statutory deductions that apply in your own country.

Assignment

For a payroll of at least five employees, produce a table showing gross pay, each deduction, net pay, employer contributions and total employer cost, then state the total liability created.

lessons.title: 9.6 Payroll Liabilities and Payments
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 9: Payroll in QuickBooks

LESSON NOTE: PAYROLL LIABILITIES AND PAYMENTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingPayroll Liabilities and PaymentsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Track payroll liabilities
  • Pay liabilities on time
  • Reconcile the liability account to zero

1. Introduction

Every pay run creates liabilities. Managing them is a separate discipline from running payroll, and it is where organisations most often fall behind.

2. The liability cycle

StageEntryBalance
Payroll runCredit Payroll LiabilitiesRises
Liability paid to authorityDebit Payroll Liabilities, Credit BankFalls
All paid—Returns to zero

A healthy liability account rises on payday and falls to zero when the payment is made. A balance that only ever grows means payments are not being made.

3. Paying on time

  1. Note the statutory due date for each liability — usually a set number of days after the pay date.
  2. Diarise the payment, do not rely on memory.
  3. Pay through the payroll liability function so the liability clears, not as a general expense.
  4. Keep the receipt and attach it to the transaction.
Note: Paying a payroll liability as a general expense is a classic error: the cost is recorded twice and the liability never clears, so the balance sheet keeps showing a debt already paid.

4. Reconciling

Example: At month end the payroll liability account should equal exactly what is genuinely still owed — this month's deductions not yet due. If it shows three months of accumulated deductions, either payments were missed or they were recorded as expenses instead of liability payments.

Summary

  • Payroll liabilities rise on payday and should return to zero when paid.
  • Pay through the liability function so the balance clears, not as a general expense.
  • A permanently growing liability balance means missed payments or mis-recorded ones.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Payroll liability accountThe account holding amounts owed from payroll.
Due dateThe statutory deadline for remitting a deduction.
RemittancePayment of withheld amounts to the authority.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What should the payroll liability balance do after liabilities are paid?

  1. Return to zero
  2. Stay the same
  3. Increase
  4. Become negative
Show answer

Answer: A. Paying the liability clears the balance.

What happens if a liability payment is recorded as a general expense?

  1. The cost is doubled and the liability never clears
  2. Nothing
  3. The liability doubles
  4. Tax is refunded
Show answer

Answer: A. The expense was already recorded at the pay run, so this records it twice.

A liability account shows three months of accumulated deductions. What does this suggest?

  1. Payments were missed or recorded incorrectly
  2. Payroll is efficient
  3. Staff were overpaid
  4. Nothing unusual
Show answer

Answer: A. A cleared liability should not accumulate across months.

When are payroll liabilities usually due?

  1. A set number of days after the pay date
  2. At year end only
  3. Immediately on the pay date
  4. Whenever convenient
Show answer

Answer: A. Statutory deadlines are typically fixed relative to the pay date.

Short answer

Describe the payroll liability cycle in three stages.

Model answer

Payroll run credits the liability; the payment debits it and credits the bank; once all are paid the balance returns to zero.

How would you investigate a payroll liability balance that never falls?

Model answer

Check whether remittances were actually made, and whether those payments were coded to the liability account or wrongly to an expense.

Class Activity

  1. Record a payroll liability payment in a sample file and check the balance clears.
  2. List the payroll liabilities an organisation you know must remit and their due dates.

Assignment

Produce a payroll liability schedule for three months showing what was created, what was paid and what remains, and reconcile the closing balance to the amounts genuinely still due.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 9.7 Payroll Reports
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 9: Payroll in QuickBooks

LESSON NOTE: PAYROLL REPORTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingPayroll ReportsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Run the main payroll reports
  • Use payroll reports for management and compliance
  • Reconcile payroll to the accounts

1. Introduction

Payroll reports serve three audiences: management wants cost, employees want accuracy, and authorities want compliance. Different reports serve each.

2. The core reports

ReportAnswersAudience
Payroll SummaryWhat did payroll cost this period?Management
Payroll DetailsWhat exactly did each employee receive?Payroll officer
Payroll Tax LiabilityWhat do we owe the authorities?Compliance
Employee DetailsWhat are each person's terms and deductions?HR and audit
Total CostWhat is the full employer cost per employee?Budgeting

3. Using them

  1. Run Payroll Summary each period and compare with the previous one; explain any movement.
  2. Run Payroll Tax Liability before each remittance date and pay exactly that figure.
  3. Reconcile total payroll expense in the Profit and Loss to the payroll reports every month.
  4. Keep a copy of each period's reports; they are the evidence for any future audit or dispute.

4. The reconciliation that matters

Example: Payroll Summary shows gross pay $18,400 for the month. The Profit and Loss salary expense should show the same $18,400 plus employer contributions. If it shows $19,200, something was posted to salaries outside payroll — find it, because it is either a duplicate or an unrecorded payment.

5. Confidentiality again

Note: Payroll reports name individuals and their pay. Share the Payroll Summary with management if needed, but never circulate Payroll Details, which exposes every person's pay to whoever receives it.

Summary

  • Different payroll reports serve management, payroll officers, compliance and budgeting.
  • Reconcile payroll reports to the Profit and Loss salary expense every month.
  • Payroll Details names individual pay and must not be circulated.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Payroll SummaryA report of total payroll cost for a period.
Payroll Tax LiabilityA report of amounts owed to authorities.
ReconciliationConfirming payroll reports agree with the general ledger.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which report tells you what to remit to the authorities?

  1. Payroll Tax Liability
  2. Payroll Summary
  3. Employee Details
  4. Balance Sheet
Show answer

Answer: A. It shows exactly what is owed and due.

Payroll Summary shows $18,400 gross but the Profit and Loss shows $19,200 in salaries. What does this suggest?

  1. Something was posted to salaries outside the payroll process
  2. Payroll is correct
  3. Tax was overpaid
  4. Nothing
Show answer

Answer: A. The difference indicates a duplicate or an unrecorded manual payment.

Which report should NOT be circulated widely?

  1. Payroll Details, because it exposes individual pay
  2. Payroll Summary
  3. Balance Sheet
  4. Profit and Loss
Show answer

Answer: A. It names each employee and their pay.

How often should payroll be reconciled to the accounts?

  1. Every month
  2. Once a year
  3. Never
  4. Only at audit
Show answer

Answer: A. Monthly reconciliation catches errors while they are still easy to fix.

Short answer

Name three payroll reports and the audience each serves.

Model answer

Payroll Summary for management, Payroll Tax Liability for compliance, and Employee Details for HR and audit.

Describe the monthly payroll reconciliation.

Model answer

Compare gross pay plus employer contributions from the payroll reports against the salary expense in the Profit and Loss, and investigate any difference.

Class Activity

  1. Run three payroll reports in a sample file and state one decision from each.
  2. Reconcile a payroll summary to a salary expense figure and explain a difference.

Assignment

Produce a monthly payroll report pack, reconcile it to the Profit and Loss, and write a short commentary for management on the period's payroll cost and any variance from the previous month.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 10.1 Sales Tax Overview
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 10: Sales Tax and VAT

LESSON NOTE: SALES TAX OVERVIEW

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSales Tax OverviewBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Explain how sales tax and VAT work
  • Distinguish tax collected from tax paid
  • Explain why sales tax is never income

1. Introduction

Sales tax and VAT operate on the same principle: the organisation collects tax from customers on behalf of the government, and passes it on. The money is never yours.

2. The basic mechanism

StepWhat happens
You sellYou add tax to the price and collect it from the customer
You buyYou pay tax to your suppliers on purchases
You fileYou remit tax collected, usually less tax paid on purchases
Net positionEither you owe the authority, or it owes you
Example: Tax collected on sales $1,200; tax paid on purchases $700. You remit $500. If instead you collected $400 and paid $700, the authority owes you $300 or you carry it forward.

3. Sales tax is never income

Output tax: Tax charged to customers on your sales.
Input tax: Tax paid to suppliers on your purchases.
Note: Output tax is a liability from the moment you collect it. Treating it as revenue makes sales look larger and profit look better, and leaves the organisation unable to pay when the filing falls due. This is a leading cause of tax arrears in small businesses.

4. Sales tax vs VAT

Sales tax is typically charged once, at the final sale to a consumer. VAT is charged at every stage, with businesses reclaiming the tax they paid. QuickBooks handles both through the same sales tax centre; the difference is in the rules of your country, not in the software.

Summary

  • Sales tax and VAT are collected on behalf of government, never earned.
  • Output tax is charged on sales; input tax is paid on purchases; you remit the difference.
  • Treating tax collected as income overstates profit and causes arrears.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Output taxTax charged to customers on sales.
Input taxTax paid to suppliers on purchases.
RemittancePaying collected tax to the authority.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Tax collected is $1,200 and tax paid on purchases is $700. What do you remit?

  1. $500
  2. $1,900
  3. $1,200
  4. $700
Show answer

Answer: A. You remit the net of output tax less input tax.

Why is sales tax collected never income?

  1. It belongs to the government from the moment it is collected
  2. It is too small
  3. It is refundable to customers
  4. It is income only at year end
Show answer

Answer: A. You act as a collector, holding the money as a liability.

What is the main difference between sales tax and VAT?

  1. Sales tax is typically charged once at final sale; VAT applies at each stage with reclaim
  2. They are identical
  3. VAT is only for exports
  4. Sales tax cannot be reclaimed ever
Show answer

Answer: A. VAT operates through the chain with input tax recovery.

What is a leading cause of tax arrears in small businesses?

  1. Treating tax collected as available income and spending it
  2. Filing early
  3. Charging too little
  4. Keeping records
Show answer

Answer: A. Spending the collected tax leaves nothing to remit at filing.

Short answer

Define output tax and input tax.

Model answer

Output tax is the tax you charge customers on sales; input tax is the tax you pay suppliers on purchases.

Explain in one sentence why sales tax must be set aside rather than spent.

Model answer

Because it is money held on behalf of the government and must be remitted in full at the filing date whatever the cash position.

Class Activity

  1. Calculate the net tax payable from a set of sales and purchases.
  2. Explain to a shopkeeper why the tax on their sales is not their money.

Assignment

Prepare a simple sales tax position for one quarter from given sales and purchase figures, showing output tax, input tax, the net amount payable, and how you would ensure the money is available.

lessons.title: 10.2 Setting Up Sales Tax
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 10: Sales Tax and VAT

LESSON NOTE: SETTING UP SALES TAX

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSetting Up Sales TaxBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Switch on and configure sales tax
  • Create tax rates and agencies
  • Set default tax treatment

1. Introduction

Sales tax must be configured before you raise your first taxable invoice. Retro-fitting tax onto invoices already issued means re-issuing documents to customers.

2. Setting it up

  1. Taxes → Sales tax → Set up sales tax.
  2. Enter the tax agency you file with.
  3. Set your filing frequency — monthly, quarterly or annually.
  4. Enter your registration number and the date registration started.
  5. Create the rate or rates that apply.

3. Rates and agencies

ConceptMeaning
Tax agencyThe authority you file and pay to
Tax rateThe percentage charged, e.g. 10%
Combined rateTwo or more rates applied together
Filing frequencyHow often a return is due
ExemptNot subject to tax at all
Zero-ratedTaxable, but at 0% — still reported
Note: Exempt and zero-rated are not the same. Zero-rated sales are reported on the return and often allow input tax recovery; exempt sales usually do not. Coding one as the other misstates the return.

4. Defaults

Set a default tax status on each product and on each customer. QuickBooks applies tax when both the item and the customer are taxable, which is why a taxable item can appear untaxed on an exempt customer's invoice — that is correct behaviour, not a fault.

Summary

  • Configure sales tax before issuing the first taxable invoice.
  • Set the agency, filing frequency, registration details and rates.
  • Zero-rated and exempt are different treatments and must not be interchanged.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Tax agencyThe authority sales tax is filed and paid to.
Zero-ratedTaxable at 0%, still reported on the return.
ExemptOutside the scope of tax entirely.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why must sales tax be configured before the first taxable invoice?

  1. Retro-fitting tax means re-issuing documents to customers
  2. QuickBooks blocks invoices otherwise
  3. It changes the price
  4. It affects payroll
Show answer

Answer: A. Invoices already sent would have to be corrected and re-sent.

What is the difference between zero-rated and exempt?

  1. Zero-rated is taxable at 0% and reported; exempt is outside the scope
  2. They are identical
  3. Exempt is taxed at 5%
  4. Zero-rated is never reported
Show answer

Answer: A. The distinction affects the return and often input tax recovery.

A taxable item shows no tax on an invoice. What is the likely reason?

  1. The customer is marked as exempt
  2. QuickBooks is faulty
  3. The rate is missing
  4. The invoice is void
Show answer

Answer: A. Tax applies only when both the item and the customer are taxable.

What does filing frequency determine?

  1. How often a sales tax return is due
  2. The tax rate
  3. The customer's terms
  4. The bank account used
Show answer

Answer: A. It sets the reporting period for the return.

Short answer

List five things set during sales tax setup.

Model answer

The tax agency, filing frequency, registration number, registration start date and the applicable rates.

Explain why a taxable product might appear untaxed on an invoice.

Model answer

Because the customer is flagged exempt, and tax is only charged when both the item and the customer are taxable.

Class Activity

  1. Set up sales tax in a sample file with one rate and one agency.
  2. Classify eight products as standard-rated, zero-rated or exempt for your country.

Assignment

Configure sales tax for an organisation, documenting the agency, frequency, rates and the default tax status of at least ten products and three customers, with reasons.

questions.question: A taxable item shows no tax on an invoice. What is the likely reason?
options: The customer is marked as exempt
questions.explanation: Tax applies only when both the item and the customer are taxable.

lessons.title: 10.3 Charging Sales Tax on Sales
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 10: Sales Tax and VAT

LESSON NOTE: CHARGING SALES TAX ON SALES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCharging Sales Tax on SalesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Apply tax correctly on an invoice
  • Handle tax-inclusive and tax-exclusive pricing
  • Deal with mixed taxable and exempt lines

1. Introduction

Once tax is configured, QuickBooks applies it automatically — but only if the item, the customer and the transaction are all set up correctly.

2. Inclusive vs exclusive

Tax exclusiveTax inclusive
Price shownBefore taxAlready includes tax
$100 at 10%Customer pays $110Customer pays $100
Tax element$10 added$9.09 extracted from the $100
Typical useBusiness-to-businessRetail, where displayed prices must be final
Note: Selecting the wrong setting changes what the customer pays or what you keep. On tax-inclusive pricing the tax comes out of your $100, so your revenue is $90.91, not $100.

3. Mixed invoices

Example: An invoice with $200 of taxable goods and $150 of exempt services at 10%: tax is $20 only. QuickBooks calculates per line, so mixed invoices need no manual work provided each item's tax status is right.

4. Getting it right

  1. Check the item's tax status is correct at setup, not on each invoice.
  2. Check the customer's tax status, especially for NGOs and government buyers who may be exempt.
  3. Confirm whether your prices are quoted inclusive or exclusive and set it once.
  4. Review the first few invoices line by line after any tax change.

Summary

  • Tax applies when the item and the customer are both taxable.
  • Tax-exclusive adds tax to the price; tax-inclusive extracts it from the price.
  • QuickBooks calculates tax per line, so mixed invoices work automatically.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Tax exclusivePrices quoted before tax is added.
Tax inclusivePrices that already contain the tax.
Mixed supplyAn invoice containing both taxable and non-taxable lines.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

A $100 item at 10% is priced tax-inclusive. What does the customer pay?

  1. $100
  2. $110
  3. $90
  4. $10
Show answer

Answer: A. Tax-inclusive means the displayed price already contains the tax.

With tax-inclusive pricing at 10%, what revenue do you keep from $100?

  1. $90.91
  2. $100
  3. $110
  4. $90
Show answer

Answer: A. The tax element of $9.09 is extracted from the $100.

An invoice has $200 taxable and $150 exempt lines at 10%. What tax is charged?

  1. $20
  2. $35
  3. $15
  4. $0
Show answer

Answer: A. Tax applies only to the taxable line.

Where should an item's tax status be set?

  1. Once, at item setup
  2. On every invoice
  3. At year end
  4. In the bank feed
Show answer

Answer: A. Setting it at the item level makes every future invoice correct automatically.

Short answer

Explain tax-inclusive versus tax-exclusive pricing with a $100 example at 10%.

Model answer

Exclusive: customer pays $110 and you keep $100. Inclusive: customer pays $100, of which $9.09 is tax, so you keep $90.91.

Why do NGOs and government buyers need special attention?

Model answer

They are often exempt, so their customer record must be flagged or you will wrongly charge them tax.

Class Activity

  1. Raise two invoices in a sample file, one tax-inclusive and one exclusive, and compare.
  2. Create a mixed invoice with taxable and exempt lines and check the tax calculated.

Assignment

Prepare five invoices covering taxable, exempt, zero-rated, mixed and tax-inclusive scenarios. For each, show the tax calculated and the revenue recognised.

lessons.title: 10.4 Sales Tax Reports
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 10: Sales Tax and VAT

LESSON NOTE: SALES TAX REPORTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingSales Tax ReportsBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Run the sales tax liability report
  • Read the tax return figures
  • Check the report before filing

1. Introduction

The sales tax reports turn a period's transactions into the figures you will put on a return. Reading them before filing is what prevents an incorrect submission.

2. The reports

ReportShows
Sales Tax LiabilityTaxable sales, tax collected and tax owed per agency
Taxable Sales DetailEvery transaction making up the taxable sales figure
Sales Tax SummaryOutput tax, input tax and the net position

3. Pre-filing checks

  1. Confirm the period matches your filing period exactly.
  2. Compare taxable sales on the report to total sales in the Profit and Loss; any large gap should be explained by exempt or zero-rated sales.
  3. Look for transactions with no tax code — usually an item or customer set up wrongly.
  4. Check for credit memos and refunds, which reduce the tax due.
  5. Investigate any negative figures before filing, not after.
Example: Total sales $50,000 but taxable sales only $18,000. That is fine if $32,000 is genuinely exempt grant income; it is a problem if taxable sales were coded as exempt by mistake.

4. The habit that protects you

Note: Print or save the report you filed from, with the date, and keep it with the return. If the authority queries the figure two years later, you can show exactly what the accounts said at the moment of filing.

Summary

  • Sales tax reports convert transactions into the figures on the return.
  • Reconcile taxable sales to total sales and explain the difference before filing.
  • Keep a saved copy of the report you filed from as evidence.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Sales Tax Liability reportA report of tax collected and owed per agency.
Taxable salesSales on which tax is chargeable.
Filing periodThe period a return covers.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What should you compare taxable sales against before filing?

  1. Total sales in the Profit and Loss, explaining any difference
  2. The bank balance
  3. Payroll
  4. Last year's tax
Show answer

Answer: A. The gap should be fully explained by exempt or zero-rated sales.

A transaction appears with no tax code. Likely cause?

  1. An item or customer is set up incorrectly
  2. The bank feed failed
  3. The invoice is void
  4. Tax rates changed
Show answer

Answer: A. Missing tax codes usually trace back to setup.

Why keep a saved copy of the report you filed from?

  1. It evidences exactly what the accounts said at the time of filing
  2. It is legally required to print
  3. It speeds up filing
  4. It reduces tax
Show answer

Answer: A. It protects you if the figure is queried later.

What effect do credit memos have on the tax due?

  1. They reduce it
  2. They increase it
  3. No effect
  4. They double it
Show answer

Answer: A. Credits reduce taxable sales and therefore the tax owed.

Short answer

Name the three main sales tax reports and what each shows.

Model answer

Sales Tax Liability — tax collected and owed; Taxable Sales Detail — the transactions behind it; Sales Tax Summary — output tax, input tax and net position.

Give two checks to perform before filing a return.

Model answer

Reconcile taxable sales to total sales, and look for transactions with a missing tax code.

Class Activity

  1. Run a sales tax liability report in a sample file and reconcile it to total sales.
  2. List the checks you would perform before submitting a return.

Assignment

Prepare a sales tax return for one period from the reports, showing every check you performed, the reconciliation to total sales, and the final figure you would submit.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 10.5 Filing and Recording Sales Tax Payments
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 10: Sales Tax and VAT

LESSON NOTE: FILING AND RECORDING SALES TAX PAYMENTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingFiling and Recording Sales Tax PaymentsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Record a sales tax filing and payment
  • Clear the sales tax liability
  • Handle a refund from the authority

1. Introduction

Filing and paying are two events. QuickBooks records the filing, which fixes the amount owed, and then the payment, which clears it.

2. The process

  1. Taxes → Sales tax → Review the period's return.
  2. Confirm the figures and choose Record payment / File return.
  3. Enter the payment date and the bank account used.
  4. Save; the liability is cleared for that period.
  5. Attach the filing confirmation from the authority.
Note: Record the payment through the sales tax centre, not as a general expense. Paying it as an expense records a cost that is not yours and leaves the liability outstanding forever.

3. The accounting

EventEntry
Tax collected on salesCredit Sales Tax Payable
Tax paid on purchasesDebit Sales Tax Payable (where recoverable)
FilingFixes the net amount owed for the period
PaymentDebit Sales Tax Payable, Credit Bank

4. Refunds and adjustments

Example: Input tax of $700 exceeds output tax of $400, so the authority owes $300. Depending on local rules this is either refunded — recorded as Debit Bank, Credit Sales Tax Payable — or carried forward against the next period's liability.

Where an adjustment is needed for a penalty, interest or a rounding difference, use the adjustment function in the sales tax centre and code penalties to a separate expense account so they remain visible to management.

Summary

  • Filing fixes the amount owed; payment clears the liability.
  • Always pay through the sales tax centre, never as a general expense.
  • A net repayment position is either refunded or carried forward, per local rules.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
FilingSubmitting the return that fixes the tax owed for a period.
Sales Tax PayableThe liability account holding tax owed.
Carry forwardApplying a repayment against a future period.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why must a tax payment be recorded through the sales tax centre?

  1. Otherwise the liability stays outstanding and a false expense is recorded
  2. It is faster
  3. It changes the rate
  4. It is legally required to use that screen
Show answer

Answer: A. Only the sales tax centre clears the liability for that period.

Input tax $700, output tax $400. What is the position?

  1. The authority owes you $300, refunded or carried forward
  2. You owe $300
  3. You owe $1,100
  4. Nothing happens
Show answer

Answer: A. When input exceeds output you are in a repayment position.

Where should a late-filing penalty be coded?

  1. A separate expense account so it stays visible
  2. Sales tax payable
  3. Sales income
  4. Equity
Show answer

Answer: A. Penalties should be visible to management, not buried in tax.

What are the two distinct events in this lesson?

  1. Filing the return and paying the amount
  2. Selling and buying
  3. Invoicing and receipting
  4. Counting and adjusting
Show answer

Answer: A. Filing fixes the amount; payment settles it.

Short answer

Give the journal entry for paying $500 of sales tax.

Model answer

Debit Sales Tax Payable $500, Credit Bank $500.

Why code penalties separately rather than to the tax liability?

Model answer

So management can see the cost of late filing and act on it, rather than having it hidden inside the normal tax charge.

Class Activity

  1. Record a sales tax filing and payment in a sample file and confirm the liability clears.
  2. Describe how you would record a refund from the authority.

Assignment

Complete a full sales tax cycle for one period: produce the return figures, record the filing, record the payment, and show the liability account before and after.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.
