lessons.title: 10.6 Common Sales Tax Mistakes
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 10: Sales Tax and VAT

LESSON NOTE: COMMON SALES TAX MISTAKES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCommon Sales Tax MistakesBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Recognise the most frequent sales tax errors
  • Explain the consequence of each
  • Build checks that prevent them

1. Introduction

Sales tax errors are rarely exotic. The same handful of mistakes account for most penalties, and each has a simple preventive check.

2. The frequent errors

MistakeConsequencePrevention
Spending tax collectedCannot pay at filing; penaltiesMove tax collected to a separate account weekly
Treating tax as incomeSales and profit overstatedNever post tax to an income account
Wrong tax status on an itemUnder- or over-charging every sale of itReview item tax status at setup and after rate changes
Charging exempt customersCustomer disputes and refundsFlag exempt customers on their record
Missing input tax on purchasesPaying more tax than necessaryEnter supplier tax on every bill
Filing lateAutomatic penaltiesDiarise filing dates for the year
Changing a filed periodThe return no longer matches the accountsLock periods with a closing date after filing

3. The single best control

Example: Each week, transfer the tax collected that week into a separate bank account and do not touch it. At filing, the money is simply there. Organisations that do this almost never fall into tax arrears; organisations that do not, frequently do.

4. After a rate change

Note: When a tax rate changes, review every item and every recurring transaction. Recurring invoices in particular keep charging the old rate silently, and the shortfall is only discovered at filing.

Summary

  • Most sales tax problems come from a small set of recurring mistakes.
  • Setting tax collected aside weekly is the single most effective control.
  • After a rate change, review all items and recurring transactions.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Tax arrearsUnpaid tax that has fallen overdue.
Rate changeA change in the statutory tax percentage.
Closing dateA lock preventing edits to filed periods.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What is the single most effective control against tax arrears?

  1. Transferring tax collected into a separate account regularly
  2. Filing early
  3. Charging more tax
  4. Hiring an accountant
Show answer

Answer: A. If the money is physically set aside, it is available at filing.

Why review recurring transactions after a rate change?

  1. They keep charging the old rate silently until discovered at filing
  2. They stop working
  3. They double the tax
  4. They delete themselves
Show answer

Answer: A. Recurring templates hold the old rate until edited.

What is the consequence of missing input tax on purchases?

  1. You pay more tax than necessary
  2. You pay less tax
  3. Nothing
  4. Sales fall
Show answer

Answer: A. Unclaimed input tax increases your net payment.

Why lock a period after filing?

  1. So later edits cannot make the accounts disagree with the submitted return
  2. To stop new sales
  3. To reduce tax
  4. To speed up reports
Show answer

Answer: A. A filed return must continue to match the underlying records.

Short answer

List four common sales tax mistakes and one prevention each.

Model answer

Spending tax collected — set it aside weekly; treating tax as income — never post to income; wrong item tax status — review at setup; filing late — diarise the dates.

Why is a filed period locked?

Model answer

Because editing transactions after filing makes the accounts disagree with the submitted return, which is very hard to explain to an inspector.

Class Activity

  1. Audit a sample file for three of the mistakes listed and report what you find.
  2. Design the weekly tax set-aside routine for an organisation.

Assignment

Write a sales tax control procedure for an organisation covering the set-aside routine, the pre-filing checks, the treatment of rate changes, and the period-locking policy.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 11.1 The Reports Centre
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 11: Reports and Financial Statements

LESSON NOTE: THE REPORTS CENTRE

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingThe Reports CentreBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Navigate the reports centre
  • Find the report you need quickly
  • Distinguish the three report families

1. Introduction

QuickBooks ships with dozens of reports. Knowing three families and four favourites is enough for almost all day-to-day management.

2. The layout

TabContains
StandardAll built-in reports, grouped by area
Custom reportsReports you have customised and saved
Management reportsFormatted packs combining several reports with a cover page

3. The four you will use constantly

  • Profit and Loss — did we make money?
  • Balance Sheet — what do we own and owe?
  • Accounts Receivable Ageing — who owes us?
  • Accounts Payable Ageing — who do we owe?

Almost every management question in a small organisation is answered by one of these four. Master them before exploring the rest.

4. Finding reports fast

  1. Use the search box at the top of the Standard tab; typing three letters is faster than scrolling.
  2. Star a report to add it to Favourites at the top.
  3. Save a customised report so the same settings are one click away next time.
Example: An owner who checks the same three reports each Monday should star all three; the weekly routine then takes seconds rather than minutes of navigation.

Summary

  • Reports are grouped into Standard, Custom and Management report packs.
  • Four reports — P&L, Balance Sheet, and the two ageings — answer most questions.
  • Star favourites and save customisations to reach reports in one click.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Standard reportsThe built-in report library.
Custom reportA saved report with your own settings.
Management reportA formatted pack of several reports.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which four reports answer most day-to-day management questions?

  1. Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, and the receivable and payable ageings
  2. Payroll, inventory, tax and budget
  3. Only the Profit and Loss
  4. The dashboard panels
Show answer

Answer: A. These four cover profitability, position, money owed to you and money you owe.

What is a management report in QuickBooks?

  1. A formatted pack combining several reports with a cover page
  2. A report only managers can see
  3. A payroll report
  4. A tax return
Show answer

Answer: A. It is a presentation-ready bundle of reports.

How do you reach a frequently used report fastest?

  1. Star it so it appears in Favourites
  2. Scroll the full list each time
  3. Export it
  4. Print it
Show answer

Answer: A. Starring puts it at the top of the reports centre.

What does saving a customised report achieve?

  1. The same settings are one click away next time
  2. It changes the data
  3. It locks the period
  4. It emails the report
Show answer

Answer: A. Saved customisations preserve date ranges, filters and columns.

Short answer

Name the three tabs of the reports centre.

Model answer

Standard, Custom reports and Management reports.

Why master four reports before exploring the rest?

Model answer

Because those four answer nearly every routine management question, and depth in them is more useful than shallow familiarity with dozens.

Class Activity

  1. Star four reports in a sample file and time how long the weekly routine takes.
  2. List the reports a manager you know would want each Monday.

Assignment

Design a weekly and monthly reporting routine for an organisation, naming each report, who reads it, and what decision it supports.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 11.2 Profit and Loss Report
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 11: Reports and Financial Statements

LESSON NOTE: PROFIT AND LOSS REPORT

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingProfit and Loss ReportBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Run and read a Profit and Loss
  • Explain each section
  • Use comparatives to interpret performance

1. Introduction

The Profit and Loss answers one question over a period of time: did we make money? Everything on it is either something earned or something consumed.

2. The structure

SectionMeaning
IncomeWhat you earned from your main activities
Cost of Goods SoldThe direct cost of what you sold
Gross ProfitIncome less COGS — the margin on trading
ExpensesThe cost of running the organisation
Net Operating IncomeGross profit less expenses
Other Income/ExpenseItems outside normal trading, e.g. interest
Net IncomeThe final profit or loss

3. Gross profit is the number to watch

Example: Sales $50,000, COGS $30,000 → gross profit $20,000, a 40% margin. If margin falls to 32% next month while sales are flat, something specific has happened: purchase prices rose, selling prices fell, or stock is being lost. Net profit alone would not have told you which.

4. Always run comparatives

A single month's Profit and Loss is nearly meaningless. Add a comparison column — previous period, or same period last year — and the report starts answering questions instead of just reporting facts.

Note: Set the report to show percentage of income. A cost that is 4% of income this month and 7% next month is a finding, even if the absolute figure barely moved.

5. Cash vs accrual

Switching the report between cash and accrual can change it dramatically. Accrual shows what was earned and incurred; cash shows what was received and paid. Know which basis you are reading before drawing any conclusion.

Summary

  • The Profit and Loss covers a period and shows income, cost of sales, expenses and net profit.
  • Gross profit margin isolates trading performance and is the first number to check.
  • Always run comparatives and percentages; a single column tells you very little.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Gross profitIncome less cost of goods sold.
Net incomeThe final profit or loss after all income and expenses.
ComparativeA prior period shown alongside for comparison.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Sales $50,000 and COGS $30,000. What is the gross margin?

  1. 40%
  2. 60%
  3. 30%
  4. 20%
Show answer

Answer: A. Gross profit $20,000 divided by sales $50,000 is 40%.

Why is a single-month Profit and Loss of limited use?

  1. Without a comparative there is nothing to judge the figures against
  2. It is always wrong
  3. It cannot be printed
  4. It omits income
Show answer

Answer: A. Interpretation requires a benchmark, usually the prior period or prior year.

Gross margin falls from 40% to 32% with flat sales. What does this suggest?

  1. Purchase prices rose, selling prices fell, or stock is being lost
  2. Sales are growing
  3. Expenses fell
  4. Nothing
Show answer

Answer: A. Margin movement isolates a trading cause rather than an overhead one.

What is the difference between the cash and accrual basis on this report?

  1. Accrual shows earned and incurred; cash shows received and paid
  2. They are identical
  3. Cash includes more expenses always
  4. Accrual excludes sales
Show answer

Answer: A. The basis changes when items are recognised, sometimes dramatically.

Short answer

Name the seven sections of a Profit and Loss in order.

Model answer

Income, Cost of Goods Sold, Gross Profit, Expenses, Net Operating Income, Other Income/Expense, Net Income.

Why show costs as a percentage of income?

Model answer

Because a cost rising as a share of income is a finding even when the absolute amount looks stable.

Class Activity

  1. Run a Profit and Loss with a prior-year comparison and note three findings.
  2. Calculate gross margin for three months and comment on the trend.

Assignment

Produce a Profit and Loss with comparatives and percentages for an organisation, then write a one-page commentary explaining the three most significant movements and their likely causes.

lessons.title: 11.3 Balance Sheet Report
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 11: Reports and Financial Statements

LESSON NOTE: BALANCE SHEET REPORT

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingBalance Sheet ReportBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Run and read a Balance Sheet
  • Explain why it balances
  • Spot warning signs in the figures

1. Introduction

The Balance Sheet is a photograph at a single moment: what the organisation owns, what it owes, and what is left for the owners.

2. The equation

Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

It always balances because every transaction has two equal sides. If a Balance Sheet does not balance in QuickBooks, the cause is almost always a damaged or unusual transaction rather than an accounting failure.

3. Reading it

SectionContainsQuestion answered
Current assetsBank, receivables, inventoryWhat can become cash within a year?
Fixed assetsVehicles, equipment, propertyWhat do we own long term?
Current liabilitiesPayables, tax, short-term loansWhat must we pay within a year?
Long-term liabilitiesLoans beyond a yearWhat do we owe long term?
EquityCapital, drawings, retained earningsWhat belongs to the owners?

4. Warning signs

  • Current liabilities exceed current assets — the organisation may not be able to pay its short-term debts.
  • Receivables growing faster than sales — customers are paying more slowly.
  • Inventory growing while sales are flat — cash is being converted into unsold stock.
  • Opening Balance Equity still holding a balance — the file was never properly set up.
  • A negative bank balance in the accounts — either genuinely overdrawn, or transactions are missing.
Example: Current assets $40,000 against current liabilities $55,000 gives a current ratio of 0.73. The organisation cannot cover its short-term obligations from short-term assets, and that is a warning that needs action, not a rounding issue.

Summary

  • The Balance Sheet is a snapshot showing assets, liabilities and equity at one date.
  • It balances because every transaction has two equal sides.
  • Watch for current liabilities exceeding current assets, growing receivables, and leftover Opening Balance Equity.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Current assetAn asset expected to become cash within a year.
Current ratioCurrent assets divided by current liabilities.
Retained earningsAccumulated profit kept in the business.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Current assets $40,000 and current liabilities $55,000. What does this indicate?

  1. Short-term obligations exceed short-term assets — a liquidity warning
  2. Strong liquidity
  3. High profit
  4. Nothing
Show answer

Answer: A. A current ratio below 1 signals difficulty meeting short-term debts.

Why does the Balance Sheet always balance?

  1. Every transaction posts two equal sides
  2. QuickBooks forces it
  3. Because assets are estimated
  4. It does not always balance
Show answer

Answer: A. Double-entry guarantees debits equal credits.

Inventory grows while sales stay flat. What is happening?

  1. Cash is being converted into unsold stock
  2. Sales are improving
  3. Profit is rising
  4. Liabilities are falling
Show answer

Answer: A. Stock build-up with flat sales ties up cash without return.

A balance still sitting in Opening Balance Equity means:

  1. The file setup was never completed
  2. Profits are high
  3. Tax is owed
  4. The bank is wrong
Show answer

Answer: A. That account is temporary and should have been cleared at setup.

Short answer

State the accounting equation and explain why it holds.

Model answer

Assets = Liabilities + Equity; it holds because every transaction records equal debits and credits.

Name three warning signs visible on a Balance Sheet.

Model answer

Current liabilities exceeding current assets; receivables growing faster than sales; inventory rising while sales are flat.

Class Activity

  1. Run a Balance Sheet and calculate the current ratio.
  2. Identify two warning signs in a sample company's Balance Sheet.

Assignment

Analyse a Balance Sheet for an organisation: calculate the current ratio, identify the three most significant risks visible, and recommend an action for each.

lessons.title: 11.4 Cash Flow Statement
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 11: Reports and Financial Statements

LESSON NOTE: CASH FLOW STATEMENT

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCash Flow StatementBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Read a statement of cash flows
  • Explain why profit is not cash
  • Identify the three activity categories

1. Introduction

A profitable organisation can still run out of money. The cash flow statement explains the gap between the profit reported and the cash actually in the bank.

2. Why profit is not cash

ReasonEffect
Sales made on creditProfit recorded, no cash yet
Stock purchasedCash gone, no expense until sold
Loan repaymentCash gone, not an expense at all
Owner drawingsCash gone, not an expense
DepreciationAn expense with no cash movement
Asset purchasedLarge cash outflow, small annual expense
Example: Profit $10,000 for the month, yet the bank fell $3,000. Receivables rose $8,000 and a $5,000 loan instalment was paid. The profit was real; it is simply sitting in customers' hands and in the lender's account.

3. The three sections

  • Operating — cash from normal trading; this should be positive over time
  • Investing — buying and selling long-term assets
  • Financing — loans received and repaid, capital introduced, drawings

4. What to look for

Note: Persistent negative operating cash flow alongside reported profit is the single most dangerous pattern in small-organisation finance. It usually means profit is trapped in receivables or stock, and it is how profitable businesses fail.

Summary

  • Cash flow explains the difference between reported profit and money in the bank.
  • The three sections are operating, investing and financing.
  • Persistent negative operating cash flow with reported profit is a serious warning.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Operating activitiesCash flows from normal trading.
Investing activitiesCash flows from buying or selling long-term assets.
Financing activitiesCash flows from loans, capital and drawings.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Profit is $10,000 but the bank fell $3,000. What could explain this?

  1. Receivables rose and a loan instalment was paid
  2. Profit was fabricated
  3. The bank made an error
  4. Sales were not recorded
Show answer

Answer: A. Profit can be tied up in receivables while cash leaves for non-expense items.

Which section should be positive over time in a healthy organisation?

  1. Operating
  2. Investing
  3. Financing
  4. None
Show answer

Answer: A. Trading should ultimately generate cash.

A loan repayment appears in which section?

  1. Financing
  2. Operating
  3. Investing
  4. It does not appear
Show answer

Answer: A. Repaying borrowings is a financing cash flow.

Why is depreciation added back in a cash flow statement?

  1. It is an expense that involves no cash movement
  2. It is not a real cost
  3. It increases cash
  4. It is a liability
Show answer

Answer: A. Depreciation reduces profit without any cash leaving.

Short answer

Give three reasons profit and cash differ.

Model answer

Credit sales record profit before cash arrives; stock consumes cash before it becomes an expense; loan repayments and drawings consume cash without being expenses.

Why is negative operating cash flow with positive profit dangerous?

Model answer

It means the profit is not converting into cash, so the organisation can exhaust its money while still appearing profitable on paper.

Class Activity

  1. Run a cash flow statement and identify the largest item in each section.
  2. Explain a month where profit rose but cash fell, using a real or invented example.

Assignment

Produce a cash flow statement for an organisation and write a commentary explaining the difference between the profit reported and the movement in the bank balance.

lessons.title: 11.5 Customizing Reports
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 11: Reports and Financial Statements

LESSON NOTE: CUSTOMIZING REPORTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingCustomizing ReportsBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Customise a report's period, columns and filters
  • Save a customised report
  • Choose customisations that reveal something

1. Introduction

A default report shows everything about everyone. Customising narrows it to the question you are actually asking, which is what turns data into an answer.

2. What can be changed

ControlUse
Date rangeThe period examined
Compare toPrior period or prior year alongside
ColumnsSplit by month, customer, class or product
FilterRestrict to certain customers, accounts or classes
Rows/columnsShow percentages of income or of the total
Header/footerTitle and notes for distribution

3. Customisations that actually reveal something

  • Profit and Loss by month — exposes seasonality and one-off spikes
  • Profit and Loss by class — shows which programme or branch is profitable
  • Profit and Loss with % of income — shows cost discipline independent of scale
  • Sales by customer — reveals concentration risk
  • Expenses filtered to one account, by month — pinpoints when a cost changed
Example: Running a Profit and Loss split by month across a year turns twelve numbers into a pattern: a cost that appears only in three months is probably annual insurance, not a monthly overhead.

4. Saving

Once customised, use Save customisation, give it a clear name, and optionally share it with other users. The report then appears under Custom reports with all settings intact, which makes a monthly routine repeatable rather than re-created each time.

Summary

  • Customise period, comparatives, columns, filters and percentages to answer a specific question.
  • Splitting by month or class usually reveals more than changing the date range.
  • Save customisations so a reporting routine is repeatable.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
FilterA restriction limiting a report to selected records.
Comparative columnA prior period shown alongside the current one.
Save customisationStoring report settings for reuse.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which customisation best exposes seasonality?

  1. Splitting the Profit and Loss by month
  2. Changing the font
  3. Filtering to one customer
  4. Hiding the header
Show answer

Answer: A. A monthly split turns totals into a visible pattern.

What does showing costs as a percentage of income reveal?

  1. Cost discipline independent of the scale of trading
  2. The bank balance
  3. Tax owed
  4. Customer names
Show answer

Answer: A. Percentages let you compare periods of different sizes fairly.

Which report reveals concentration risk?

  1. Sales by customer
  2. Balance Sheet
  3. Payroll summary
  4. Bank reconciliation
Show answer

Answer: A. It shows whether too much revenue depends on too few customers.

Why save a customisation?

  1. The monthly routine becomes repeatable rather than rebuilt each time
  2. It changes the data
  3. It locks the period
  4. It emails the report
Show answer

Answer: A. Saved settings preserve dates, filters and columns.

Short answer

Name four things you can customise on a report.

Model answer

Date range, comparative columns, the column split, filters, percentage display and header text.

Give an example of a customisation that turns data into an answer.

Model answer

A Profit and Loss split by month across a year, which reveals whether a cost is monthly or a one-off annual charge.

Class Activity

  1. Customise and save three reports in a sample file.
  2. Design the customisation that would answer 'which branch is most profitable?'

Assignment

Create a set of at least five saved custom reports for an organisation. For each, state the question it answers and the customisations applied.

lessons.title: 11.6 Memorizing and Scheduling Reports
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 11: Reports and Financial Statements

LESSON NOTE: MEMORIZING AND SCHEDULING REPORTS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingMemorizing and Scheduling ReportsBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Save and schedule a report
  • Build a management report pack
  • Automate a reporting routine

1. Introduction

Reports that must be remembered often are not run. Scheduling turns a good intention into something that happens whether or not anyone remembers.

2. Scheduling

  1. Open a saved custom report.
  2. Choose Edit schedule or Set email schedule.
  3. Set the frequency and the recipients.
  4. Add a short covering note explaining what the reader should look at.
  5. Save.
Note: Send scheduled reports to people who will actually act on them. A report emailed to twelve people is usually read by none; a report emailed to the one person who can act on it gets acted on.

3. Management report packs

ElementPurpose
Cover pageOrganisation name, period, who prepared it
Table of contentsNavigation for a multi-report pack
Selected reportsUsually P&L, Balance Sheet and cash summary
Notes pageYour commentary on what the numbers mean

The notes page is the part that matters. Numbers without interpretation get filed; numbers with three sentences of explanation get discussed.

4. A workable routine

Example: Weekly: receivables ageing to the person who chases debts. Monthly: a management pack with P&L, Balance Sheet and commentary to the owner or board. Quarterly: the same pack with year-to-date comparatives. Set once, delivered automatically.

Summary

  • Scheduling converts a reporting intention into an automatic routine.
  • Send each report only to those who can act on it.
  • A management pack's notes page is what makes the numbers get discussed.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Scheduled reportA report emailed automatically on a set frequency.
Management report packA formatted bundle of reports with a cover and notes.
CommentaryWritten interpretation accompanying the figures.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why send a report only to those who can act on it?

  1. A report sent to everyone is usually read by no one
  2. To save data
  3. It is legally required
  4. Reports cost money to send
Show answer

Answer: A. Diffused responsibility means nobody owns the action.

Which part of a management pack makes the numbers get discussed?

  1. The notes and commentary page
  2. The cover page
  3. The table of contents
  4. The page numbers
Show answer

Answer: A. Interpretation is what turns figures into decisions.

What is the benefit of scheduling over manual running?

  1. It happens whether or not anyone remembers
  2. It is more accurate
  3. It changes the figures
  4. It reduces tax
Show answer

Answer: A. Automation removes reliance on memory.

A sensible weekly scheduled report for collections would be:

  1. The receivables ageing, sent to whoever chases debts
  2. The Balance Sheet to all staff
  3. The payroll details to everyone
  4. The chart of accounts
Show answer

Answer: A. It reaches the person who can act, at the frequency the task needs.

Short answer

Describe a sensible reporting routine across week, month and quarter.

Model answer

Weekly receivables ageing to the collector; monthly management pack with P&L, Balance Sheet and commentary to the owner or board; quarterly the same with year-to-date comparatives.

Why does a notes page matter more than the reports themselves?

Model answer

Because most readers cannot interpret raw figures quickly, and a short written explanation is what prompts a decision.

Class Activity

  1. Schedule one report in a sample file and build a two-report management pack.
  2. Draft the commentary you would write for a month where profit fell but cash improved.

Assignment

Design a complete automated reporting routine for an organisation: which reports, to whom, how often, and a sample commentary page for one month.

lessons.title: 11.7 Exporting Reports to Excel
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 11: Reports and Financial Statements

LESSON NOTE: EXPORTING REPORTS TO EXCEL

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingExporting Reports to ExcelBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Export a report to Excel or PDF
  • Choose the right format for the purpose
  • Work with exported data safely

1. Introduction

QuickBooks reports are flexible, but sometimes you need to reshape figures, build a chart, or send something that cannot be altered. Exporting handles both cases.

2. Which format

FormatKeepsUse for
ExcelLive figures you can edit and recalculateAnalysis, charts, reshaping data
PDFA fixed image of the reportSending to banks, funders and boards
PrintPaperMeetings and filing
EmailPDF attachedRoutine distribution
Note: Send a PDF to anyone outside the organisation. An Excel file can be edited by the recipient, and you cannot later prove what you actually sent.

3. Exporting well

  1. Set the report exactly as you want it before exporting; fixing layout in Excel is slower.
  2. Export to Excel for analysis, PDF for distribution.
  3. Name the file with the organisation, report and period, e.g. 'TIH_P&L_2026-01'.
  4. Keep exports in a dated folder so the version sent is always identifiable.

4. The danger of exports

Example: An exported Excel file is a snapshot. If a transaction is later corrected in QuickBooks, the export does not change. A board discussing last week's spreadsheet may be discussing figures that have since been superseded — always state the export date on any distributed file.

Summary

  • Export to Excel for analysis and PDF for distribution.
  • Set the report fully before exporting; reshaping afterwards is slower.
  • An export is a snapshot; always label it with the date it was produced.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
ExportSaving a report outside QuickBooks in another format.
SnapshotA fixed copy of data as it stood at one moment.
Version controlKeeping track of which copy is current.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which format should you send to a bank or funder?

  1. PDF, because it cannot easily be altered
  2. Excel
  3. A screenshot
  4. A text message
Show answer

Answer: A. A fixed format protects the integrity of what you sent.

Why label an export with its date?

  1. It is a snapshot and may be superseded by later corrections
  2. It is legally required
  3. It reduces file size
  4. It speeds up opening
Show answer

Answer: A. Later corrections in QuickBooks do not update an exported file.

When should you export to Excel?

  1. When you need to analyse, reshape or chart the figures
  2. When sending to a funder
  3. When printing
  4. Never
Show answer

Answer: A. Excel keeps figures live and editable for analysis.

What should be done before exporting?

  1. Set the report exactly as required
  2. Nothing
  3. Delete old data
  4. Lock the period
Show answer

Answer: A. Fixing layout in the source is faster than reworking it afterwards.

Short answer

Give the right format for analysis and for sending to a board, with reasons.

Model answer

Excel for analysis because figures stay editable and can be charted; PDF for the board because it is fixed and cannot be altered.

Explain the risk of a board discussing an exported spreadsheet.

Model answer

The export is frozen at the moment it was produced, so later corrections in QuickBooks are not reflected and the meeting may rely on superseded figures.

Class Activity

  1. Export three reports in two formats and compare what each preserves.
  2. Design a file-naming convention for exported reports.

Assignment

Produce a monthly reporting pack as exports, applying a clear naming convention, and write a short policy on which formats go to which audiences and why.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 11.8 Reading Reports to Make Decisions
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 11: Reports and Financial Statements

LESSON NOTE: READING REPORTS TO MAKE DECISIONS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingReading Reports to Make DecisionsBeginner to Advanced45 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Turn report figures into decisions
  • Apply a simple review sequence
  • Write a short commentary for management

1. Introduction

This lesson is the point of the whole course. Every earlier skill exists so that someone can look at a report and decide something with confidence.

2. A review sequence that works

  1. Cash first. Bank balance and cash flow — can we meet obligations for the next month?
  2. Then who owes us. Receivables ageing — is anything hardening past 60 days?
  3. Then who we owe. Payables ageing — is anything about to damage a supplier relationship?
  4. Then margin. Gross profit percentage against last period — is trading still healthy?
  5. Then overheads. Expenses as a percentage of income — is any category drifting up?
  6. Then position. Balance Sheet — current ratio and anything unusual.

Six checks, in that order, take about fifteen minutes and cover almost every way a small organisation gets into trouble.

3. From figure to decision

FindingDecision
Gross margin down 6 pointsReview purchase prices and selling prices this week
Receivables over 60 days risingStop further credit to those customers; escalate collection
Operating cash flow negative for three monthsCut discretionary spending; accelerate collections
One customer is 45% of salesActively seek new customers to reduce dependence
An expense category up 40% with no explanationInvestigate before approving further spend

4. Writing the commentary

Example: Good commentary is short and specific: 'Gross margin fell from 41% to 35% because cement purchase prices rose 12% in January and selling prices were not adjusted. Recommendation: raise prices 8% from 1 March or renegotiate supply.' Three sentences: what happened, why, and what to do.

5. The discipline

Note: A report you do not act on is a cost, not an asset. If the same finding appears three months running with no action, either the finding is not important or the reporting routine has failed.

Summary

  • Review in a fixed order: cash, receivables, payables, margin, overheads, position.
  • Every finding should produce a decision, not just an observation.
  • Good commentary states what happened, why, and what to do — in three sentences.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Review sequenceA fixed order for examining reports.
CommentaryA short written interpretation of the figures.
Concentration riskOver-dependence on a small number of customers.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What should be checked first in the review sequence?

  1. Cash — can we meet obligations next month?
  2. Net profit
  3. The chart of accounts
  4. Payroll
Show answer

Answer: A. Cash is what an organisation actually runs out of.

One customer represents 45% of sales. What is the concern?

  1. Concentration risk — losing them would be severe
  2. Nothing, it is efficient
  3. Tax will rise
  4. Margin will fall
Show answer

Answer: A. Heavy dependence on one customer is a structural risk.

What three things should a good commentary state?

  1. What happened, why it happened, and what to do
  2. The date, the author and the page count
  3. Only the figures
  4. Only the recommendation
Show answer

Answer: A. Cause and action are what make figures useful.

The same finding appears three months running with no action. What does this mean?

  1. Either the finding is not important or the reporting routine has failed
  2. The report is wrong
  3. Profit is rising
  4. Nothing
Show answer

Answer: A. Reporting without action is a cost rather than a benefit.

Short answer

List the six checks in the review sequence in order.

Model answer

Cash; receivables ageing; payables ageing; gross margin; overheads as a percentage of income; balance sheet position.

Write a three-sentence commentary for a month where margin fell due to rising purchase prices.

Model answer

Gross margin fell from 41% to 35%. Purchase prices rose 12% while selling prices were unchanged. Recommend an 8% price increase or renegotiating supply terms.

Class Activity

  1. Apply the six-step review to a sample company and write one decision per step.
  2. Draft a three-sentence commentary for a month of your choice.

Assignment

Carry out a complete monthly review of an organisation using the six-step sequence. Produce a one-page commentary with at least four findings, each paired with a specific recommended action.

modules.title: Module 12: Advanced Features and Closing the Books

lessons.title: 12.1 Journal Entries in QuickBooks
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 12: Advanced Features and Closing the Books

LESSON NOTE: JOURNAL ENTRIES IN QUICKBOOKS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingJournal Entries in QuickBooksBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create a journal entry
  • Identify when a journal is appropriate
  • Avoid using journals to bypass proper forms

1. Introduction

A journal entry posts debits and credits directly, bypassing the friendly forms. It is powerful, occasionally necessary, and frequently misused.

2. When a journal IS appropriate

  • Depreciation charges
  • Accruals and prepayments at period end
  • Correcting a misposting between accounts
  • Recording payroll calculated outside QuickBooks
  • Reclassifying an amount between accounts
  • Opening balances during setup

3. When it is NOT

Do not journalUse insteadWhy
A customer saleInvoice or sales receiptA journal does not update the customer's balance properly
A supplier purchaseBill or expenseThe payable and vendor history are bypassed
A bank paymentExpense or chequeReconciliation becomes far harder
Inventory movementItem-based transactionsQuantities are not updated at all
Note: Journalling directly to Accounts Receivable, Accounts Payable or Inventory breaks the link between the control account and the underlying records. The Balance Sheet may still balance while the customer, supplier and stock detail is wrong.

4. Creating one

  1. + New → Journal entry.
  2. Enter the date and a journal number.
  3. Enter each line with an account, a debit or credit, and a description.
  4. Confirm total debits equal total credits.
  5. Write a clear memo explaining why the entry exists.
Example: Monthly depreciation: Debit Depreciation Expense $250, Credit Accumulated Depreciation $250. Memo: 'Monthly depreciation on delivery van, straight line over 5 years.'

5. The memo rule

Every journal needs a memo that would let a stranger — an auditor, or you in two years — understand why it exists. An unexplained journal is the first thing an auditor questions and the hardest thing to defend.

Summary

  • Journals suit depreciation, accruals, corrections and externally calculated payroll.
  • Never journal sales, purchases, bank payments or inventory movements.
  • Every journal needs a memo explaining why it exists.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Journal entryA direct posting of debits and credits.
AccrualA cost incurred but not yet invoiced.
Control accountA summary account such as Accounts Receivable backed by detailed records.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Which of these is an appropriate use of a journal entry?

  1. Recording monthly depreciation
  2. Recording a customer sale
  3. Recording a bank payment
  4. Recording an inventory purchase
Show answer

Answer: A. Depreciation has no form of its own and is a classic journal.

Why should you not journal directly to Accounts Receivable?

  1. It breaks the link between the control account and the customer records
  2. It is impossible
  3. It doubles the balance
  4. It deletes the customer
Show answer

Answer: A. The total may balance while the customer detail becomes wrong.

What must every journal entry include?

  1. A memo explaining why it exists
  2. A customer name
  3. An attachment
  4. A tax code
Show answer

Answer: A. An unexplained journal is indefensible under audit.

Journalling an inventory movement causes what problem?

  1. Quantities on hand are not updated
  2. Nothing
  3. Sales are doubled
  4. The bank changes
Show answer

Answer: A. Only item-based transactions move stock quantities.

Short answer

List four legitimate uses of a journal entry.

Model answer

Depreciation, accruals and prepayments, correcting a misposting, and recording payroll calculated outside QuickBooks.

Why is an unexplained journal a problem under audit?

Model answer

Because nobody can verify why it was posted, and unexplained direct postings are the classic route for concealing errors or manipulation.

Class Activity

  1. Post a depreciation journal in a sample file with a proper memo.
  2. Identify three transactions that should never be journalled and say what to use instead.

Assignment

Prepare the month-end journals for an organisation: depreciation, one accrual and one prepayment. Show each entry with a memo, and explain why each could not have been recorded through a standard form.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 12.2 Budgets in QuickBooks
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 12: Advanced Features and Closing the Books

LESSON NOTE: BUDGETS IN QUICKBOOKS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingBudgets in QuickBooksBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Create a budget
  • Run a budget versus actual report
  • Use variances to manage

1. Introduction

A budget is a plan expressed in money. Its value is not the plan itself but the monthly comparison against reality, which tells you early when something is drifting.

2. Creating one

  1. Gear → Budgeting → Add budget.
  2. Choose the fiscal year and the interval, usually monthly.
  3. Optionally subdivide by class, customer or location.
  4. Enter figures per account per month, or enter a year total and let QuickBooks spread it.
  5. Save and name it clearly, e.g. 'FY2026 Operating Budget'.
Note: Pre-fill from last year's actuals where possible, then adjust. Building a budget from a blank sheet takes far longer and is usually less realistic than adjusting what actually happened.

3. Budget versus actual

ColumnMeaning
ActualWhat really happened
BudgetWhat you planned
Over/UnderThe variance in money
% of BudgetThe variance in proportion

Read the percentage column first. A $500 overspend on a $600 budget is far more serious than a $500 overspend on a $50,000 budget, even though the money is identical.

4. Acting on variances

Example: Fuel budget $1,000 per month; actual $1,650 — 65% over. That is not a rounding issue: either the budget was unrealistic, fuel prices moved, or usage has changed. All three demand a different response, so investigate before adjusting the budget.

5. The discipline

Note: Do not quietly revise the budget to match actuals. That converts a management tool into a record of what happened, which is what the Profit and Loss already is.

Summary

  • A budget's value is in the monthly comparison against actuals, not the plan itself.
  • Read variances as percentages, not just absolute amounts.
  • Investigate variances rather than revising the budget to match reality.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
BudgetA financial plan for a future period.
VarianceThe difference between budget and actual.
Budget versus actualA report comparing planned and real figures.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why read the percentage variance rather than the money?

  1. A $500 overspend on a $600 budget is far more serious than on a $50,000 budget
  2. Percentages are easier
  3. Money is unreliable
  4. It is required
Show answer

Answer: A. Proportion shows the significance of the variance.

What is the recommended starting point for a budget?

  1. Last year's actuals, then adjusted
  2. A blank sheet
  3. The bank balance
  4. A competitor's figures
Show answer

Answer: A. Adjusting real history is faster and more realistic.

Fuel is budgeted $1,000 but actual is $1,650. What should you do first?

  1. Investigate whether prices, usage or the budget itself caused it
  2. Increase the budget
  3. Ignore it
  4. Stop buying fuel
Show answer

Answer: A. The cause determines the correct response.

Why not revise the budget to match actuals?

  1. It turns a management tool into a record of what already happened
  2. It is not allowed
  3. It changes tax
  4. It deletes the variance
Show answer

Answer: A. The Profit and Loss already records what happened; the budget exists to challenge it.

Short answer

Name the four columns of a budget versus actual report.

Model answer

Actual, Budget, Over/Under variance, and percentage of budget.

Explain why a budget's value lies in the comparison rather than the plan.

Model answer

Because the plan alone changes nothing; the monthly comparison is what reveals drift early enough to act on it.

Class Activity

  1. Create a simple budget in a sample file and run budget versus actual.
  2. Analyse three variances and propose a response for each.

Assignment

Build an annual budget for an organisation, then produce a budget versus actual report for one month with a written explanation of every variance over 15%.

lessons.title: 12.3 Class and Location Tracking
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 12: Advanced Features and Closing the Books

LESSON NOTE: CLASS AND LOCATION TRACKING

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingClass and Location TrackingBeginner to Advanced40 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Turn on and use classes and locations
  • Report profitability by segment
  • Choose between class, location and project

1. Introduction

Classes and locations cut across the whole file, letting you report income and cost by programme, branch or funder without creating separate accounts for each.

2. The three segment tools

ToolCuts acrossBest for
ClassAny transactionProgrammes, funders, departments, product lines
LocationAny transactionBranches, sites, regions
ProjectCustomer-related workA specific job with income and cost

3. Turning them on

Gear → Account and settings → Advanced → Categories. Switch on Track classes and, if needed, Track locations. Set 'Warn me when a transaction is not assigned a class' — without this, unclassified transactions accumulate silently and every segment report becomes incomplete.

4. Why NGOs need this

Example: An NGO runs three funded programmes from one bank account. Without classes, the accounts show total income and total expenditure and no funder can be told how their money was spent. With a class per funder, a Profit and Loss by Class produces each funder's report directly from the accounts — no spreadsheet, no guesswork.

5. Discipline

Note: Segment reporting is only as good as its weakest habit. One unclassified month makes the annual report unusable, so the warning setting and a monthly check for unclassified transactions are essential, not optional.

Summary

  • Classes and locations tag transactions so income and cost can be reported by segment.
  • Enable the warning for unassigned transactions or reports will silently be incomplete.
  • Classes suit programmes and funders; locations suit branches; projects suit specific jobs.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
ClassA tag for reporting income and cost by programme or department.
LocationA tag for reporting by branch or site.
UnclassifiedA transaction with no class assigned.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

An NGO must report spending to three funders from one bank account. What should it use?

  1. Class tracking, with a class per funder
  2. Separate companies
  3. Separate accounts per funder
  4. Projects only
Show answer

Answer: A. Classes cut across all transactions and produce a Profit and Loss per funder.

Why enable the warning for unassigned transactions?

  1. Unclassified transactions accumulate silently and make segment reports incomplete
  2. It is legally required
  3. It speeds up entry
  4. It reduces tax
Show answer

Answer: A. Without the warning, gaps appear only when the annual report is wrong.

Which tool best suits reporting by branch?

  1. Location
  2. Class
  3. Project
  4. Customer
Show answer

Answer: A. Locations are designed for sites, branches and regions.

Segment reporting quality depends most on:

  1. Consistent tagging of every transaction
  2. The number of classes
  3. The plan tier
  4. Report formatting
Show answer

Answer: A. One unclassified month undermines the whole year's analysis.

Short answer

Distinguish class, location and project in one sentence each.

Model answer

Class tags any transaction by programme or department; location tags by branch or site; project tracks income and cost for a specific customer job.

Why is a monthly check for unclassified transactions necessary?

Model answer

Because gaps are invisible in normal reports and only surface when a segment report is produced, by which time the data may be months out of date.

Class Activity

  1. Turn on classes in a sample file and run a Profit and Loss by Class.
  2. Design the class structure for an NGO with three funders and two departments.

Assignment

Design and implement segment tracking for an organisation with multiple programmes or branches. Produce a Profit and Loss by segment and explain the monthly discipline needed to keep it reliable.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 12.4 Attachments and Document Management
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 12: Advanced Features and Closing the Books

LESSON NOTE: ATTACHMENTS AND DOCUMENT MANAGEMENT

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingAttachments and Document ManagementBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Attach documents to transactions
  • Build a paperless record system
  • Explain the audit value of attachments

1. Introduction

An accounting record without its supporting document is an assertion. With the receipt attached, it is evidence. Attachments turn QuickBooks into the filing cabinet as well as the ledger.

2. What to attach

TransactionAttach
ExpenseReceipt or till slip
BillSupplier invoice
InvoiceDelivery note, signed contract
Journal entryThe calculation supporting it
Bank depositDeposit slip
PayrollApproved timesheet

3. How

  1. Open the transaction and use the Attachments box, or drag a file onto it.
  2. Or use the mobile app to photograph a receipt at the moment of purchase.
  3. Or email receipts to the QuickBooks receipts address and match them later.
  4. Files stay with the transaction permanently.

4. Why it matters

Example: Two years later a tax inspector questions a $900 expense. With the supplier invoice attached, the query takes thirty seconds. Without it, someone searches a box of fading paper, and if it is not found the deduction may be disallowed and penalties added.

5. Practical limits

Note: Attachments have per-file and total storage limits depending on your plan. Photograph receipts at reasonable rather than maximum resolution, and attach the document that evidences the transaction rather than every related email.

Summary

  • Attachments convert an assertion into evidence tied to the transaction.
  • Capture receipts at the point of purchase using the mobile app or email-in.
  • Attach what evidences the transaction, mindful of storage limits.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
AttachmentA file stored against a transaction.
Supporting documentEvidence that a transaction occurred as recorded.
PaperlessKeeping records digitally rather than on paper.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Why is an attached receipt described as evidence?

  1. It proves the transaction occurred as recorded, years later
  2. It looks professional
  3. It reduces tax
  4. It speeds up entry
Show answer

Answer: A. Evidence is what survives a query long after memory fades.

What is the best moment to capture a receipt?

  1. At the point of purchase, using the mobile app
  2. At year end
  3. When the auditor asks
  4. Never
Show answer

Answer: A. Immediate capture prevents loss and fading.

What should you attach to a journal entry?

  1. The calculation supporting it
  2. A photo of the office
  3. Nothing
  4. A customer invoice
Show answer

Answer: A. Journals need their workings to be defensible.

What is a practical limit on attachments?

  1. Per-file and total storage limits depending on the plan
  2. They cannot be deleted
  3. Only one per transaction
  4. Only PDFs are allowed
Show answer

Answer: A. Storage is finite, so capture sensibly rather than at maximum resolution.

Short answer

Name four transactions and the document you would attach to each.

Model answer

Expense — receipt; bill — supplier invoice; journal — the calculation; payroll — the approved timesheet.

Explain the audit value of attachments in one sentence.

Model answer

They let any query about a transaction be answered immediately from the record itself, rather than depending on paper that may be lost or illegible.

Class Activity

  1. Attach documents to five transactions in a sample file.
  2. Design a document capture routine for a team of three who all spend money.

Assignment

Create a document management policy for an organisation: what is attached to each transaction type, who captures it and when, and how the policy would be evidenced to an auditor.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 12.5 Apps and Integrations
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 12: Advanced Features and Closing the Books

LESSON NOTE: APPS AND INTEGRATIONS

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingApps and IntegrationsBeginner to Advanced30 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Explain what integrations add
  • Evaluate an app before installing it
  • Manage connected apps safely

1. Introduction

QuickBooks connects to hundreds of other applications. Used well, integrations remove double entry; used carelessly, they create duplicate transactions faster than any human could.

2. Common categories

  • Payment processing — customers pay invoices online
  • Point of sale — shop sales flow into QuickBooks
  • Payroll — where the built-in payroll is unavailable
  • Expense capture — receipt scanning
  • E-commerce — online store orders
  • Time tracking — hours flow into invoices and payroll

3. Evaluating before installing

QuestionWhy it matters
What data does it read and write?An app that writes transactions can create duplicates
Is the sync one-way or two-way?Two-way sync is powerful and riskier
Can it be undone?Some integrations post transactions that are tedious to reverse
What is the ongoing cost?App subscriptions accumulate quietly
Who supports it if it breaks?The app vendor, not Intuit, usually owns the problem
Note: Trial any transaction-writing app in a sample company first, never in the live file. An app that misposts a week of sales can take longer to unwind than it would have taken to enter them by hand.

4. Managing connections

Gear → Manage apps shows everything connected. Review it periodically and disconnect anything no longer used. Every live connection is both a running cost and a route into your financial data, so an unused connection is pure risk.

Summary

  • Integrations remove double entry but can create duplicates if misconfigured.
  • Evaluate what an app reads and writes, and trial it in a sample company first.
  • Review connected apps periodically and disconnect what is unused.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
IntegrationA connection between QuickBooks and another application.
Two-way syncData flowing in both directions between systems.
Connected appA third-party application with access to your file.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

Where should a transaction-writing app be trialled?

  1. In a sample company, never the live file
  2. In the live file
  3. At year end
  4. It needs no trial
Show answer

Answer: A. A misposting app can take longer to unwind than manual entry would have taken.

Why review connected apps periodically?

  1. Each live connection is a cost and a route into your financial data
  2. Apps expire
  3. It speeds up QuickBooks
  4. It reduces tax
Show answer

Answer: A. Unused connections are pure risk with no benefit.

What is the main risk of a badly configured integration?

  1. Duplicate transactions created automatically at speed
  2. Slower reports
  3. Higher tax
  4. Loss of customers
Show answer

Answer: A. Automation multiplies an error far faster than a person could.

Who usually supports an integration that breaks?

  1. The app vendor rather than Intuit
  2. Intuit only
  3. The bank
  4. Nobody
Show answer

Answer: A. Third-party apps are supported by their own vendors.

Short answer

List five questions to ask before installing an app.

Model answer

What data does it read and write; is the sync one- or two-way; can it be undone; what does it cost; who supports it?

Why is an unused connected app a risk?

Model answer

It still has access to financial data and may still be charged for, while delivering no benefit.

Class Activity

  1. Review the connected apps in a sample file and identify one you would remove.
  2. Evaluate one real integration against the five questions.

Assignment

Evaluate two integrations an organisation might use. Apply the five questions to each, recommend one, and set out how you would trial and monitor it.

lessons.title: 12.6 Year-End Closing Procedures
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 12: Advanced Features and Closing the Books

LESSON NOTE: YEAR-END CLOSING PROCEDURES

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingYear-End Closing ProceduresBeginner to Advanced45 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Complete a year-end closing checklist
  • Set a closing date
  • Explain what QuickBooks does automatically at year end

1. Introduction

Year end is not a button. It is a checklist that confirms the year's records are complete and correct, after which the period is locked and the accounts can be relied upon.

2. The checklist

#Task
1Reconcile every bank and credit card account to December
2Review the receivables ageing; write off genuinely bad debts
3Review the payables ageing; confirm all bills are entered
4Count inventory and post the adjustment
5Post depreciation for the year
6Post accruals and prepayments
7Confirm payroll liabilities agree to what was remitted
8Review the Profit and Loss for anything odd or miscoded
9Confirm Opening Balance Equity is zero
10Run and save the year's financial statements
11Set the closing date with a password
12Back up and store the year's reports

3. What QuickBooks does automatically

At the fiscal year end QuickBooks automatically rolls net income into Retained Earnings. There is no closing journal to post for this — it happens as part of how the reports are constructed.

Note: Because it is automatic, a transaction dated into a prior year will silently change that year's retained earnings. This is exactly why the closing date matters.

4. The closing date

Example: Set the closing date to 31 December with a password. QuickBooks then warns, and requires the password, before anyone can save a transaction dated on or before that date. Without it, a colleague entering a January invoice with a mistyped year silently changes accounts you have already reported to a bank.

Summary

  • Year end is a twelve-point checklist ending in a locked, backed-up period.
  • QuickBooks rolls net income into retained earnings automatically at year end.
  • A password-protected closing date is what stops prior-year figures changing afterwards.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Closing dateA date before which transactions cannot be saved without a password.
Retained earningsAccumulated profit carried forward into equity.
Year-end checklistThe sequence of tasks completing a financial year.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does QuickBooks do automatically at fiscal year end?

  1. Rolls net income into retained earnings
  2. Deletes old transactions
  3. Files the tax return
  4. Locks the file
Show answer

Answer: A. The roll-over is built into how the reports are constructed.

Why is a closing date essential?

  1. A mistyped date could silently change a year already reported
  2. It speeds up reports
  3. It reduces tax
  4. It backs up data
Show answer

Answer: A. Without a lock, prior-year figures can change after they were relied upon.

Which task confirms setup was completed correctly?

  1. Confirming Opening Balance Equity is zero
  2. Counting inventory
  3. Posting depreciation
  4. Reconciling the bank
Show answer

Answer: A. A remaining balance there means setup was never finished.

What should be done immediately after the checklist?

  1. Set the closing date and back up the year's reports
  2. Start the new year's invoices
  3. Delete the old year
  4. Change the fiscal year
Show answer

Answer: A. Locking and preserving the position completes the year end.

Short answer

List any six year-end checklist tasks.

Model answer

Reconcile all accounts; review receivables and payables; count inventory; post depreciation; post accruals; verify payroll liabilities; confirm Opening Balance Equity is zero; set the closing date.

Explain why the automatic retained earnings roll-over makes a closing date more important, not less.

Model answer

Because a transaction dated into a closed year silently changes that year's retained earnings without any visible journal, so only a lock prevents it.

Class Activity

  1. Work through the twelve-point checklist against a sample company and note what is incomplete.
  2. Set a closing date in a sample file and test that it warns you.

Assignment

Complete a full year-end close for a practice organisation. Evidence each checklist item, produce the year's financial statements, and confirm the closing date and backup are in place.

Printable: use your browser’s Print → Save as PDF to keep an offline copy.

lessons.title: 12.7 Backing Up and Protecting Your Data
lessons.html:
QuickBooks AccountingModule 12: Advanced Features and Closing the Books

LESSON NOTE: BACKING UP AND PROTECTING YOUR DATA

SubjectTopicLevelLesson duration
QuickBooks AccountingBacking Up and Protecting Your DataBeginner to Advanced35 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Explain how QuickBooks Online protects data
  • Create your own independent backup
  • Protect access to the file

1. Introduction

QuickBooks Online is backed up by Intuit, which protects against their servers failing. It does not protect against the far more common risks: someone deleting data, an integration corrupting it, or losing access to the account.

2. What Intuit does and does not cover

RiskCovered by Intuit?
Their server failsYes
A user deletes a year of transactionsNo
An app posts corrupt dataNo
You lose access to the loginNo
The subscription lapsesNo — access is lost while data is retained for a limited period
Note: This is the crucial point: automatic backup protects the provider's infrastructure, not you from yourself.

3. Your own backup routine

  1. Export the key reports monthly: Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, trial balance, and the general ledger detail.
  2. Export the master lists yearly: chart of accounts, customers, vendors, products.
  3. On QuickBooks Advanced, use the built-in backup and restore feature.
  4. Store exports in two places, at least one off the office premises or in separate cloud storage.
  5. Test once a year that you could actually rebuild from what you hold.

4. Protecting access

  • Use a strong, unique password on the Intuit account.
  • Turn on two-step verification.
  • Ensure at least two trusted people can reach the account, so a single person leaving cannot lock the organisation out.
  • Remove users the day they leave.
  • Keep the billing card current — a lapsed subscription eventually costs access.
Example: A church treasurer resigned holding the only login and could not be reached. The congregation lost access to three years of records until Intuit's recovery process completed. Two administrators would have prevented it entirely.

Summary

  • Intuit's backup protects their infrastructure, not you from deletion, corruption or lost access.
  • Export key reports monthly and master lists yearly, stored in two places.
  • Ensure at least two trusted people can access the account and remove leavers promptly.

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Two-step verificationA second check, usually a phone code, required at login.
ExportA copy of data saved outside QuickBooks.
Access continuityEnsuring more than one person can reach the account.

Review Questions

Multiple choice

What does Intuit's automatic backup NOT protect against?

  1. A user deleting a year of transactions
  2. Their server failing
  3. A data-centre fire
  4. Hardware failure
Show answer

Answer: A. Provider backup covers their infrastructure, not your own actions.

Why should at least two people have access?

  1. A single person leaving could lock the organisation out of its records
  2. It is legally required
  3. It reduces the subscription cost
  4. It speeds up reports
Show answer

Answer: A. Sole access is a single point of failure for the whole organisation.

How often should you test that you could rebuild from your backups?

  1. At least once a year
  2. Never
  3. Every ten years
  4. Only after a loss
Show answer

Answer: A. An untested backup is only an assumption.

What happens if the subscription lapses?

  1. Access is lost while data is retained only for a limited period
  2. Nothing
  3. Data is deleted instantly
  4. The file becomes free
Show answer

Answer: A. Losing access can be as damaging as losing the data itself.

Short answer

List four items you would export as part of a backup routine.

Model answer

Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, trial balance, general ledger detail, and the chart of accounts, customer, vendor and product lists.

Explain why automatic backup is not enough on its own.

Model answer

It protects against the provider's systems failing, but not against deletion, corrupt data from an app, or the organisation losing access to the login.

Class Activity

  1. Export a full backup set from a sample company and store it in two places.
  2. Review the access arrangements of an organisation you know and identify the single points of failure.

Assignment

Write a data protection plan for an organisation covering the backup routine, storage locations, access continuity, the leaver process, and how the plan will be tested each year.
